articles.title: Ukraine invests in firepower as it inflicts a new Russian casualty record
articles.body:
Ukraine invests in firepower as it inflicts a new Russian casualty record
Recent Starlink suspension did not much affect Ukrainian lethality, but Kyiv shows it is losing trust in the US.
Ukraine’s military says Russian casualties reached 49,040 in October – a new monthly record.
The General Staff’s estimate of dead and incapacitated Russian troops, as of October 28, comes close to fulfilling Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s goal set in January of at least 50,000 enemy casualties a month by the end of 2026.
Zelenskyy had said that was “a level of destruction of the occupier at which Russian losses exceed the number of reinforcements they can send.”
The previous monthly high of 46,230 was set in September, with both records marking a sharp increase in reported Russian dead and wounded since the summer.
Ukrainian Unmanned Systems Forces commander Robert Brovdi called it a “massive industrial slaughter”.
Al Jazeera cannot independently verify casualty estimates by either side. Ukraine’s military says it has video documentation of each strike.
Aerial drones are responsible for most of the casualties Ukraine inflicts, and Ukrainian Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara this week asked his European allies for funding to double drone production next year to about 16 million units.
The goal, he said, was “to scale up joint production of Ukrainian drones in other countries”.
Zelenskyy has said Ukraine could even triple drone production given enough money. Ukraine has decided that mass is the key to winning the war against Russia in terms of firepower.
“We see signs that mass production is preferred over technological sophistication,” said Ukrainian Defence Ministry adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov. “Mass production and simplicity will overcome technology.”
On October 28, the Netherlands and UK took steps to help Ukraine achieve its goal.
The Netherlands said it would provide 500 million euros ($560m) in immediate additional military aid and 1.2 billion euros ($1.34bn) in additional financing.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham upped Britain’s commitments by 10 billion pounds ($13.4bn) over three years, of which 3 billion pounds ($4bn) will be for weapons.
Ukraine announced its Starlink satellite navigation services were back to normal on October 24. “Communication remains stable at speeds exceeding 400km/h,” said the Defence Ministry.
On October 14, Ukraine had reported it was losing control of its drones above about 150km/h (100mph), making it difficult to mount defence against Russian jet-powered drones travelling above 500km/h.
After initially denying involvement, Starlink owner Elon Musk said on October 24 that he had “closed a loophole” that had allowed Ukraine to use Starlink offensively.
But Ukraine appeared to be thinking beyond Starlink and its Pentagon-owned military-grade service, Starshield.
On October 22, Ukraine and Finland announced they were jointly developing an independent sovereign military satellite system. Poland-based ICEYE and Finnish Nokia said they were partnering to realise the system, which would begin to launch satellites in 2028.
Other Europeans may be interested. On October 28, Zelenskyy also discussed satellite technology collaboration with Dutch premier Rob Jetten.
Ukraine said while they lasted, Starlink’s speed restrictions damaged its interception of Russian jet-powered Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones.
The Institute for the Study of War, a Washington-based think tank, said the 10-day outage caused Ukraine’s interception rate to fall from 77 percent to 74 percent.
Yet the rate seemed to be improving regardless.
According to Ukrainian Air Force data, Ukraine managed to shoot down at least 75 percent of jet-powered drones during the week ending October 29.
That was far above the three-month average shoot-down rate of 60 percent for jet-powered drones, suggesting that Ukraine is adapting fast.
Still, many Russian drones are getting through. One struck a train platform in the central city of Dnipro on October 29, killing at least 14 people.
Ukraine is also concerned that the US administration is hesitating about sending ballistic missile interceptors European allies have paid for.
“The artificial and prolonged delays in the delivery of interceptor missiles for Patriot and NASAMS systems, which unfortunately have been occurring recently, are directly helping Russia achieve the goals of its terrorist campaign,” Zelenskyy said, after Russian ballistics hit a university campus in downtown Kyiv on October 27.
The previous day, Khmara had asked European allies to transfer 10 percent of their existing stocks of interceptors as an advance on future orders.
Ukraine struck Russia during the past week, too.
On October 23, Ukrainian missiles destroyed the main microchip production building of Proton-Electrotex in the city of Orel, which makes missile components.
During the week, Ukraine damaged five chemical plants, NAK Azot, Toliattykauchuk, Omskiy Kauchuk, Energiya and Voronezhsintezkauchuk, which make solid rocket propellants used in missiles.
It also damaged the Voronezh Aircraft Company and VSMPO-AVISMA, two factories building airframes or the metals for them.
Notes from underground
Ukraine has also been developing underground warfare, far from the battlefields monitored by drones, planes and satellites.
On October 22, its Khartiia Corps, originally a volunteer unit but now part of the National Guard, announced it had successfully completed an operation to flush Russian infiltrators out of a disused gas pipeline.
The Russians were using the pipeline to move troops from occupied parts of Kharkiv to the front line city of Kupiansk.
“The Russians tried to use underground gas pipelines to move past our positions. Our warriors turned this tactic against the Russians and used this system of underground pipelines against the occupiers with extraordinary success,” said Zelenskyy.
Ukraine’s Operation Veles advanced 15km (10 miles) underground through the pipeline and tunnels to emerge behind Russian positions, said Brigadier General Ihor Oboloenskyi.
Khartiia Corps said it coordinated underground attacks from pipes and tunnels with overland attacks and drones to surprise the enemy from several different directions at once, killing or wounding 100 Russian soldiers and capturing 30.
Russian forces had used the pipelines to evacuate their wounded, too, and were filmed marching Ukrainian civilians among them as human shields, said Viktor Tregubov, United Forces Group spokesman.
Ukraine’s forces besieged the Russians inside the pipeline, said Vladimir Dektyarev, an officer of Khartiia Corps. “Even after they were surrounded, they sat for over a month, until their food ran out, waiting for a command from their command for permission to surrender.”
Veles marked the third operation this year where Ukrainian forces have pushed Russian forces back and reclaimed land.
In the south of the country, too, Ukrainian forces were reported to have liberated three settlements – Peredubova, Komar and Fedorivka – on the Donetsk-Zaporizhia border, expanding an area of reclaimed territory there.
Although the US is still on track to bring Ukrainian and Russian technical teams to the negotiating table on November 10, and Zelenskyy supported a ceasefire on energy infrastructure and grain exports, Russia downplayed expectations.
Russian President Vladimir Putin spoke of Ukraine as “the territory of historical Russia” on October 22, denying the existence of a Ukrainian people and refusing a ceasefire on energy infrastructure.
His foreign policy adviser, Valery Ushakov, said the talks “will not resolve much”.
When Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store and Finnish President Alexander Stubb held a call with Putin on October 27 – their first contact with him since assuming office – Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov dismissed the conversation as “Europeans’ desire to squeeze into the negotiation process.”

articles.title: Seoul fears being left out as US reaches out to North Korea
articles.body:
Seoul fears being slighted as US reaches out to North Korea
October 30, 2026
South Korea's relationship with the North, always strained, seems to be going through a particularly hostile patch in recent weeks.
Last month, Seoul accused North Korea of planting a mine on the southern side of the heavily fortified border. The device exploded, injuring three South Korean soldiers. Pyongyang refused to apologize and insisted this was a false-flag incident designed to tarnish the isolated nation. The North Korean regime has since conducted multiple weapons tests, held its first-ever exhibition of military drones attended by Kim Jong Un, brought up self-propelled artillery units to the border and started preparing loudspeaker systems that will blast propaganda into the South.
On Thursday, North Korea also fired around 10 short-range ballistic missiles towards the Sea of Japan just before a scheduled visit to South Korea by German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
On top of South Korea's issues with its archrival, however, many in Seoul are growing increasingly wary of their most important ally, the United States. South Korean politicians are worried that the US could push for a diplomatic breakthrough with North Korea to the point of ignoring South Korea's security, or even leave it exposed to Pyongyang's nuclear arsenal.
Who gets a voice on South Korea's future?
US President Donald Trump famously claimed he and Kim Jong Un "fell in love" during Trump's first term. More recently, Trump has indicated he would like to resume talks and there have been suggestions that a meeting could take place on November 18 in the Chinese city of Shenzhen, where Trump is expected to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.
The North Korean side has made no official response to Washington's hints, although South Korea's National Intelligence Service informed a closed-door meeting of Seoul's intelligence committee on Thursday that Kim Jong Un discussed the possibility of meeting Trump when he met with senior members of China's politburo in Dandong on Saturday.
Seoul's fears were also fueled by the US proposing three-way talks with Russia and China on the fate of Ukraine, without inviting a representative of Kyiv to attend. The worry in Seoul is that President Donald Trump may similarly bypass Seoul to discuss the future of the Korean Peninsula with China and North Korea.
Washington-Seoul relationship shaken by tariffs, funding disputes
"Right now, there is a problem of trust between the two governments," said Kim Sang-woo, a former politician with the left-leaning South Korean Congress for New Politics and now a member of the board of the Kim Dae-jung Peace Foundation.
A security and trade relationship that was previously considered secure has been rocked by tariffs, trade restrictions and demands from Washington that the South pay more for the US troops stationed in the country, Kim told DW.
President Lee's diplomats have lost access to key decision-making personnel in this White House, he added.
"I do not think this US administration is thinking long-term in the relationship with South Korea," Kim said. "They do not see South Korea as a part of their wider national security network and I do not think they are listening to experts on the importance of allies in the region."
"I also think that Trump is eager to meet with Kim because of his personal quest to obtain a Nobel Peace Prize," he added.
Trump's widely publicized efforts to secure a Nobel have been thwarted so far. However, this might change if Trump somehow manages to formally end the Korean War that was put on hold by the 1953 armistice.
The fear in Seoul is that Trump would trade South's security to achieve this goal.
South Korea eyeing its own nuclear deterrent
"The most serious concern is that the US recognizes Pyongyang as a nuclear power, which would legitimize the North's program and undermine efforts to convince it to abolish its nuclear weapons as well as the broader non-proliferation system," said Lim Eun-jung, a professor of international studies at Kongju National University.
In parallel, she said, there are fears that Trump could reach an agreement with North Korea that requires it to scrap its long-range nuclear missiles — those that are capable of hitting targets in the United States — but permits it to retain short-range weapons that can still easily reach South Korea and Japan.
That would raise questions about the US commitment to defend South Korea in case of a nuclear attack. That uncertainty, in turn, is likely to give credence to voices arguing that South Korea needs to develop its own nuclear deterrent.
"For years, we have depended on US extended deterrence guarantees under the nuclear umbrella, but this US administration is unpredictable and there are more and more people asking why we don't just go it alone," Lim told DW.
"Virtually, all our neighbors have nuclear weapons, and while no-one wants the dominoes to start falling, it could happen," she added.
Merz says Korean security affects Europe
The latest escalation between Seoul and Pyongyang comes amid repeated attempts by South Korean President Lee to improve communication with Pyongyang. The perceived outreach has irritated South Korea's European allies, who are angry over North Korea deploying soldiers and supplying munition and missiles to help Russia in the Ukraine war.
Moscow is believed to be repaying for Pyongyang's support with money, military technology and security guarantees.
During his visit to South Korea, Germany's Merz pointed out that "Korea's security affects Europe's security. And Europe's security also affects the security of Korea."
"The world is small — even in war," Merz added.
South Korea needs allies
Berlin, just like Seoul, has been disoriented by the Trump administration turning hostile on many of its allies while seeking reproachment with geopolitical rivals such as Russia and China. During his Asia tour, Merz pushed for an alliance of middle powers to protect free trade and oppose "unilateralism, autocratic power politics and violations of international law."
"The fact remains that the United States is shifting its foreign policy, its foreign economic policy, and redefining its interests. As they do so, we must do the same," Merz said in South Korea.
It was not clear if Seoul will respond to Merz's appeal by moving closer to the European Union. At the moment, however, it seems apparent that the South Korean government is struggling to communicate with either North Korea or the US.
"It is a very difficult situation," said Kim Sang-woo. "There is no trust and no connections and that, to me, is very worrisome."

articles.title: Tanker hit by explosives in Strait of Hormuz as Iran claims two vessels disabled
articles.body:
An oil tanker was struck by explosives attached to its hull in the Strait of Hormuz, setting its engine room ablaze and temporarily disabling the vessel, Reuters reported, as Iran's Revolutionary Guard claimed Friday that two tankers attempting to cross the strategic waterway without Tehran's authorization had been forced to stop.
The latest incidents underscore the growing threat to commercial shipping in one of the world's most important oil transit routes, where Iran has intensified attacks on vessels in an apparent effort to frustrate a U.S.-led operation to reopen the strait without a negotiated agreement.
According to Reuters, citing shipping industry sources, a small boat approached the Panama-flagged tanker Louise 1 on Thursday and attached two limpet mines, explosive devices designed to adhere to the hull of a vessel. The mines detonated, igniting a fire in the ship's engine room and temporarily putting it out of operation.
No crew members were injured, the fire was extinguished and no environmental damage was reported. The tanker has since resumed its voyage.
The attack occurred approximately 46 kilometers (29 miles) northeast of Khasab, Oman, on the southern side of the Strait of Hormuz.
Reuters said it was not immediately clear who was responsible for the attack.
The incident marks the first reported successful use of such explosives in the strait since the outbreak of the war with Iran in late February, according to Reuters. A similar attempt to disable a vessel last month failed when the explosives did not detonate, two sources told the news agency.
The apparent ability of attackers aboard a small vessel to approach a moving tanker, attach explosives and escape has raised serious concerns about the vulnerability of commercial shipping in the narrow and heavily trafficked waterway.
Marisks, a Greece-based maritime risk management company, warned that the method could pose a particularly difficult challenge for shipping operators because of its simplicity and low cost.
"The apparent ability of a small craft to approach a transiting tanker, deploy explosive devices and withdraw presents a significant security concern, particularly in the Strait's congested shipping lanes," the company said.
Marisks noted that limpet mines are relatively inexpensive and readily available, describing their deployment against moving ships from small boats as a technologically simple but highly effective method of attack.
Iran claims two tankers stopped in Hormuz
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps' navy said Friday that two oil tankers had been stopped off the strait's southern coast after attempting to cross without coordinating their movements with Iranian authorities.
In a statement, the Guard claimed the vessels had disabled their navigation and positioning systems and attempted to leave the strait through an unauthorized route with assistance from the U.S. military.
"After several unanswered radio warnings, the two tankers entered an unsafe area, became involved in incidents and were stopped off the southern coast of the Strait of Hormuz," the statement said.
The Guard did not identify the vessels or explain what it meant by the incidents that caused them to stop.
It was not immediately clear whether the Louise 1 was one of the two tankers mentioned in the Iranian statement. The Guard's account could not be independently verified.
The reported location of the vessels, near the southern shore of the strait, is notable because Iran's coastline lies along the northern side of the waterway, while Oman occupies much of its southern shore.
In recent weeks, Iranian authorities have repeatedly claimed that tankers crossing the strait were damaged after striking mines.
The incidents come amid reports that Tehran has stepped up deliberate attacks on commercial vessels in an effort to disrupt Washington's campaign to restore maritime traffic and the flow of oil to international markets.
The United States has sought to reopen the waterway without reaching an agreement with Iran while maintaining a naval blockade of Iranian ports.
Washington has so far refrained from directly responding to the latest reported Iranian attacks, potentially to avoid an escalation that could drive fuel prices higher just days before Tuesday's U.S. midterm elections.
President Donald Trump has recently dismissed some Iranian claims of damage to vessels as "fake hits."
The continued disruption of shipping through the strait has become a central point of contention between Washington and Tehran, with both sides seeking to use maritime access as leverage in negotiations over ending the conflict.
Trump says Iran deal possible as Qatari mediators arrive
Despite the continued attacks, diplomatic efforts to prevent a renewed American military offensive against Iran appeared to be gaining momentum Friday.
Speaking to a local radio station in Kansas, Trump was asked about his ultimate objective in Iran and whether military action could resume after Tuesday's midterm elections.
"It will be over soon," Trump said, while suggesting that a negotiated settlement remained possible.
"They want to make a deal, they have to make a deal with a guarantee. We have to have a guarantee that they will never have a nuclear weapon," he said.
Earlier Friday, Reuters reported, citing a source familiar with the discussions, that Qatari mediators had arrived in Tehran in an effort to advance negotiations and prevent further escalation.
Qatar presented Iran with a draft agreement Sunday, according to an earlier Reuters report, but a senior Iranian official rejected the proposals Wednesday as "unacceptable" and said Tehran would maintain its position on the nuclear issue.
The central dispute concerns the sequence of concessions each side is prepared to make.
Washington wants Iran's nuclear program included in negotiations from the outset, while Tehran insists that the United States must first lift its naval blockade of Iranian ports, remove sanctions on Iranian oil exports and meet additional conditions included in an Iranian proposal Trump rejected last month.
CBS News also reported Friday that a Qatari delegation had arrived in Tehran, citing a source familiar with the negotiations who said the mediators were carrying revisions to the proposed agreement to end the war.
The source said there were signs of progress and that an Iranian response was expected by the end of the week.
"The goal of the proposal is to prevent a return to U.S. military action against Iran, which Trump has repeatedly threatened to resume in recent weeks," CBS reported.
Meanwhile, The Washington Post reported that Vice President JD Vance recently sent a letter to senior Iranian official Mohsen Rezaei offering to meet him personally to advance the negotiations.
Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, is a close associate of Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei and is widely regarded as a hard-liner.
Despite his hawkish positions, the Trump administration reportedly views Rezaei as its "best hope for peace."
The diplomatic contacts come as Washington weighs whether to resume military operations against Iran, with a decision widely expected to come only after the U.S. midterm elections.
Air defenses deployed around Trump's Florida estate
Amid the heightened tensions with Iran, U.S. media reported that security around Trump's private Mar-a-Lago estate in Palm Beach, Florida, has been significantly reinforced at the direction of the Secret Service.
Photographs circulated in American media show two Avenger air defense systems equipped with Stinger missiles positioned on a floating platform in a lake adjoining the presidential estate.
The systems were first spotted near Mar-a-Lago on Oct. 23, shortly before Trump arrived at the property that day, according to the reports.
The Palm Beach Daily News reported that an additional Avenger system had been deployed in the southern section of Palm Beach's international airport, which was renamed after Trump earlier this year.
That system was reportedly positioned near the area where Air Force One typically parks during presidential visits.
In a statement to the local newspaper, the Secret Service said it continued to operate in an elevated threat environment.
"The U.S. Secret Service continues to operate in a heightened threat environment, and the agency continually adapts its protective operations to incorporate the most advanced tools, technologies and methods to protect those in its care," the agency said.
The Avenger system, manufactured by Boeing, consists of a modified Humvee equipped with a rotating turret carrying two missile launchers, each holding four Stinger missiles.
The short-range surface-to-air missiles use infrared guidance to track the heat signatures of their targets. The system also carries a heavy machine gun.
According to the U.S. military, the Avenger is designed to counter aerial threats including cruise missiles, drones, helicopters and low-flying aircraft.
Neither the Secret Service nor the U.S. military has publicly explained why the additional defenses were deployed.
Local media noted that placing such conspicuous air defense systems in a civilian area, where they are clearly visible to people passing the estate, is highly unusual.
Retired Lt. Col. Octavio Perez, a security intelligence expert, told NBC's Miami affiliate that the deployment could reflect concerns about a drone attack on the property or even an attempt to strike it using a larger aircraft, such as a helicopter or small plane.
Perez also pointed to the upcoming Group of 20 summit, scheduled to take place at Trump's golf resort in Miami in December, as a possible factor behind the heightened security.
He suggested that the deployment could also be connected to threats from Iran, whose leadership has previously threatened to assassinate Trump or members of his family.
With Washington considering renewed military operations against Tehran, Perez warned that an escalation could create incentives for an attack on the president's Florida residence.
If the war resumes, "a sleeper cell or a lone actor in the United States could try to do something at Mar-a-Lago," Perez said. "That's essentially what's behind this preparation."
The deployment highlights the broader security concerns accompanying the standoff with Iran, even as negotiators attempt to reach an agreement that would end the war, reopen the Strait of Hormuz and avert another round of military confrontation.

articles.title: Ukraine Destroys Russian Iskander-M Launcher Near Key Transit Point
articles.body:
Ukraine’s Defense Forces struck a Russian Iskander-M ballistic missile launcher near a missile transshipment point in Russia’s Kursk region early on Friday, Oct. 30, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported.
“An Iskander-M tactical missile system launcher was struck in the vicinity of a ballistic missile transshipment point, near Fatezh in the Kursk region of the Russian Federation,” the General Staff said on Telegram.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The military said the strike would reduce Russia’s capacity to launch ballistic missile attacks on Ukrainian cities.
Ukraine’s Defense Forces also struck several other Russian military targets, including ammunition depots near Maloyanysol in the Donetsk region, Novoiehorivka in the Kharkiv region, and Hanusivka in the Luhansk region.
Other targets included a logistics and supply depot near Bilovodsk, an enemy repair unit near Rubizhne, and a repair and restoration base near Pysarivka – all in the Luhansk region.
The General Staff said destroying ammunition depots reduces Russian forces’ firepower, while strikes on repair facilities make it harder for them to restore damaged equipment and return it to the battlefield.
In a separate attack, Ukraine struck a Russian Iskander ballistic missile launcher and destroyed two Su-34 fighter-bombers on Thursday, Oct. 29, according to President Volodymyr Zelensky.
The Ukrainian Navy’s Neptune coastal missile system hit the aircraft at the Marinovka airfield in Russia’s Volgograd region, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) reported. The Su-34s are used by Russian forces to launch guided and unguided aerial bombs, including KABs.
Russian Ballistic Missile Strike on Kyiv Kills One, Sparks Fires
Zelensky added that Ukrainian intelligence had information indicating Russia was preparing to launch another wave of ballistic missile attacks.
He urged international partners to provide additional interceptor packages for Patriot air defense systems, warning that Ukraine faced a critical shortage.
“We are waiting for the relevant decisions,” Zelensky said.
He made a similar appeal during his visit to the Netherlands on Wednesday, Oct. 28, describing Patriot interceptors as Ukraine’s most pressing weapons shortage.
He urged Washington not to delay deliveries under the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL), a mechanism through which allies fund purchases of US-made weapons for Ukraine.
As winter approaches, Russia is increasingly using ballistic missiles to target Ukraine’s critical infrastructure, including electricity and water supply facilities. Kyiv had reportedly depleted its stocks of Patriot interceptors as of Oct. 15, amid limited deliveries from allies.
PAC-3 interceptors are among the few weapons capable of destroying Russian ballistic missiles, including the Iskander-M, which carries a warhead weighing around half a ton and can cause extensive damage to residential buildings.
“Another aspect of our anti-ballistic work is the interceptor packages, primarily for Patriots, that partners can provide to us,” Zelensky said on Wednesday.

articles.title: Russian troops liberate three communities in Ukraine operation over week — top brass
articles.body:
MOSCOW, October 30. /TASS/. Russian troops liberated three communities in the Kharkov, Sumy and Zaporozhye Regions over the week of October 24-30 in the special military operation in Ukraine, Russia’s Defense Ministry reported.
"During the week, Battlegroup North units liberated the settlements of Alisovka in the Kharkov Region and Barilovka in the Sumy Region through active offensive operations. <…> During the past week, Battlegroup East units continued advancing deep into the enemy’s defenses and liberated the settlement of Obshcheye in the Zaporozhye Region through decisive operations," the ministry said in a statement.
Russian troops deliver 11 precision strikes on Ukrainian military sites over week
Russian troops delivered two massive and nine combined strikes by precision-guided weapons and unmanned aerial vehicles on Ukrainian military-industrial enterprises, energy and transport sites over the week, the ministry reported.
"On October 24-30, the Russian Armed Forces delivered two massive and nine combined strikes, hitting Ukraine’s military-industrial enterprises, logistics centers, energy and transport infrastructure facilities used to support the Ukrainian army’s operations, workshops producing and sites storing ground robotic platforms, unmanned aerial vehicles and uncrewed boats, and also temporary deployment areas of Ukrainian armed formations and foreign mercenaries," the ministry said.
In addition, the strikes degraded Ukraine’s port infrastructure facilities used to receive, store and distribute military cargo, it said.
"During the week, 11 dry cargo ships involved in the delivery of armament, military hardware and dual-use products for the needs of the Ukrainian army were hit," the ministry said.
Russia’s Battlegroup North inflicts over 1,575 casualties on Ukrainian army in week
Russia’s Battlegroup North inflicted more than 1,575 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed eight enemy armored combat vehicles in its areas of responsibility over the week, the ministry reported.
Over the week, Battlegroup North units "inflicted losses on formations of eight mechanized brigades, three motorized infantry brigades, two airmobile brigades, two assault regiments of the Ukrainian army and four territorial defense brigades," the ministry said.
The Ukrainian army lost more than 1,575 personnel, eight armored combat vehicles, 68 motor vehicles, three field artillery guns and six electronic warfare stations in the areas of responsibility of Russia’s Battlegroup North over the week, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup West inflicts over 1,585 casualties on Ukrainian army in week
Russia’s Battlegroup West inflicted more than 1,585 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed eight enemy armored combat vehicles in its area of responsibility over the week, the ministry reported.
"During the past week, Battlegroup West units gained better lines and positions and inflicted losses on manpower and equipment of four mechanized brigades, an airmobile brigade, an assault brigade of the Ukrainian army and two territorial defense brigades," the ministry said.
The Ukrainian army lost more than 1,585 personnel, eight armored combat vehicles, 108 motor vehicles, six field artillery guns and 12 electronic warfare stations in that frontline area over the week, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup South inflicts over 1,155 casualties on Ukrainian army in week
Russia’s Battlegroup South inflicted more than 1,155 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed 24 enemy armored combat vehicles in its area of responsibility over the week, the ministry reported.
"During the past week, Battlegroup South units improved their forward positions and inflicted losses on formations of five mechanized brigades, a motorized infantry brigade, an airmobile brigade, an air assault brigade, a mountain assault brigade, two assault regiments of the Ukrainian army, a marine infantry brigade and two territorial defense brigades," the ministry said.
The Ukrainian army lost more than 1,155 personnel, 24 armored combat vehicles, 217 motor vehicles, 12 field artillery guns and eight electronic warfare stations in that frontline area over the week, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup Center inflicts over 2,400 casualties on Ukrainian army in week
Russia’s Battlegroup Center inflicted more than 2,400 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed 38 enemy armored combat vehicles in its area of responsibility over the week, the ministry reported.
"During the week, Battlegroup Center units gained better lines and positions and inflicted losses on manpower and equipment of four mechanized brigades, a jaeger brigade, an assault brigade, an airborne brigade, two assault regiments of the Ukrainian army, three marine infantry brigades and five National Guard brigades," the ministry said.
Overall, the Ukrainian army lost more than 2,400 personnel, 38 armored combat vehicles, 67 motor vehicles, five field artillery guns and 13 electronic warfare stations in the responsibility area of Russia’s Battlegroup Center over the week, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup East inflicts over 1,390 casualties on Ukrainian army in week
Russia’s Battlegroup East inflicted more than 1,390 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed 12 enemy armored combat vehicles in its area of responsibility over the week, the ministry reported.
During the past week, Battlegroup East units "inflicted losses on manpower and equipment of two assault brigades, three air assault brigades, three assault regiments of the Ukrainian army and a marine infantry brigade," the ministry said.
The Ukrainian army lost more than 1,390 personnel, 12 armored combat vehicles, 42 motor vehicles, three field artillery guns and three electronic warfare and counterbattery radar stations in that frontline area over the week, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup Dnepr eliminates 205 Ukrainian troops in week
Russia’s Battlegroup Dnepr eliminated roughly 205 Ukrainian troops and destroyed two enemy armored combat vehicles in its area of responsibility over the week, the ministry reported.
"During the week, Battlegroup Dnepr units improved their tactical position and inflicted losses on formations of two mechanized brigades, a mountain assault brigade, an assault regiment of the Ukrainian army and a territorial defense brigade," the ministry said.
"As many as 205 Ukrainian military personnel, two armored combat vehicles, 65 motor vehicles and 10 electronic warfare and counterbattery radar stations were destroyed," it said.
Russian air defenses intercept 6,900 Ukrainian UAVs, nine cruise missiles in week
Russian air defense forces intercepted and destroyed 6,900 Ukrainian unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and nine cruise missiles over the week, the ministry reported.
"Air defense capabilities shot down six guided aerial bombs, three air-launched cruise missiles, among them two UK-made Storm Shadow missiles and one French-made SCALP missile, six Neptune long-range cruise missiles and 6,900 fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles," the ministry said.
Russian forces destroy over 275,000 military drones in Ukraine operation
Russian forces have destroyed over 275,000 Ukrainian military drones since the beginning of the special military operation in Ukraine, according to the latest data released by Russia’s Defense Ministry.
"In all, the following targets have been destroyed since the start of the special military operation: 674 aircraft, 284 helicopters, 275,728 unmanned aerial vehicles, 672 surface-to-air missile systems, 31,455 tanks and other armored combat vehicles, 1,794 multiple rocket launchers, 36,839 field artillery guns and mortars and 75,947 special military motor vehicles," the ministry said.

articles.title: Report: US deploys 10 military cargo planes to Israel amid preparations for possible strike on Iran
articles.body:
The US has transferred 10 military cargo aircraft to Israeli air bases in the southern Negev region amid preparations for a possible military strike against Iran, the Israeli public broadcaster KAN reported Thursday, Anadolu Agency reported.
The broadcaster said the aircraft landed at Ovda and Nevatim air bases, while additional US military planes were reportedly dispatched to bases in Jordan, Saudi Arabia and Qatar.
According to KAN, the planes departed from Fort Bliss in the US state of Texas, which houses one of the US military’s largest air defense centers, including facilities associated with interceptor missiles and air defense batteries.
There was no immediate US confirmation of the reported deployments, and it remained unclear what cargo the aircraft were carrying or whether Washington had decided to launch an attack against Iran.
An Israeli official told the broadcaster that Israel and the US were closely coordinating their military preparations.
“Israel and the United States are coordinating closely, and although no decision has yet been made on the matter, the Americans and Israel are preparing for any decision President Donald Trump makes,” the official said.
The official did not specify the nature or timing of any potential decision.
Earlier this week, KAN reported that Washington had warned Gulf countries about the possibility of a short, limited military campaign against Iran.
According to the broadcaster, the US military has also transferred a Patriot missile defense system from Texas to reinforce its air defenses in the Gulf region.
The report said US troops stationed at bases across the region had been instructed to leave as a precaution against a possible military escalation.
It added that US forces were replenishing their weapons stockpiles, with an additional aircraft carrier and Marine Corps unit expected to arrive in November.
The reinforcements would reportedly join approximately 20 US warships already operating in the Middle East.
Separately, The Wall Street Journal reported earlier Thursday that US Central Command (CENTCOM) Commander Gen. Brad Cooper had briefed Trump on options for potential strikes against Iran.
The newspaper suggested that the briefing could indicate that Washington was moving closer to launching major military operations.
Democratic US Sen. Chris Murphy said he and several other senators had received a briefing on possible plans to attack Iran, describing them as “insane.”
Murphy warned that such an operation would lead to a devastating escalation and could undermine the US commitment to the rule of law.
The US and Israel launched attacks against Iran on Feb. 28, prompting Tehran to retaliate against Israel and US targets across the region before a ceasefire agreement was reached in April.
The US and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding in June concerning freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, but its implementation has stalled over disagreements related to the waterway’s security.
The latest reported military deployments come amid renewed concerns over a possible escalation between the US and Iran.

articles.title: Houthis continue to engage in ‘fierce battles’ in mountains near Aden, Taiz - report
articles.body:
The Houthis continue to attack Saudi Arabia and are also continuing to engage in “fierce battles” in Yemen. This is an important issue because any talks with Iran, which appear to be happening, will take the Houthis into account. Arab News in Saudi Arabia said on October 30 that the “Saudi-led coalition said on Friday it intercepted and destroyed in the Makkah region a drone fired by Yemen’s Houthis.”
According to the Saudis, “a drone launched by the terrorist Houthi militia has been intercepted and destroyed in the Makkah region.” The report noted that “the Iran-backed militia has for weeks targeted airports, energy infrastructure and cities across the Kingdom with drones and missiles.”
Now, Al-Ain media in the UAE also says that “dozens of government forces and Houthis were killed and wounded on Friday in fierce battles in Al-Maqatra district of Lahj, following a large-scale attack by the militias.”
Sources in Yemen told Al-Ain News that the Houthi militias launched a large-scale ground attack on government forces’ positions in Al-Maqatirah district, the northern gateway to Lahj, in an attempt to make progress on the ground and control key mountain ranges in the area.
This is an area in southern Yemen where the Houthis are fighting a tough and complex war against the Yemeni government and also other factions aligned with the government. Some of these factions were linked to the Southern Transitional Council, which had been backed by the UAE.
The UAE has excellent sources in this area.
“The sources confirmed that the Houthi militias aim, through the attack, to control the ‘Al-Muqatara Tunnel’ area and the strategically important Al-Muqatara mountain fortress, as well as to reach the Al-Rubu’ market located in the Heijah Al-Abd valley, where the main road linking Taiz and Aden is located.” The sources explained that the battles extended to the Haifan front, where the militias are trying to reach Mount An’an, which overlooks large areas between Haifan and Al-Maqatirah.
Events in Yemen could affect Iran, UAE, Qatar, US
This area appears to be only around 40 to 50 miles from Aden. This means the battles in these mountains, amid palm trees and scrub brush and steep terrain, could determine the next moves in Yemen. What happens here, could also matter in Tehran, Doha, Riyadh and Washington.
Let’s recall why the Houthis matters. The Iran-backed Houthis have emerged as one of the most important armed terrorist armies in the Middle East, using Yemen as a base to threaten Saudi Arabia, Israel and international shipping. The movement, also known as Ansar Allah, emerged from northern Yemen's Zaydi Shi'ite community and seized the capital, Sanaa, in 2014.
In early 2015, Houthi forces advanced south toward Aden, forcing Yemen's internationally recognized government to flee. Saudi Arabia intervened in March 2015 at the head of an Arab coalition seeking to restore the government and prevent the Houthis from consolidating control over Yemen.
The war devastated the country but failed to defeat the Houthis. Iran's support helped the movement develop an increasingly sophisticated arsenal of ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and drones. These weapons enabled the Houthis to strike Saudi Arabia and eventually target Israel.
Following the Hamas attack on Israel on October 7, 2023, the Houthis began launching missiles and drones toward Israel and attacking commercial shipping in the Red Sea. Israel, the United States and Britain subsequently carried out strikes against Houthi targets. The Houthis resumed attacks on Israel during the 2026 conflict involving Iran.
Yemen's war escalated again in July 2026, when the Houthis renewed attacks on Saudi targets and shipping. In September, Houthi forces advanced along the Red Sea coast, capturing Mocha and reaching the strategically important Bab al-Mandab Strait. The strait connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and is a vital route for international trade and energy shipments.
Fighting has also intensified around Taiz, where the Houthis have sought to threaten the road linking the city to Aden, the internationally recognized government's main base.
The renewed conflict illustrates how Yemen's civil war has become intertwined with the wider regional confrontation involving Iran, Saudi Arabia and Israel. Control of territory around Bab al-Mandab gives the Houthis additional leverage over regional security and international commerce.
Al-Ain says that as the battles in the mountains have continued, “warplanes launched a series of raids on Houthi positions and gatherings to repel the militia's attack on Al-Maqatirah district in Lahj governorate.” Al-Ain concludes that “by attacking Al-Maqatirah, the Houthi militias are trying to reach Tur Al-Bahah district in Lahj, a coastal province that is the main gateway to the capital, Aden.”
Yemen has been witnessing fierce battles since the beginning of last September, following a large-scale, multi-pronged attack launched by the Houthis on areas of the western coast, Bab al-Mandab and Taiz, which resulted in thousands of deaths and injuries.
Houthis lay seige to Taiz
The Houthis are also laying siege to the city of Taiz in the mountains. Arab News says that the Houthis are also facing growing international criticism over their detention of United Nations personnel and the worsening humanitarian crisis in Taiz, Yemen's third-largest city.
According to Arab News, the Houthis are holding 71 UN staff members, severely restricting the organization's ability to operate in areas under their control. “These actions render the delivery of humanitarian aid in areas under the control of the Houthis untenable at this time,” Shirin Yaseen, associate spokesperson for UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, told Arab News.
The reports indicate that the humanitarian situation has deteriorated further around Taiz, where more than 800,000 people have been cut off from essential supplies. The Houthis intensified their siege in early October after seizing the road connecting Taiz with Aden, the seat of Yemen's internationally recognized government. According to the World Food Programme, approximately three-quarters of the affected population depend on humanitarian assistance. Taiz has faced varying degrees of Houthi siege since 2015.

articles.title: Explosion at Spanish ammunitions factory supplying Ukraine injures 3
articles.body:
National Police officers are securing the area around the munitions factory where a powerful explosion has taken place in Granada, Andalusia, Spain, on Oct. 30 2026. (Alex Camara/Europa Press/Getty Images)
An explosion at the Fabrica de Municiones de Granada (FMG), an ammunition factory on the outskirts of Granada, Spain, injured three people on the morning of Oct. 30, Spanish newspaper ABC reported.
The explosion occurred shortly before 9 a.m. in the plant's gunpowder-burning area, a restricted site where no one is normally supposed to be present, Granada's local police said, according to ABC.
Emergency services received multiple calls reporting the blast, which was felt in nearby towns, including Fuente Vaqueros and La Zubia, Spanish outlet El Espanol reported.
All three people sustained minor injuries, including hearing damage, ABC reported.
Sources from UGT, one of Spain's two major trade unions, said the explosion occurred during a routine test in a fenced-off area of the factory.
The incident was the second at the facility in two weeks. On Oct. 13, a company truck carrying mortar rounds overturned on the road to El Fargue, ABC reported.
Since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion, the Spanish factory has produced ammunition of various calibers and missile components for Ukraine.
The factory is owned by Slovakia's MSM Group, which is part of the defense division of Czechoslovak Group (CSG), one of Central Europe's largest defense holdings. The Czech holding is a key supplier of ammunition to Ukraine under the Czech ammunition initiative, according to CSG Executive Director Michal Strnad.
Launched in early 2024 amid severe ammunition shortages in Ukraine, the Czech-led program has been hailed by its proponents as one of Prague's most significant international efforts and has since delivered millions of shells to Ukrainian forces.

The sports court's ruling means that Russia will be able to participate in a sweep of forthcoming ice hockey tournaments in Canada, Czechia, the U.S., and Germany.

President Volodymyr Zelensky signed decrees on Oct. 30 imposing sanctions on 10 companies and 19 Russian citizens involved in developing the Rassvet satellite system, as well as 39 vessels in Russia's shadow fleet, according to a statement on the Presidential Office's website.
"This is not just our personal story. This is the story of a country and a society that are being crushed in exactly the same way," the Novaya Gazeta staff wrote.
Russia deliberately targeted a "civilian enterprise" where people were working at the time of the strike, Hryhorov said, without specifying the facility's location or the business it housed.
Euroclear is facing "multiple proceedings in Russian courts," including a case launched by the Russian Central Bank that seeks to challenge the immobilization of its assets.
Beyond strikes on Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, Russia launched ballistic missiles, four guided aerial missiles, and 113 Shahed-type drones, including 83 jet-powered drones, against Ukraine overnight on Oct. 30, according to Ukraine's Air Force.

articles.title: Russia-Africa Summit: Four days of dealmaking the West wanted Africa to skip
articles.body:
Russia-Africa Summit: Four days of dealmaking the West wanted Africa to skip
Delegations from 48 African countries, including 21 leaders, gathered in Moscow this week for the third Russia-Africa Summit under the motto “For Peace, Security and Development.” The gathering concluded on Thursday with the final declaration, a new cooperation plan and more than 60 agreements signed across the summit and its accompanying Economic and Humanitarian Forum.
Organizers reported over 3,500 participants from 74 countries, including more than 1,200 business representatives from around 630 companies. The signing total excludes confidential commercial documents, Russian presidential adviser Anton Kobyakov said. The forum hosted more than 40 sessions.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has already held at least nine bilateral meetings with African leaders, including the presidents of Egypt, Equatorial Guinea, Mozambique, Namibia, the Republic of the Congo, Burundi, and Kenya, as well as Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed and Libya’s Presidential Council Chairman Mohamed Al-Menfi.
Bilateral talks continued on Friday, with the day’s lineup including the leaders of Sudan, Madagascar, Ghana, Mali, South Sudan, the Central African Republic, DR Congo, and Eritrea, as well as Togo’s prime minister.
The October 28-29 summit capped four days of events, beginning with Monday’s media forum and including Tuesday’s separate gas exporters’ summit. Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov told RT that Western governments had tried to discourage African leaders from attending.
An overnight Ukrainian drone attack also prompted temporary restrictions at three Moscow airports before Thursday’s proceedings. Mayor Sergey Sobyanin reported 231 drones destroyed on the approaches to the capital. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov questioned the timing during an international gathering and praised air defenses.
Here are the main outcomes and key moments.
A framework through 2029
Putin and Burundian President Evariste Ndayishimiye, the African Union chair, co-chaired Wednesday's and Thursday’s proceedings. Leaders addressed a plenary session in Kremlin before continuing over a working breakfast.
They adopted the Moscow Declaration, a Russia-Africa Partnership Forum action plan for 2027-2029 and a declaration on civilian applications of artificial intelligence.
The political declaration backed greater African representation in international institutions, opposed unlawful unilateral sanctions, and supported efforts to address colonial-era damage. It also called for South Africa’s full G20 participation to be restored, following its exclusion from meetings under the US presidency. Pretoria remains a member.
At their closing press conference, Putin emphasized the potential for further cooperation, while Ndayishimiye pressed for measurable benefits. Another summit will follow, with its date and location to be agreed.
Partnership: ‘Africa has not come to ask for aid’
Russia and Africa are “natural allies in building a multipolar, genuinely democratic world order,” Putin told the plenary. He backed stronger African representation in global decision-making and described Russian businesses as partners investing in host countries rather than pursuing colonial exploitation.
African leaders also stressed that cooperation should strengthen their ability to make independent decisions and develop their economies.
“Contrary to what malevolent forces might think, Africa has not come to ask for aid,” Ndayishimiye told the Kremlin plenary. He called for commitments to become concrete investment programs and for international cooperation to follow African priorities.
Democratic Republic of Congo President Felix Tshisekedi made a similar distinction. “Diversifying our partnerships is not about choosing sides: it is about strengthening our freedom of decision-making in the service of our populations,” he said.
Zimbabwean President Emmerson Mnangagwa highlighted the need to turn agreements into action while processing more minerals domestically. Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi presented his country’s cooperation with Russia, including the El Dabaa nuclear plant and planned Suez Canal industrial zone, as a model for wider partnerships.
Russia also signed several documents to deepen cooperation with African regional organizations. These included memorandums with the East African Community, the Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa, and the African Continental Free Trade Area Secretariat, alongside an action plan with the African Union Commission.
Sergey Lavrov met counterparts from 41 African states.
Ghanaian Foreign Minister Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa said Lavrov pledged support for Accra’s application for BRICS partner status and would seek consensus among founding members.
Peskov said Putin presented country-specific cooperation roadmaps during bilateral meetings. Putin also highlighted expanding diplomatic representation: eight Russian embassies have opened in Africa since 2023, bringing the total to 48. Six trade missions cover 16 countries, while Botswana, Seychelles, and Togo plan embassies in Moscow.
Financing and nuclear cooperation
Signings included a Wednesday memorandum between Russia’s development institution VEB.RF and BCID-AES, the joint investment bank serving Burkina Faso, Mali, and Niger, to identify and assess development and integration projects.
Rosatom also signed a peaceful nuclear cooperation memorandum with Togo, establishing working groups to examine potential projects and training. Floating nuclear power units are among the possibilities.
Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed sought priority for nuclear cooperation, including financing, engineering training and medical isotopes. A roadmap for Ethiopia’s first nuclear plant was signed in March, Rosatom chief Aleksey Likhachev said in an interview published Friday. Site-selection preparations are underway. Burundi expressed interest in small modular reactors. Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi highlighted El Dabaa and the planned Russian industrial zone near the Suez Canal as examples of bilateral cooperation.
Trade and technology at Gostiny Dvor
Wednesday’s Economic and Humanitarian Forum at Gostiny Dvor in the Russian capital set much of the practical agenda. Putin proposed at least doubling Russia-Africa trade to more than $50 billion. On Thursday, he reported that the ruble accounted for up to 85% of commercial transactions between the two sides.
Putin and African leaders toured the “Platform for Sovereign Development” exhibition, showcasing energy, healthcare, agricultural, and digital technologies.
Elsewhere, Kenyan President William Ruto visited Sberbank’s smart city development and highlighted potential AI cooperation in healthcare and education.
Gas diplomacy alongside the summit
Tuesday’s eighth Gas Exporting Countries Forum summit adopted its own Moscow Declaration, separate from the Russia-Africa documents. It reaffirmed sovereign rights over gas resources and supported supply security, investment, and a balanced transition toward lower-carbon energy.
At Monday’s ministerial meeting, Russian Energy Minister Sergey Tsivilev promoted a proposed gas bank for long-term infrastructure financing, including in Africa. The initiative remained under discussion.
Media cooperation and liberation legacies
The Russia-Africa Media Forum ran from Monday to Thursday, organized by RT alongside Sputnik and TASS. Organizers welcomed more than 200 participants from 46 African countries for discussions on reporting, professional cooperation, and media sovereignty.
The forum also produced several media partnerships. These included Ethiopia’s Fana renewing its agreement with RT and Libya’s national news agency signing with RT Arabic. Rossiya Segodnya concluded partnerships with outlets in Algeria, Chad, Morocco, Ghana, and Zimbabwe, as well as Ethiopia’s Debre Markos University and Niger’s Higher School of Journalism and Communication.
RT’s Thursday session, “Forging Independence: Lessons from the Founders of African Nations,” featured descendants of African liberation leaders. Samia Nkrumah, daughter of Ghana’s first president Kwame Nkrumah, credited Russian support during Africa’s independence struggles, saying, “We are all here in Russia for a reason.” Ndileka Mandela, granddaughter of South Africa’s Nelson Mandela, recalled first meeting him through a prison window on Robben Island in 1981, aged 16: “I touched the window on one side and he touched on the other.”
Education and healthcare commitments
Putin extended Russia’s epidemic-control assistance program for Africa through 2029.
Eight countries have received 15 mobile laboratories, and around 450 African specialists have been trained under the program, he said.
Among the healthcare agreements was a five-year memorandum with DR Congo covering training, research, maternal and child health, nuclear medicine, and digital healthcare.
Nearly 40,000 Africans study at Russian universities, up 50% since 2020, according to Putin. Government-funded scholarship places have nearly tripled over that period, reaching 5,500 for 2026-2027. Announced initiatives include ten centers helping African applicants enter Russian universities and vocational training programs.
Andrey Maslov, director of HSE University’s Center for African Studies, told RT that extended visits by African leaders and their separate business programs showed political ties with Moscow are gaining practical substance.

articles.title: Su-57 Fighter Reportedly Burned Down at Russia’s Akhtubinsk Airfield
articles.body:
A Russian Su-57 (NATO: Felon) fighter jet burned down at the Akhtubinsk airfield in Russia’s Astrakhan region on Thursday, a Ukrainian channel has claimed.
Russia has not confirmed the loss.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The Ukrainian open-source intelligence (OSINT) channel, titled Absolutely Reliable Source, said on Friday that the aircraft caught fire “as a result of an emergency situation during engine start-up” and burned completely.
The channel posted a satellite image showing the faint outline of a burned-out fighter jet surrounded by a patch of scorched earth near the airfield.
Kyiv Post could confirm, based on Google Maps imagery, that the photo shows the Akhtubinsk airfield, which is known to have hosted Su-57s. However, it could not independently verify when the new photo was taken or whether the wreckage is that of a Su-57.
Russian investigative outlet The Insider noted that Russia lost 11 fighter jets and one helicopter in October thus far, including the Su-57.
On Thursday, Ukraine said it destroyed two Russian Su-34 bombers in the Volgograd region using a domestically produced Neptune missile.
The suspected Su-57 lost on Thursday would make it the fourth Su-57 Russia has lost in 2026. Two were hit at Russia’s Shagol airfield in April, alongside a Su-34 bomber, while another was lost after it crashed near Moscow in July.
Moscow said the latter was a Su-57 on a training flight with no weapons on board, and that the Investigative Committee opened a criminal case.
‘Get Them There Alive’: Ukraine’s Railways Under Russian Barrage
Akhtubinsk is home to Russia’s State Flight Test Center, where Su-57s have been tested and delivered.
It was also the site of the first reported strike on the jet. In June 2024, Ukraine’s military intelligence (HUR) said a drone attack damaged a Su-57 at the airfield. A Russian military channel, reportedly run by a retired pilot, acknowledged at the time that fragments had damaged the aircraft.
The Su-57 is Russia’s fifth-generation multirole fighter and its most advanced aircraft currently in service. It first flew in 2010, with serial production beginning in 2019 following a troubled development process that included India’s withdrawal from the project in 2018.
The first serial-production aircraft crashed on Dec. 24, 2019. It was the only known crash until July. As of early 2026, The National Interest estimated that Russia had around 32 Su-57s, including prototypes, against the 76 originally envisioned.
Russia has also attempted to promote the export versions of the Su-57 in 2026, with Algeria identified as the only foreign operator as of summer 2026.

articles.title: Zelensky Ready to Discuss Territory With Putin, Sybiha Says
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky is ready to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin and discuss territorial issues as part of efforts to end the war, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said.
Speaking to Finnish newspaper Helsingin Sanomat in an interview published after his two-day visit to Finland, Sybiha said Kyiv had coordinated the decision to hold a call between Putin, Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The Nordic leaders conveyed two main messages, he said: Ukraine’s demand for a ceasefire and its proposal for a face-to-face meeting between Zelensky and Putin.
“We want this meeting, and we are ready for it,” Sybiha said. “Probably only a meeting between Zelensky and Putin can bring a new quality to the negotiations. Zelensky is ready to discuss the most difficult and sensitive issues, including the territorial question.”
Sybiha said direct talks could lead to confidence-building measures, including prisoner exchanges and the return of Ukrainian children abducted by Russia.
The venue was not important to Kyiv, provided it was neither Moscow nor Belarus, Sybiha said, joking that North Korea could also be ruled out. He dismissed Russia’s invitation for Zelensky to visit Moscow as “not serious.”
Kyiv sees Nordic call as diplomatic opening
“Our assessment is that the call was a step forward in our peace efforts,” Sybiha said, adding that he hoped the channel of communication with Putin would remain open.
80% of Ukrainians Back Refinery Strikes Despite Risks of US Aid Cut
The roughly 90-minute conversation also confirmed that trilateral negotiations involving Ukraine, the US and Russia were expected to continue in Abu Dhabi in November, he said.
“Those talks will show whether Russia has serious intentions to end the war through diplomatic means,” Sybiha said, adding that Kyiv currently saw no signs of such intentions.
Asked whether Putin had made any important statements during the conversation, he replied: “At least it [the call] happened.”
The call drew criticism from some European officials. Stubb and Støre said they had acted in their national capacities, rather than on behalf of Europe.
Sybiha said the initiative reflected a shared decision with Kyiv to use every available diplomatic channel. He also urged Europe to establish a stronger role in negotiations and speak with one voice.
Stubb’s close relations with both US President Donald Trump and Zelensky already gave him an important role, Sybiha said. The Finnish president had now also heard Putin’s position directly.
Asked whether Stubb could represent Europe in the peace process, Sybiha said EU leaders would have to decide, adding: “Why not?”
Europe should reinforce US peace efforts, Sybiha says
Sybiha said greater European involvement was particularly important because he believed the Trump administration had moved further toward accommodating Russia’s demands.
He cited what he described as US pressure for a change in Ukraine’s leadership, sanctions relief and renewed US purchases of Russian diesel.
Despite those concerns, Sybiha said Ukraine had no alternative to keeping Washington involved.
“It is not realistic to end the war without them, or to obtain real security guarantees for the future without them,” he said.
Europe’s role should complement, rather than replace, US-led diplomacy, he added.
Sybiha said intensified Russian attacks were another reason Kyiv had sought additional diplomatic channels through Finland and Norway. Russia had launched 100 ballistic missiles at Ukraine over two weeks, he said.
He said he was returning from Finland more hopeful, praising the country’s support for Ukraine.
“We have hope that things will move forward after that call,” he said.
Moscow continues to insist on talks in Russia
Trump said on Oct. 28 that he hoped to hold a summit with Putin and Zelensky “very soon.”
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov did not rule out a meeting but said the timing was flexible and that talks would require “extensive, meticulous preparation.”
Zelensky had proposed meeting Putin on the sidelines of the G20 summit in the US in December. Peskov called that option “impossible,” saying Zelensky could accept Putin’s invitation to Moscow if he “truly desires” direct talks.
In early June, Zelensky proposed a summit in a neutral country in a rare open letter to Putin. He said the meeting should be backed by broader European and US security guarantees. The Kremlin dismissed the proposal and reiterated its invitation to Moscow.
Putin first issued that invitation in September 2025 while questioning Zelensky’s legitimacy and the value of a meeting. Zelensky rejected it and proposed Kyiv instead.
Putin did not respond to that proposal and has continued to insist that Moscow is the “best place” for talks, claiming Zelensky’s safety would be guaranteed.

articles.title: Ukraine sanctions companies, individuals linked to Russia's Rassvet satellite system, shadow fleet
articles.body:
Ukraine sanctions companies, individuals linked to Russia's Rassvet satellite system, shadow fleet
President Volodymyr Zelensky signed decrees on Oct. 30 imposing sanctions on 10 companies and 19 Russian citizens involved in developing the Rassvet satellite system, as well as 39 vessels in Russia's shadow fleet, according to a statement on the Presidential Office's website.
Since February, Russian Starlink terminals have been blocked, with only verified devices allowed to connect. The Rassvet low-Earth orbit satellite network could provide Russian forces with their own satellite communications link, enabling them to control drones and missiles over long distances.
The Rassvet system could pose a threat to the entire world, Vladyslav Vlasiuk, the presidential commissioner for sanctions policy, said.
"The (Rassvet) project depends on foreign technologies, equipment, and components, so we are targeting these supply chains at the development stage and calling on our partners to coordinate sanctions," Vlasiuk added.
Among the sanctioned entities are Bureau 1440, the developer, coordinator, and system integrator of the Rassvet system, and two affiliated companies: Labs 1440, which manufactures solar panels for spacecraft, and FAB Rassvet, which develops low-Earth orbit communications satellites, the Presidential Office said.
The sanctions also targeted Belarusian company Aerospace Instruments, which develops components for aerospace systems, the office added.
Ukraine's military intelligence agency (HUR) said on Oct. 28 that 49 Russian and Belarusian companies were involved in developing Russia's Rassvet low-Earth orbit satellite communications system.
Besides the satellite system-related entities, the sanctions target 39 vessels belonging to Russia's shadow fleet. The vessels sail under the flags of Russia, Barbados, Liberia, the Marshall Islands, Panama, Hong Kong, Djibouti, the Bahamas, Equatorial Guinea, Zimbabwe, Cameroon, Palau, and Sierra Leone, the Presidential Office said.
The vessels transport Russian oil, petroleum products, and gas condensate to China, India, Egypt, Turkey, and other countries, the office said.
One tanker, the Vasily Dinkov, made 15 voyages carrying approximately 726,000 tons of Russian crude oil in the first half of 2026 alone. Some of the vessels are already under sanctions imposed by the EU, U.K., U.S., Canada, Switzerland, and Australia, the statement read.
Russia's shadow fleet consists of aging, poorly insured tankers used to transport Russian oil in violation of international sanctions. Western governments have also accused Moscow of using the fleet to support its hybrid war against Europe.

articles.title: Destinus says it now makes more cruise missiles a month than Europe did a year before 2022, but engines are what Ukraine’s strike programs are short of
articles.body:
Destinus has completed 1,750 Ruta B1 cruise missiles and reached monthly output of nearly 300, the company said on 29 October, telling Reuters this exceeds Europe’s annual cruise-missile production before Russia’s full-scale invasion.
That gives a date for easing a shortage. A looming shortage of mini jet engines threatened to hold back Ukraine’s deep-strike drones, Reuters reported in April. Czech maker ZofiTech was then producing about 200 a month, nearly all for Ukraine, and expected demand to reach thousands within months. Both Ruta versions use the 1.5-kN engines Destinus is promising. Ukraine plans to build more jet drones and cruise missiles, so engine output next year will have to keep up, Defense Express notes.
Destinus builds its own engines, but hasn’t said how many
Destinus CEO Mikhail Kokorich said the company already produces turbojets in the roughly 1.5-kilonewton class in series, supplying them both for its own missiles and to other manufacturers. The Ruta B1 runs on the company’s own T150 engine. In June, Destinus announced its 1,000th T150 and said the line was designed to sustain production of thousands of missile systems a year. The company has not disclosed its current engine output.
Block 2 enters production, Block 3 is due to fly in 2027
Meanwhile, Destinus said it has begun production of the larger Ruta Block 2, designed to carry a 250-kg payload more than 700 km. Unlike the roughly 300-km Block 1, Block 2 is designed to be stored, transported, and launched from the same container. A third version, Block 3, is planned with a 2,000-km range, with flight tests scheduled for 2027.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy acknowledged the Ruta’s combat use in October 2025. Days later, he said Ukraine expected mass production of Ruta and Flamingo missiles by the end of that year. In June 2026, then-Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov said the Netherlands was ready to finance about 700 Rutas for Ukraine, without specifying the version.
Deterrence takes “tens of thousands of missiles”
At the same time, Kokorich said Europe’s problem is shifting from production to integration.
“To have sufficient deterrence, you need to have tens of thousands of missiles,” he said.
European customers, he added, still need to build the military units and logistics to operate missiles in such numbers. Those arsenals would also need storage, transport, maintenance, and targeting infrastructure, he said, and European militaries would need to rethink how they stockpile and deploy precision-strike weapons.
No Chinese parts, and a bet on cheaper, shorter-range missiles
Kokorich said Destinus uses no Chinese components, unlike wartime production in Ukraine, and said access to Chinese suppliers would make manufacturing cheaper, faster, and easier.
Kokorich also argued that cheaper missiles with ranges under 1,000 km would make up most future demand. Separately, Destinus is working with Rheinmetall on cruise missiles and ammunition for multiple-launch rocket systems, including a planned European equivalent of the GMLRS rockets fired by HIMARS.

articles.title: Estonia's Russia expertise is respected by the US, says foreign minister
articles.body:
Estonia's Russia expertise is respected by the US, says foreign minister
Minister of Foreign Affairs Margus Tsahkna (Eesti 200) said the United States has not made any proposals to Estonia to change its tone when discussing the Russian threat. He said Estonia is respected in America because the country is an expert on Russia.
On Friday, Reuters news agency, citing anonymous sources, reported that Pentagon officials had urged several NATO allies, including Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, to tone down their public rhetoric on the threat posed by Russia.
Tsahkna and outgoing Ministry of Foreign Affairs Secretary General Jonatan Vseviov pushed back on the media reports on Friday afternoon.
"The United States has not made any official proposal to us that we should in any way change our foreign policy or our communication," Tsahkna told ERR.
"These are anonymous sources. I cannot comment on them, and I do not want to comment on them. However, Estonia is highly respected in the eyes of the United States and more broadly within NATO, because we are, after all, experts when it comes to Russia. Likewise, we can see very far into Russia, and our expert assessments and intelligence are highly valued," the minister said.
He pointed out that Russia is "organizing terrorist attacks and acts of sabotage" against Europe and that Estonia has not been afraid to point this out, publicly.
"Estonia has always been very clear and honest when it comes to the Russian threat and Russia's aggression against Ukraine. Also about the fact that we do not currently see Russia preparing for large-scale aggression against NATO, because we do not see any major movements of Russian troops or increases in their capabilities beyond our borders. At the same time, however, we see Russia increasingly organizing terrorist attacks and acts of sabotage against Europe. And here, too, we have been very clear in publicly attributing these acts and punishing the perpetrators. However, what Russia is doing is trying to undermine Western unity. It is trying to play on that same fear of escalation, which Russia has constantly done, while continually accusing NATO and the Western world of preparing some kind of aggression against Russia, which is absolutely not true," Tsahkna said.
'Russia is provoking us'
One source told Reuters that Elbridge Colby, the Pentagon's top policy official, recently told an official from one of the Baltic states that Russia should not be provoked.
Tsahkna denied that Estonia is provoking Russia.
"We are in constant contact with the United States on security policy, on the deployment of their troops here and on NATO defense plans. And it is certainly not in our interests to provoke Russia in any way; rather, Russia is provoking us. So we are not under any pressure one way or the other. We discuss these matters together. The United States is a NATO ally and Article 5 works, so this communication takes place daily," Tsahkna said.
Tsahkna stressed that neither the Baltic states nor Estonia have been aggressive in their messages in any way. "This entire narrative is connected to Putin's desire to undermine the political unity of our Western world," he said.
Ministry of Defense spokesperson Ines Edur told ERR that the ministry does not comment on a story based on anonymous sources and that no such request has been received by the ministry through official channels.
