articles.title: Binance says $6.3bn stolen in biggest crypto heist in history: What we know
articles.body:
Binance says $6.3bn stolen in biggest crypto heist in history: What we know
The world’s largest crypto exchange halts withdrawals as the theft is linked to North Korean hackers.
Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, says hackers have stolen about $6.3bn in what appears to have been the biggest crypto heist on record.
The company, which was co-founded by the Chinese-born Canadian billionaire Changpeng Zhao, suspended deposits and withdrawals on Thursday and said it would cover all losses, telling Al Jazeera in a statement that user funds were “safe”.
Two United States blockchain analysis firms have claimed the attack originated in North Korea.
So how did it happen, and what does it mean for the crypto market? Here’s what you need to know:
What happened?
Blockchain analysis firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis say most of the theft unfolded over about 20 minutes, starting late on Thursday.
“An attacker moved approximately 6.36 billion USD out of Binance wallets on 10 blockchains,” TRM reported.
That dwarfs the previous record of $1.5bn, which was stolen from the exchange Bybit in February 2025.
Binance said about $3bn of that has since been frozen, including more than $2.3bn by stablecoin issuers Tether and Circle, according to the Reuters news agency.
Binance has not stated what has happened to the remaining $3.3bn.
It also warned on X that the $6.3bn figure “may continue to increase” as the company works to trace and freeze more assets.
Who carried out the heist and how?
North Korean hackers, according to the firms tracking the funds.
TRM said it had assessed with “high confidence” that the attack was carried out by TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking unit linked to the Lazarus Group.
According to the Council on Foreign Relations (CFR), the Lazarus Group “targets and compromises entities primarily in South Korea and South Korean interests for espionage, disruption, and destruction”.
It also conducts cyberoperations for financial gain, including targeting cryptocurrency exchanges, the CFR says.
The US Department of the Treasury sanctioned the Lazarus Group in 2019, saying it was controlled by North Korea’s primary intelligence bureau. North Korea routinely denies involvement in hacking.
Chainalysis reached the same conclusion, however.
The FBI also blamed the Bybit hack in 2025 on the same unit.
TRM said the attackers ordered Binance’s wallets to empty into wallets they controlled, mirroring the Bybit hack.
Binance has been more cautious, however. “Our investigation has not attributed responsibility to any individual,” co-CEO Richard Teng said on X.
The company initially said the breach may have started with a hacked laptop belonging to one of its engineers. But on Friday, it said further investigation had uncovered “additional points of breach”.
Binance said it had found no evidence that any wallet’s private key, the digital password that controls a crypto wallet, had been leaked.
But Mark Karpeles, former head of the collapsed Tokyo exchange Mt Gox, told Reuters the attackers had probably accessed keys for at least two Binance wallets.
What was the purpose of the attack?
Money.
While North Korea denies involvement in crypto theft, it has become a much-needed source of foreign currency for Pyongyang, helping to prop up its economy and fund its nuclear programme, which is under United Nations sanctions, experts say.
In December 2022, South Korea’s spy agency estimated that North Korean hackers had stolen about 1.5 trillion won ($1.1bn) in crypto and other virtual assets over five years.
“When North Korea steals at this scale, the money funds weapons proliferation and other destabilising activity,” Ari Redbord, TRM’s global head of policy, told Al Jazeera, adding, “That makes this a global security issue, not just a crypto theft.”
What does this mean for the crypto market?
Prices have fallen, though markets steadied after the initial shock.
Bitcoin hit a six-week low of $76,368, while Ether fell more than 3 percent to a two-month low of $2,178.
Shares in crypto exchange Coinbase, which said it was unaffected, fell 4.8 percent.
The hack comes as crypto had already been under pressure from higher US interest rates and weaker demand from exchange-traded fund buyers, analysts told Reuters.
The stolen sum is more than six times Binance’s $1bn emergency fund, the Secure Asset Fund for Users, set up in 2018 and held entirely in Bitcoin to protect users in case of a breach.
Teng said company funds would also cover losses.
Is crypto an inherently unsafe investment?
The hack has exposed one particular weak point: Large, centralised exchanges, which hold users’ assets on their behalf.
“Any assets held at a centralised exchange are only as safe as the exchange itself, and the larger the exchange’s holdings, the larger a target it becomes,” Sean Foley, an expert in crypto markets at Macquarie University in Sydney, told Al Jazeera.
Insurance offers limited protection as most crime- and cyber-insurance policies do not cover stolen cryptocurrency, and crypto-specific cover remains a niche business offered largely by specialist insurers.
Thefts are frequent. Hackers stole $2.87bn in crypto in nearly 150 attacks in 2025, according to TRM’s 2026 Crypto Crime Report.
Binance itself has faced legal trouble. Founder Changpeng Zhao pleaded guilty in 2023 to a felony linked to failing to prevent money laundering on the platform. US President Donald Trump pardoned him in 2025.
On Friday, Binance said it was coordinating with law enforcement and remained on track to resume withdrawals within 45 hours.

articles.title: Poland may reconsider transferring additional MiG-29s to Ukraine if Bulgaria deal falls through – expert
articles.body:
Poland may reconsider transferring additional MiG-29s to Ukraine if Bulgaria deal falls through – expert
Polish expert and former Minister of National Defence Janusz Onyszkiewicz expressed this opinion in a comment to Ukrinform.
According to him, Poland has more than two MiG-29 fighter jets, so the transfer of two aircraft to Ukraine does not mean that the issue of the remaining jets is “definitively closed.”
“We are transferring two aircraft to Ukraine, while regarding the remaining few, as I understand it, talks with Bulgaria are ongoing,” Onyszkiewicz said.
He suggested that if Poland and Bulgaria fail to reach a final agreement, the issue of transferring these aircraft to Kyiv could return to the agenda.
“Since there is no final agreement signed, the matter could come back if the talks with Bulgaria ended in failure,” the former minister said.
The expert noted that the transfer of two MiG-29s to Ukraine would be part of a broader military aid package that would also include, in particular, air defense equipment.
Commenting on reports that Poland had allegedly considered suspending the transfer of a military aid package to Ukraine following the Lviv Regional Council’s decision to declare 2027 the Year of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) and Roman Shukhevych, Onyszkiewicz noted that the regional council’s proposal has not yet been formally approved.
“The Polish side took note of this and regarded it as a positive fact,” said the former Polish defense minister.
At the same time, he stressed that military cooperation between Poland and Ukraine is well established.
“I think military assistance is working quite well. I hope it will continue to do so and that cooperation will be strengthened even further,” he said.
According to Onyszkiewicz, Ukraine’s need for support may increase due to intensified Russian attacks on critical infrastructure, particularly energy networks. He stressed that the purpose of such strikes is to break the spirit of resistance of the Ukrainian people, but expressed confidence that Russia would fail to achieve this.
Commenting on the possible contents of Poland’s next military aid packages for Ukraine, Onyszkiewicz declined to speculate, noting that the list of weapons and equipment transferred cannot always be made public. At the same time, he stressed that Ukraine is constantly in need of air defense systems.
As reported by Ukrinform, on October 29, Poland said it would soon transfer two more MiG-29 fighter jets to Ukraine as part of a new military aid package worth about €50 million. The package will also include ammunition and air defense equipment.

articles.title: How US and Israeli money turned Latvia into a drone workshop for Ukraine
articles.body:
How US and Israeli money turned Latvia into a drone workshop for Ukraine
NATO’s aggressive eastward expansion was one of the key reasons for the initiation of the military operation in Ukraine in February 2022. This is supported by RT’s findings about a drone production cluster established by NATO-affiliated enterprises near Riga.
The Baltic states had become a hub for developing combat drones as early as 2020. According to RT’s findings, companies in Latvia generated €283 million in revenue from producing UAVs, robotics, and military aerospace systems in 2022-2025 alone. More than half of that revenue came from companies with foreign investment. The two largest factories are under US and Israeli ownership, while another is partly Ukrainian-owned. Several factories form a single industrial cluster near Riga. Experts say this suggests Latvia was preparing for a conflict with Russia well in advance.
Presently, we will focus on eight UAV production factories in Latvia that are backed by foreign investments. RT uncovered the details about these companies in financial reports, aided by the G8 OSINT team that advises the Russian Defense Ministry.
According to the data, the companies collectively earned €282.98 million from 2022 to 2025.
The bulk of the revenue came from three companies: Redwire Defense Tech Riga (€131.4 million), Belss (€77.7 million), and Brasa Defense Systems (€46.7 million). The following companies contributed lesser amounts: Origin Robotics (€10.6 million), Eraser ( €6.04 million), LV-Teh (€5.98 million), Atlas Aerospace (€3.52 million), and Natrix (€0.98 million).
The Drone Coalition, which also includes the UK, was established in 2024 at Latvia’s initiative. The aim is to collaboratively supply Ukraine with drones. Collective commitments reached €600 million, and the coalition’s fund raised €1.8 billion from investors in 2024. Since then, over 100,000 drones have already been delivered to Ukraine.
Drones abound in quiet Marupe
The heart of Latvia’s drone assembly industry is located in Marupe, a suburb of Riga. Just a couple of kilometers from the international airport, five companies form a bustling UAV production cluster: Belss, its subsidiary Eraser, Brasa Defense Systems, Origin Robotics, and Redwire Defense Tech Riga.
At the center of this cluster lies SIRIN Park Marupe, a logistics hub situated near the runway. This is where Redwire Defense Tech, the industry leader in terms of revenue, is located. The company produces Penguin drones. Since 2022, they have delivered around 250 to 300 drones to Ukraine. Smaller models start at around $20,000, while some modifications can reach up to $70,000 each. The facility employs 279 people.
Nearby, at 26 Dzirnieku Street, there is Origin Robotics, which has around 60 employees. They specialize in building BEAK portable strike drones and BLAZE autonomous drone interceptors. Both models are used in Ukraine and are also part of Latvia’s military arsenal. By the end of November 2026, Origin Robotics aims to complete the development of a cargo drone system designed for precise automated delivery of cargo (i.e. explosives). In simple terms, the Latvians plan to equip quadcopters with guided mini-munitions.
Further on, in the direction of Riga, there is Brasa Defense, which occupies around 6,000 square meters of warehouse and office space at 16 Plienciema Street. They manufacture UNHUMAN ground robotic platforms designed to support infantry on the battlefield.
Located furthest from the airport, Belss operates in Ezisi Industrial Park. It is the largest defense communications integrator in Latvia (operating since 1994). The company formerly focused on secure military communications but pivoted in 2023 to develop its own line of UAVs. By 2024, they were supplying thousands of modular military drones to Ukraine. In June 2024, Belss spun off its drone division into a separate subsidiary named Eraser.
There are no doubts as to who is the primary consumer of Belss products: Latvian and Ukrainian flags are proudly displayed at the entrance. A satellite view reveals a private runway just 100 meters from the fence, used for testing equipment.
The other production facilities are located in Riga, but the difference isn’t critical since Marupe is very close to Riga. The area is home to the NATRIX, LV-Teh, and AeroVictory Baltic factories. The latter is a Baltic subsidiary of a Ukrainian company that has relocated UAV production to Latvia and has yet to submit financial reports.
Also registered in Riga is Atlas Aerospace – a company with Ukrainian roots and Israeli ownership – producing reconnaissance drones like the AtlasPRO, Atlas UAVs, and AtlasTETHER tethered systems. These devices are supplied to Ukraine and NATO countries. The company has 43 official employees.
The choice of location is strategic, according to specialists from the G8 group. In addition to proximity to the airport, a railway runs through Marupe that will soon connect with tracks leading to Ukraine via Moldova.
The father of ‘Penguins’ in the service of NATO
Latvia has its own key figure uniting several companies backed by American and European capital: Konstantins Popiks, a serial entrepreneur in the military industry. He was introduced to aeromodeling as a child and even represented Latvia in aeromodeling competitions. After enrolling at the University of Liverpool in 2005, he graduated in 2009 with a Master’s degree in aerospace engineering.
The Penguin reconnaissance drone and its combat versions, which are in service with the Latvian military and are being sold in large quantities to Ukraine, originated as Popiks’ student project. Upon returning to his homeland, he founded UAV Factory, which produces Penguin drones. Within ten years, the company reached the international level, and in 2021, it attracted an investor from the US: AE Industrial Partners. By 2022, Popiks departed, and the factory changed ownership and rebranded as Edge Autonomy.
In June 2025, the facility announced plans to double its production footprint, enabling it to produce up to ten heavy fixed-wing UAVs per month. According to documents, there were 270 employees at the time, and the company had contracts with the Latvian Defense Ministry.
In 2025, Edge Autonomy Holdings signed a merger agreement, becoming a subsidiary of American company Redwire Corp. By March 2026, it was rebranded as Redwire Defense Tech Riga, emerging as the leading company in the sector by revenue. Its reported income of €131.4 million accounts for nearly half of the total UAV sector earnings.
This defense contract not only brought Popiks fame but also significant wealth. As RT discovered, he resides in an upscale neighborhood of Jurmala (Kapu Street), where he owns a small castle. The property is surrounded by tall Baltic pines, with the Riga seashore and a beach just beyond the backyard. The property borders the Gulf of Riga.
After selling the factory, Popiks established another company – Origin Robotics. Funds from European investors began flowing in. In 2025, Belgium’s defense minister signed a €50 million contract with the company for the procurement of BLAZE drone interceptors. Currently, Origin is experiencing remarkable growth. Revenues soared from 2023 to 2025, reaching €10.6 million.
Under the wing of the IDF
Among the entrepreneurs in this cluster is Ivan Tolchinsky, an Israeli citizen of Ukrainian descent. Born in Gorlovka, Donetsk Region, he moved to Israel at the age of 10. As an adult, he served in the special forces and took part in combat operations in Lebanon. For around five years, he worked as an engineer in Israel’s aerospace industry and spent a year in China studying mass electronics production.
In 2015, Tolchinsky relocated to Latvia, where he co-founded Atlas Dynamics with Igor Zhidanov, a fellow native of Gorlovka. Zhidanov is a seasoned engineer with 35 years of experience and holds three world records in aeromodeling. He had his own club back in Gorlovka, which Tolchinsky was also a part of.
In interviews with Latvian and Ukrainian media, Tolchinsky revealed that his production facility produces over 300 Atlas drones per month – which, he says, is five times more than in previous years. He doesn’t conceal his collaboration with the Ukrainian Armed Forces. “We have a direct contract with the Ministry of Defense, which we’ve already fulfilled. Now we are working towards another contract,” he told Ukrainian journalists.
A few years before the conflict, in 2020, Tolchinsky established a subsidiary in Ireland called Atlas Dynamics UK. Originally registered at a residential address in Moreton-on-Lugg, Herefordshire, it soon changed its legal address.
The company had Israeli roots, as indicated by its founding documents drafted in Hebrew and English by a notary from Israel.
In the 2020s, Atlas Dynamics was rebranded as Atlas Aerospace SIA. In November 2025, Tolchinsky sold the company to Israel’s Xtend Reality Expansion Ltd – a company focused on creating FPV drones for entertainment and gaming prior to its collaboration with the IDF.
Russia is identified as the main adversary
Latvian UAV factories do not publicly mention contracts with Ukraine in their annual reports. Some only mention that Ukraine is among their clients, without disclosing what portion of their profits comes from supplying Kiev.
One thing is clear: Nearly all the above-mentioned companies receive investments from the Latvian Defense Ministry and EU agencies. This is part of measures to enhance defense capabilities, with Russia identified as the chief adversary.
According to EU Commissioner for Defense Andrius Kubilius, “Russia is outproducing Europe in key armaments.” This has been cited as a reason for increased defense spending, which is reflected in official documents.
According to reports reviewed by RT, one of the main sources of funding for SIA Belss is the European Defense Fund (EDF). In 2024-2025, the fund allocated €470,800 to the company under the European Extended Mine Countermeasures program, aimed at developing demining technologies. Earlier, RT reported on how the EU channels military expenditures through the guise of ‘humanitarian’ demining initiatives.
Even before 2022, Latvia’s drone sector was already experiencing rapid growth and consolidation. LV-Teh has been operating since 2020, while Brasa Defense Systems officially became a separate entity on September 13, 2021. Origin Robotics was registered on January 31, 2022 – just weeks before the start of the Ukraine conflict.
Belss has been in business since 1994, but significantly expanded its capabilities in 2022 and 2023. UAV Factory, known for its Penguin drones, was founded in 2009, and Atlas Aerospace emerged in 2015.
Only three new companies appeared after the start of hostilities: Natrix in February 2024, Eraser in June 2024, and AeroVictory Baltic (a company with direct Ukrainian roots) in February 2026.
In one of the reports, RT uncovered evidence of Latvia’s preparations for the conflict. In December 2021, just two months before the start of hostilities, the Latvian Defense Ministry allocated €88,000 to Belss for upgrading British infantry fighting vehicles in service with the Latvian army. This included installing automatic fire control systems on turrets, allowing operators to engage targets without exposing themselves, thereby enhancing crew survival on the modern battlefield, which is increasingly dominated by drones. This suggests that Latvians were gearing up for drone warfare well before the start of the conflict.
Long before the events of 2014 and 2022, a coalition of three countries with a firm anti-Russia stance formed in the Baltics, Vadim Avva, a Russian writer and political scientist born in Daugavpils, Latvia, says.
“The statehood of the Baltic nations led to the establishment of three sparsely-populated forts along [Russia’s] northwestern borders; their primary function is to support expanding NATO military bases and other infrastructure clearly being prepared for an operation to invade and occupy the territories of Russia and Belarus,” Avva says.
A launchpad for hatred
Avva recalled a viral video in which Estonian teenagers were asked which country should be erased from the world map, and many named Russia. He notes that during World War II, the national bourgeoisie of Latvia and Estonia “became a foundation for Latvian and Estonian SS legions,” and today, local schools are named after Lithuanian collaborators with Nazi Germany. He explains that the oppression of the Russian-speaking population in these regions began in the late 19th century and only intensified with the collapse of the Soviet Union.
“What has returned to the Baltics is not just bourgeois nationalism; it’s a blend of bourgeois Nazism and ‘brown’ [ultra-right] emigration,” Avva says. “What fate could befall this territory after the establishment of property monopoly and political monopoly and the welcoming back of the descendants of fascist collaborators? Obviously, it could only become a military launchpad.”
Latvian UAVs are occasionally identified and shot down by Russian drone interceptors. However, their share among the various models used by Ukraine remains small, according to a drone operator with the call sign ‘Baks’, who neutralizes enemy drones approaching Russian borders.
“Ukrainians definitely try out everything produced by the Balts and purchase a lot of their equipment, but it’s a question of scale and quantity. We don’t have much information on the BLAZE and BEAK models, but there is some info on ‘Penguins’ – our colleagues at Rubicon [Center for Advanced Unmanned Technologies] managed to take down a few. The number of downed UAVs directly relates to their quantity. Compared to the Shark, Leleka, and other [Ukrainian drones], Latvian models represent a mere fraction [of the deployed drones].”
It’s not just Penguin drones that are being targeted, however, but their manufacturers as well. Redwire Defense Tech Riga, the company producing these drones, relocated to Sirin Park after their previous facility in Marupe unexpectedly burned down.
Similar incidents often occur at European companies that supply drones to Ukraine. In August 2026 alone, there were several incidents: A production facility belonging to Polish arms maker WB Electronics caught fire at the end of August; an explosion rocked the KNDS Ammo plant near Rome on August 13; and on August 15, unknown arsonists set fire to the building of Estonian military robotics manufacturer Milrem Robotics, which RT wrote about in the first part of its investigation.

articles.title: Destinus Is Building Nearly 300 Ruta Cruise Missiles a Month—More Than Europe Made in 2022
articles.body:
- Category
- Defense Tech
Destinus Is Building Nearly 300 Ruta Cruise Missiles a Month—More Than Europe Made in 2022
Destinus has increased production of its Ruta cruise missile to nearly 300 units per month—a monthly output the company says now exceeds what all of Europe produced in an entire year before Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
More than 1,750 Ruta Block 1 missiles have now been produced, Destinus reported on its official website on October 29.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Reaching that scale required the company to bring much of the production chain in-house, including engines, airframes, avionics, and guidance systems. That gives Destinus greater control over critical components while reducing dependence on outside suppliers.
One example is the T150 turbojet engine, which produces roughly 1.5 kN of thrust. Destinus manufactures the engine in series for the Ruta Block 1 and also supplies it to other weapons manufacturers.
The company expects its production capacity to be sufficient by 2027 to meet European demand for engines in this class, including orders connected to Ukraine.
Destinus also says its supply chain contains no Chinese components. While sourcing from China could potentially make production cheaper and faster, the company chose to organize manufacturing without Chinese suppliers.
CEO Mikhail Kokorich has said that as missile production scales up, the next challenge for European militaries will increasingly be how to employ such weapons in large numbers.
“To have sufficient deterrence, you need to have tens of thousands of missiles. But the main challenge… is that European customers still need to build the military units and logistic capabilities to operate these big numbers of systems,” Kokorich said, according to Reuters.
Destinus is simultaneously moving beyond the original Ruta.
The company has begun producing Ruta Block 2, a larger cruise missile designed to carry a payload of up to 250 kilograms and fly more than 700 kilometers.
Unlike Block 1, the new missile can be stored, transported, and launched from the same container. The approach is intended to simplify deployment and logistics, particularly when militaries need to stockpile large numbers of weapons.
The Block 2 features a box-shaped fuselage and an integrated folding-wing mechanism that allows the missile to fit inside its transport-launch container.
It also uses a solid-fuel booster to provide initial acceleration at launch.
That means Ruta Block 2 can be fired directly from its container instead of requiring a separate launch rail, making the system easier to transport, conceal, store, and deploy.
Earlier, Destinus accelerated development of the Ruta Block 3 long-range strike missile together with Rheinmetall, aiming to create a 2,000-kilometer-class precision weapon that will be tested in Ukraine.
Discuss this article:

articles.title: Shadows, roofs, job ads give Ukrainian arms plants away to Russian analysts, Ukrainian experts warn
articles.body:
Russian analysts can locate Ukrainian weapons plants from details in published photos and TV footage, Ukrainian defense outlet Oboronka reported on 29 October. Open-source researchers told the outlet how to hide those details.
Ukraine plans to build 7 million drones this year, and Russia is hunting the plants that make them. In June, the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) said Russia’s GRU military intelligence was gathering data to prepare air strikes on defense plants and attacks on their engineers.
A TV clip, then missiles
On 7 April 2022, Ukrainian channel 1+1 aired a report from a workshop at the Kyiv Armored Plant converting captured Russian military equipment for Ukraine’s forces. On 14 April, Rybar, an anonymous pro-Russian Telegram channel, posted the factory’s location. Russian missiles hit the workshop on 16 April, killing at least three civilians, the Centre for Information Resilience (CIR) found.
Retracing the likely method, CIR wrote that wall colors, window size, and ceiling height could single out the plant, and Google Earth imagery the workshop. InformNapalm researcher Andrii Lisitsyn told Oboronka that matching a frame with old photos, satellite images, job ads, or staff profiles quickly narrows the search.
A Gaussian blur smears pixels but keeps part of the information, Oboronka wrote. In a 2020 blog post, aerospace engineering student Gonçalo Raposo showed it can be fully reversed if the exact filter and edge handling are known. Pixelation fails too: a 2022 neural network reconstructs plausible faces from pixelated images. Lisitsyn advises cropping or fully opaque masking instead, plus checking file metadata.
Leaks beyond photos
Some Ukrainian defense enterprises still keep accounts and procurement records in Russian 1C software, Oboronka wrote. Since 6 January 2026, 1C products have been on the State Special Communications Service’s list of banned software. The ban covers systems with state information resources and critical information infrastructure owned or managed by state bodies, state enterprises, and local governments, the service said.
Oboronka also wrote that days before the full-scale invasion, Spanish journalist Pablo González photographed production lines at engine maker Motor Sich. Poland held him from February 2022 until a prisoner swap sent him to Russia in August 2024. Prosecutors then indicted him under both his names, Pablo González and Pavel Rubtsov, for spying for Russian military intelligence.
Read also
- “Whole family fell from third floor”: Strike on Flamingo missile company employee signals Russia is hunting Ukraine’s defense innovators at their homes
- Ukraine says it hit drone hangars at Crimea’s Hvardiiske. Now an OSINT channel spots 20+ bermed shelters there
- Ukrainian OSINT channel: Russia turned a bare field into a Geran-5 launch site in a month—and drones are already arriving

articles.title: Gulf states must rethink trillion-dollar defence in light of US-Iran war, says report
articles.body:
Gulf states are going to have to reconfigure their trillion-dollar defences given the damage inflicted on their economies and the questionable continued value of US bases in the face of Iranian attack, according to a study by the International Institute for Strategic Studies.
The report says that in the weeks before the 8 April ceasefire, 12 regional states, overwhelmingly in the Gulf, faced 4,670 Iranian one-way attack drones and more than 1,400 ballistic missiles. Nearly half were aimed at the United Arab Emirates. Although the vast majority were repelled, one estimate of the damage to energy infrastructure cited by the report is put as high as $58bn (£43bn).
Iran would portray either a reduction or complete withdrawal of US forces from the region as “a strategic success and vindication of its steadfastness, but also use it to embarrass the Gulf states about their decades-long courtship of US protection”.
The report says the war also highlights another “uncomfortable truth for the Gulf states: not only has their trillion-dollar acquisition of US weapons not translated into US protection at the crucial time, but their respective militaries are also not adequately prepared for the new kind of attritional air war to which they are being exposed”.
Despite huge investment in mainly US armaments, the report identified significant shortcomings: “overwhelming reliance on US-supplied air- and missile-defence systems and munitions; a failure to achieve regional defence integration; a shortage of minesweeping capability; limited retaliatory options; and the prohibitive costs stemming from an overdependence on expensive, high-end systems to take down relatively inexpensive drones and missiles”.
The report is neutral on whether the divided Gulf states should seek a new non-aggression pact with Iran, but notes that the US-Iran war has shown longstanding defence and security partnerships with the US “have failed to ensure adequate protection against Iranian aggression”.
It adds: “If anything, US military bases and defence partnerships with the US have provided Iran with another pretext for attacks against the Gulf states.”
Public opinion on the US in the Gulf has also been shifting, it says, “from security provider to strategic liability”.
Any reduction or withdrawal of US forces from the Gulf region would be portrayed by Iran “as a strategic success and vindication of its steadfastness” and would also be used “to embarrass the Gulf states about their decades-long courtship of US protection,” the report notes.
The study comes after Chris Murphy, the Democrat senator and member of the senate foreign relations committee, said a debate was under way in the US military about the value of seeking to rebuild the damaged US bases in the Gulf.
Murphy said the Gulf state leadership “want us to rebuild” and “to keep a presence in the region”, but asked: “What good is it to have a base in the region to protect American interests if within 24 hours of a hot war starting, it is wiped off the map?
“We would be criminally incompetent as stewards of taxpayer dollars if we were to rebuild bases that are blown up within hours of the next war starting.
“So clearly, we are going to have to have a smaller footprint in the region, and the limiting principle on the footprint that we rebuild will be ‘what can we protect?’ because we clearly cannot protect the scope of our footprint today and if we can’t protect it, it is useless.”
Murphy suggested that, at the very least, the US may need to relocate its bases in the eastern Mediterranean further away from Iranian missiles.

articles.title: French patrol plane spots sea drones before strike on ship off Bulgaria
articles.body:
- A French Navy Atlantique 2 detected three sea drones targeting the container ship Contship Jet off Bulgaria on Oct. 28, helping save all 18 crew.
- The ship sank the next day; Bulgaria’s navy said it could not intercept the drones, which struck in its exclusive economic zone.
A French Navy Atlantique 2 maritime patrol aircraft spotted three Russian uncrewed surface vessels heading for a civilian container ship in the Black Sea on Oct. 28 and raised the alarm, helping Bulgarian naval forces rescue all 18 crew members after the drones struck, the French military said in a post.
The Liberian-flagged container ship Contship Jet was hit about 16 nautical miles east of Cape Kaliakra, inside Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone but outside its territorial waters, the Bulgarian Navy said. The Greek-managed ship was sailing from Haifa, Israel, to Constanța, Romania, with 421 containers, some carrying fuel and other hazardous cargo. It sank the following day, Bulgaria’s maritime administration said.
The French military said the Atlantique 2, flying a routine maritime surveillance mission, detected the threat and warned the ship’s crew, passed the vessel’s position to Bulgarian authorities, helped coordinate the rescue with Bulgarian naval forces and alerted other ships in the area.
Photos released by the French military also show the Bulgarian Navy corvette Reshitelni, hull number 13, one of the ships sent to the scene.
Bulgarian Navy commander Rear Adm. Kiril Mihaylov said the French crew first saw two uncrewed boats and then a third, all heading west toward several merchant ships crossing the area, Bulgarian news site Dnes.bg reported. The first strike hit the Contship Jet at exactly noon, followed by two more, and he said the third drone was destroyed with small-arms fire. The open-source account GeoInsider said the aircraft spotted the drones about 40 minutes before they reached the ship, a figure Bulgarian and French officials have not confirmed.
The drones were traveling at about 26 knots (48 km/h), and the Bulgarian Navy said it had no forces able to react that quickly or any technical means to destroy them before impact, 24 Chasa reported. Mihaylov said the early warning likely helped save the crew. The corvette Reshitelni, the rescue ship Proteo and fast boat 223 joined the search, and all 18 sailors, 14 Filipinos and four Ukrainians, were taken aboard the Proteo and brought to Varna without injuries.
The Atlantique 2 is a twin-turboprop patrol aircraft that the French Navy uses to hunt submarines and watch surface shipping over long distances. France deployed the aircraft to Constanța earlier this month to support search and rescue after the attacks began, while a U.S. Navy P-8A Poseidon started patrolling the Black Sea at Bulgaria’s request. Their job is to detect and track threats; the decision to intercept rests with the coastal state, and the attack took place in waters patrolled by Bulgaria.
The strike was the fifth drone attack in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone this month, the Associated Press reported. On Oct. 6, sea and aerial drones hit two Turkish-owned ships about 70 nautical miles east of Byala, sinking one. On Oct. 13, drones struck two more cargo ships off Bulgaria, damaging the Ukrainian-owned Chelsea 3 and sinking a second vessel with 11 crew missing. On Oct. 23, a cargo ship capsized and sank off Romania after a drone strike, killing one sailor, and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen blamed Russia.
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev told parliament earlier this month that “the logic points” toward Russia but that Bulgaria cannot prove it. The Bulgarian Navy commander declined to say whether the drones’ course indicated where they came from or whether debris had been recovered.
The attack came as the defense ministers of Bulgaria, Romania and Turkey met in Sofia. The three NATO countries condemned the attacks on merchant shipping and agreed to strengthen intelligence sharing, early warning and coordination in the Black Sea, but did not announce new patrols or air defense measures.

articles.title: Dozens of Russian drones fell to gun turrets over Kyiv in a month, Ukraine’s Defense Ministry says
articles.body:
Automated gun turrets now serve in Ukraine’s Air Force and are destroying Russia’s jet-powered weapons, the Defense Ministry reported on 29 October. It gave no count for those jet kills, and it did not say what type of drones the turrets downed over Kyiv.
Jet drones are where Ukraine struggles most. From 1 to 26 September, Ukraine downed 55% of jet-powered drones against 90% of slower ones, partly because its interceptor drones fly at about 300 km/h, too slow to catch them. Yurii Cherevashenko, Deputy Commander of the Air Force, told a parliamentary inquiry commission on 6 October that jet-drone interceptors would arrive in the needed numbers no earlier than late November. Guns have limits too. On 5 October, Air Force spokesman Yurii Ihnat said turrets had already downed Geran-5s, but that their range is short because their main weapon is a machine gun.
Air Force turrets against jet weapons
According to the ministry, Brave1, a defense innovation cluster, began developing automated turrets in 2024. The systems have since “moved beyond the experimental stage and become an integral part of air defense,” it said. In Air Force service, the turrets are destroying jet-powered Banderol munitions and Geran-5 drones.
To scale up air defense without straining the front, Ukraine enlists business. In under year nearly 100 companies have joined, their crews downing 60-plus targets
Russia first used the Geran-5, a 6-meter jet-powered strike drone, in early 2026. The Banderol, a jet-powered cruise missile, flies at 520–560 km/h and can reach 650 km/h.
Private teams, a familiar number
Separately, the ministry said turrets have destroyed more than 60 targets within the private air defense project. The project lets companies form anti-drone teams that work under Air Force command.
Postal service Nova Post says it has already shot down Russian Shahed drones, as Ukrainian businesses take air defense into their own hands
Yet on 14 October, the ministry gave the same 60-plus total for all private teams. At the time, it named interceptor drones and heavy machine-gun turrets as their main weapons. Groups from six companies were on combat duty, about 50 groups had been formed in total, and some were still training. Nearly 100 companies had joined by then, up from 81 in mid-September.
The ministry says the project expands air defense “without placing an additional burden” on the military’s own air defense. It and Brave1 say they will keep integrating automated turrets into the air defense system.
Read also
- From making interceptors to guarding sky: Ukrainian drone maker gets its own private air defense unit and will pay for it from weapon sales
- Ukraine’s private air defense has quadrupled since spring: businesses are now shooting down Shaheds over their own sites
- Ukraine just caught a Geran-5 at 425 km/h—the jet drone that has often outrun Ukrainian interceptor drones since January

articles.title: Pentagon tells Baltic hawks to stop ‘poking’ Russia – Reuters
articles.body:
Pentagon tells Baltic hawks to stop ‘poking’ Russia – Reuters
The Pentagon has privately urged the Baltic NATO states to rein in their increasingly aggressive war of words against Russia, warning that the rhetoric is undermining European security, Reuters reported on Friday, citing sources. The reported rebuke comes as the US intensifies its diplomatic push to settle the Ukraine conflict through negotiations with Moscow.
The message was delivered by Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby, a key figure in an ongoing review of US troop levels in Europe, who advised a Baltic official against “poking” Moscow, four people familiar with the matter told the agency. Among the nations that received the warning were Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia – countries that have been more hawkish on Russia than most of their NATO counterparts.
“We are helping you. The Americans are there,” one European official told Reuters, describing Washington’s message. “Just don’t be loud. Don’t make noise.” The Pentagon also reportedly urged an Estonian delegation to be “measured” in its public communications. It is unclear whether other NATO nations received a similar warning.
One European official told Reuters that Washington’s advice was “baffling,” claiming that Baltic intelligence services have already played down the likelihood of a direct Russian assault on NATO. The Pentagon declined to comment on private communications with NATO allies.
The warning came after Baltic officials issued a frenzy of aggressive statements against Moscow. In September, Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal likened Russian President Vladimir Putin to a “rat in a corner.” Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda made similar remarks as he warned that Ukrainian strikes deep into Russia – many of which target civilian facilities – could trigger Moscow’s retaliation. The jabs came despite Moscow’s forces making steady progress on the battlefield.
Meanwhile, Latvian Foreign Minister Baiba Braze went so far as to accuse Russia of “state-sponsored terrorism” over an explosives-laden drone discovered at Germany’s Leipzig airport.
Putin denied Moscow was responsible, saying that Berlin failed to provide any proof while suggesting that the incident was linked to the country’s own domestic woes. The Russian leader has also repeatedly dismissed speculation that Moscow could attack NATO and the EU, describing it as “political schizophrenia.”
The reported Pentagon intervention comes amid US President Donald Trump’s renewed diplomatic overtures to Moscow. Following an October 9 call with Putin, Washington temporarily eased sanctions to allow Russian diesel shipments to the US and global markets, with Trump suggesting the move would alleviate pressure on American truckers and farmers.
US envoy Steve Witkoff subsequently met Putin in St. Petersburg to discuss new Ukraine peace proposals, with Moscow agreeing in principle to restart trilateral talks with Washington and Kiev in November.
Trump’s deal with Putin triggered backlash from Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky, who denounced it as a “weak decision,” prompting the US president to suggest that Zelensky should be ousted to open the path to peace. Some of Ukraine’s EU backers have also sounded the alarm over the US-Russia agreement, describing it as risky and undermining NATO unity.

articles.title: Kiev ‘ignoring’ Trump – Kremlin
articles.body:
Kiev ‘ignoring’ Trump – Kremlin
Ukraine, emboldened by continued European support, is ignoring US President Donald Trump’s calls to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries, Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov has said.
Three Russian oil refineries and a gas chemical complex were targeted in overnight attacks on Friday, according to Deputy Prime Minister Aleksandr Novak.
Commenting on the latest attacks, Ushakov told journalist Pavel Zarubin that Kiev had once again defied Trump. “I would even say they are simply ignoring him,” he added.
According to Novak, one of the targeted facilities sustained minor damage, but Russian air defenses largely repelled the attacks. Samara Region Governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said on Friday that two people involved in dealing with the aftermath of the drone strikes had been killed, while several others were injured.
Trump has repeatedly demanded that Kiev stop targeting Russian oil refineries, accusing it of worsening the global fuel crisis and driving up prices for American consumers and farmers – a sensitive issue ahead of the November 3 US midterms. Vladimir Zelensky rejected the criticism, calling Trump’s claims “totally false.”
Ushakov suggested that Kiev was emboldened by continued European support. “They would hardly have dared to do this on their own,” he said.
“Trump has been persistent on this issue and continues to be, but they are not listening,” Ushakov said. The aide noted that trilateral talks are being planned under US mediation, which he described as crucial to resolving the conflict.
Moscow agreed in principle to a fourth round of trilateral talks with the US and Ukraine following last week’s meeting between Russian President Vladimir Putin and US special envoy Steve Witkoff in St. Petersburg. The negotiations could take place in Abu Dhabi in November, with European countries not invited, according to the Kremlin.
Ukraine’s European backers have been excluded from all three rounds of trilateral negotiations so far and have increasingly sought direct participation in the peace process. Moscow has accused the EU of acting as the principal side arming Ukraine and prolonging the conflict.
Novak said on Friday that the Russian government was preparing to extend its diesel export ban until the end of January 2027, while maintaining exemptions for certain shipments to international markets.
Tankers carrying Russian diesel have been dispatched to the US under an agreement reached between Putin and Trump following their October 9 phone call. Washington temporarily waived sanctions on Russian fuel imports to facilitate the deliveries.

articles.title: Ukraine destroys Iskander-M missile launcher in Russia's Kursk Oblast, General Staff says
articles.body:
Ukraine destroys Iskander-M missile launcher in Russia's Kursk Oblast, General Staff says
Ukrainian forces struck an Iskander-M missile launcher in Russia's Kursk Oblast, along with several ammunition depots and repair facilities in Russian-occupied Ukrainian territories between Oct. 29 and Oct. 30, the General Staff said.
Ukraine struck the missile launcher near the town of Fatezh, at a site used to reload ballistic missiles, the General Staff said.
The Iskander-M is a short-range ballistic missile system that Russia uses to attack Ukrainian cities. During its overnight attack on Oct. 30, Russia launched ballistic missiles from Voronezh, Kursk, and Bryansk oblasts as part of a combined assault that mainly targeted Kyiv, Poltava, and Dnipropetrovsk oblasts, Ukraine's Air Force said.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Aug. 5 that Ukrainian forces would prioritize strikes on Russian missile launchers as Moscow steps up its use of ballistic missiles. Zelensky also said international deliveries of air-defense interceptors to Ukraine had fallen threefold from 2025 levels.
Ukraine's military also reported strikes on Russian ammunition depots in the occupied parts of Donetsk, Kharkiv, and Luhansk oblasts.
Ukrainian forces hit several other Russian military targets in occupied Luhansk Oblast, including a logistics depot near Bilovodsk, a repair unit near Rubizhne, and a repair and recovery base near Pysarivka, the General Staff said on Oct. 30.
The General Staff did not specify which weapons were used in the strikes.
The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the extent of the damage.
Zelensky said on Oct. 29 that Ukraine had carried out two missile strikes, destroying an Iskander-M missile launcher and two Russian Su-34 fighter-bomber jets.
On Oct. 29, Ukraine's Navy also struck two Russian Su-34 fighter-bomber jets at the Marinovka military airfield in Russia's Volgograd Oblast using domestically produced Neptune missiles, the Navy reported.

articles.title: U.S. Navy seeks “super intelligence” for future SSN(X) attack submarine
articles.body:
- The U.S. Navy’s SSN(X) program office asked companies on Oct. 30 to express interest in using AI to design the submarine’s internal arrangement.
- Responses are due Nov. 6, and a formal call for proposals under other transaction authority could open as early as next week.
The U.S. Navy plans to ask industry for artificial intelligence tools to help lay out the interior of its next-generation attack submarine, SSN(X), and on Oct. 30 told companies to register their interest by Nov. 6. The submarine program office said a formal call for proposals could open as early as next week.
The notice comes from Naval Sea Systems Command’s Director, Submarine Programs, acting through the SSN(X) program office, PMS 351. It is a presolicitation: companies are asked for a short, non-proprietary expression of interest giving their capabilities and whether they are a traditional or non-traditional defense contractor. The notice gives no dollar value, number of awards or schedule beyond the response deadline.
“This forthcoming opportunity will solicit competitive industry concepts to leverage Super Intelligence to advance the design of a novel SSN(X) System Arrangement Concept Design and reduce technical risk associated with its integration within a hydrostatically balanced Whole-Ship Submarine Concept Design,” the notice says.
Super intelligence is the U.S. Navy’s new official term for artificial intelligence. In October, the service issued a memo ordering all commands to use “Super Intelligence” and “SI” in place of “Artificial Intelligence” and “AI” in official documents, following President Donald Trump’s Sept. 29 announcement retiring the older term. The SSN(X) notice is one of the first U.S. Navy acquisition documents to apply it.
The work itself centers on the submarine’s system arrangement: where reactor, propulsion, weapons, sensors, crew spaces and other equipment sit inside the hull. That layout drives the hull’s size, and every change shifts the boat’s weight and center of gravity. A submarine design has to stay hydrostatically balanced, meaning its weight and buoyancy match closely enough that the boat can hold depth and trim when submerged. The U.S. Navy wants competing concepts that use AI to explore arrangements quickly and check them against that whole-boat balance before engineers commit to a design.
The U.S. Navy will run the effort as an other transaction under 10 U.S.C. § 4022, a prototype authority that skips most standard procurement rules. To use it, the law generally requires at least one non-traditional defense contractor or nonprofit research institution to take a significant part in the project, an all-small-business or all-non-traditional team, or a one-third cost share from non-government participants. The notice points vendors to those conditions, and its question about each company’s status suggests the program office expects software firms from outside the submarine industrial base to bid.
Future SSN(X) attack submarine is the planned successor to the Virginia class. U.S. Navy officials have said they want it to combine the speed and payload of the Seawolf class, the quietness and sensors of the Virginia class, and the availability and service life of the Columbia-class ballistic missile submarine. In its fiscal 2025 budget, the U.S. Navy pushed procurement of the first boat from fiscal 2035 to fiscal 2040, citing limits on its overall budget. In January 2025, the Congressional Budget Office estimated the average SSN(X) at $8.7 billion per boat in fiscal 2024 dollars, against the U.S. Navy’s own estimate of $7.1 billion, based on a submerged displacement of about 10,100 tons.
Funding has moved in the other direction since. The U.S. Navy requested $622.8 million for SSN(X) research and development in fiscal 2026, including $256.8 million for next-generation attack submarine nuclear propulsion. Its fiscal 2027 request cut SSN(X) development funding by about $121 million to roughly $315 million, Naval News reported this month, as the program shifts to settling design requirements and an acquisition strategy.
Only two U.S. shipyards can build nuclear-powered submarines: General Dynamics Electric Boat in Groton, Connecticut, and Quonset Point, Rhode Island, and Huntington Ingalls Industries’ Newport News Shipbuilding in Virginia. In July, the U.S. Navy awarded the two yards $76.6 billion to build nine Virginia-class attack submarines and five Columbia-class ballistic missile submarines, work that runs through July 2038. The U.S. Navy has warned that the delay between finishing Columbia design work and starting SSN(X) design creates a gap for the submarine design workforce. The new notice does not say how AI-generated arrangement concepts would feed into work by the two shipbuilders.

articles.title: North Korea warns South Korea with ballistic missiles as Seoul calls for talks to ease border tensions
articles.body:
Missile launches and a dispute over a landmine incident have heightened tensions between the two Koreas. Seoul is seeking military talks to prevent accidental clashes, but Pyongyang has yet to respond.
North Korea fired around a dozen short-range ballistic missiles towards the sea on Thursday, South Korea’s military said, a day after Seoul renewed its call for talks to prevent accidental clashes along their heavily fortified border.
The missiles were launched from the eastern coastal area of Wonsan at about 12.30pm local time and travelled around 250 kilometres, according to South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff.
South Korea said it had stepped up surveillance for further launches and was sharing information with the United States and Japan.
Seoul proposed military talks on 23 October to jointly verify the location of the Military Demarcation Line, which separates the two Koreas, restore military communication lines and agree measures to prevent accidental clashes.
Unification Minister Chung Dong-young renewed the appeal on Wednesday in an address read on his behalf at a forum in Goyang, near Seoul.
“South and North Korea should align their positions on the MDL through dialogue,” Chung said, calling for communication channels to be restored so the area could be managed peacefully.
North Korea has not responded to the talks proposal.
Mine blasts deepen border tensions
The offer follows landmine explosions in the Demilitarised Zone on 21 September that injured three South Korean soldiers, two of them seriously.
Seoul accused North Korean troops of planting the mines south of the demarcation line. North Korea denied responsibility and accused the South of fabricating the incident in a letter to the UN Security Council.
The US-led United Nations Command, which oversees the armistice, said a joint investigation with South Korea had identified an active North Korean mine south of the line and determined that an armistice violation had occurred.
North Korean troops have been reinforcing the border with roads, fences and landmines. South Korea says they have repeatedly crossed the demarcation line during the work, prompting warning broadcasts and warning shots.
Seoul says differing interpretations of the boundary could lead to accidental clashes. Many of the markers installed under the 1953 armistice have deteriorated or disappeared, with only about 200 of the original 1,292 still identifiable, according to Yonhap.
Direct military communication between the two Koreas remains suspended, although the command maintains a separate channel with the North Korean military.

articles.title: Russia’s naval symbol Pyotr Velikiy deemed too worn out to repair
articles.body:
- Pyotr Velikiy, a symbol of the Russian Navy and flagship of the Northern Fleet, cannot be restored, a commission has preliminarily decided, a naval support group head said.
- A final decision has not been announced; the refitted sister ship Admiral Nakhimov is expected to join the Northern Fleet by the end of 2026.
The nuclear-powered battlecruiser Pyotr Velikiy, one of the best-known symbols of the Russian Navy and the flagship of its Northern Fleet, is too worn out to repair, a Russian commission has preliminarily decided, the head of a Russian naval support organization told state news agency TASS on Oct. 30.
Vladimir Maltsev, who leads the All-Russian Navy Support Movement, said a special commission had concluded that repairing and modernizing the ship was not worthwhile, but that a final decision had not yet been announced, Meduza reported. He spoke on the sidelines of a forum marking 330 years of the Russian Navy. The Russian Defense Ministry and the Navy have not commented.
“The commission has already made a preliminary decision, the final one has not yet been announced: the cruiser cannot be restored. The ship has a certain degree of wear,” said Maltsev.
Maltsev himself said he believes the ship should be modernized if at all possible, calling the Project 1144 Orlan cruisers, known in NATO as the Kirov class, among the most successful designs in the history of shipbuilding.
The Pyotr Velikiy was laid down in Leningrad in 1986 and joined the fleet in 1998, the last of four Orlan-class cruisers and the only one to stay in active service through the post-Soviet decades. The Orlan ships are often described as the largest surface combatants ever built apart from aircraft carriers. At about 251 meters (823 feet) long and roughly 28,000 tons, the Pyotr Velikiy carries P-700 Granit anti-ship missiles and S-300F long-range air defense missiles, and it has served as the Northern Fleet’s flagship and led its major exercises for more than two decades. The ship has been laid up at a pier in Severomorsk since autumn 2022, The Barents Observer reported.
Its fate is tied to its sister ship, the Admiral Nakhimov. Russia planned to modernize the Pyotr Velikiy as soon as work on the Nakhimov was finished, so the Navy would always keep at least one cruiser of the class in service, a source in the defense industry told TASS. The Sevmash shipyard in Severodvinsk, which handles the work, can take only one of the ships at a time. The Nakhimov’s overhaul was supposed to end in 2018 but ran about eight years late, and its cost doubled to more than 200 billion rubles. By the time it neared completion, the Pyotr Velikiy’s service life had run out, according to the TASS source.
The Admiral Nakhimov left Severodvinsk for final sea trials at the end of May 2026 after nearly three decades out of service, and Russian Navy commander Adm. Alexander Moiseyev has said it should join the Northern Fleet by the end of the year. If the Pyotr Velikiy is retired, the Nakhimov will be Russia’s only nuclear-powered cruiser. The two other ships of the class, the Admiral Ushakov and Admiral Lazarev, have already been taken out of service, and Russia dropped earlier plans to bring all four back.
TASS reported plans to retire the Pyotr Velikiy in 2023, but a source quoted by RIA Novosti said the same year that there were no plans to decommission it.
Russia’s only aircraft carrier faces a similar outlook. The Admiral Kuznetsov has been under repair since 2017 and was badly damaged by a fire in 2019, and Russian media have reported that work on it has largely stopped while the Navy decides whether to return the carrier to service or scrap it. No official decision on the Kuznetsov has been announced either.

articles.title: Russia’s Geran-5 has hit 1,000 km/h in maneuvers, and Chinese engineers help develop some technical solutions for Russia’s drones
articles.body:
Russia’s Geran-5 jet drones have sped up to 1,000 km/h while maneuvering, Ukraine’s presidential adviser on defense technology Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov said in Kyiv on 29 October. He added that Chinese engineers help develop Russia’s Geran drones.
When Russia moved to faster Geran versions, Ukrainian developers had to look for new ways to intercept them, Beskrestnov said, and Ukraine must learn to stay a step ahead. From 1 to 26 September, air defenses downed only 55% of Russia’s jet-powered drones. On 29 October, one such drone hit Dnipro’s railway station, and the death toll has since risen to 15. Over the past three months, air defenses downed nearly 60% of the jet-powered Geran-4, the General Staff said on 27 October, noting a shortage of guided anti-aircraft missiles. That update gave no Geran-5 figure.
A peak well above cruise speed
That peak, about 620 mph, came during maneuvers. Ukraine’s military intelligence (HUR) puts the Geran-5’s cruise speed at 450–600 km/h. By Beskrestnov’s count, the earlier Geran-3 flew at 280–300 km/h.
Ukraine intercepts nearly 60% of Russia’s Geran-4 jet drones, General Staff says, as Kyiv races to counter evolving threat
Russia’s best engineers work against Ukraine, and China’s do too, Beskrestnov told journalists. Russia’s Alabuga drone plant sets Chinese engineers tasks such as work on the control module, he said. Key components inside Russia’s Shahed-type drones are Chinese, he said. Meanwhile, China will require licenses for Geran engines from 18 November, Ukraine’s sanctions commissioner Vladyslav Vlasiuk said. Licensing is not a ban, he stressed.
Speed is the easy part
Some interceptors are being designed to match the Geran-5’s cruise speed. US firm CHAOS Industries claims a top speed of 540 km/h for its Vespid Mk 1 interceptor. On 14 October, Ukrainian defense outlet Defense Express judged that may be enough against the Geran-5’s 450–600 km/h cruise speed.
Russia equips Geran attack drones with image-based navigation using Google map imagery, reducing reliance on satellite navigation that Ukraine can jam, defense adviser warns
Ukrainian manufacturers have already shown jet-powered interceptor drones, Beskrestnov said. But they have run into problems with control, guidance, automatic target lock, and scaling up production. A model that flies fast is only one part of the job, he said, and an easy-to-use serial product is a different question entirely.

- Russia is launching a faster Geran-5 at Ukraine that satellite jamming may no longer knock off course, a monitoring channel says
- Ukrainian OSINT channel: Russia turned a bare field into a Geran-5 launch site in a month—and drones are already arriving

articles.title: Latvia Lets Border Guards Open Fire to Defend Infrastructure From Hybrid Attacks
articles.body:
- Category
- World
Latvia Lets Border Guards Open Fire to Defend Infrastructure From Hybrid Attacks
Latvian border guards will be allowed to use weapons not only in self-defense but also to repel attacks on border infrastructure, under amendments adopted by the Saeima , LSM reported on October 29.
The changes expand the State Border Guard’s powers to respond to hybrid attacks targeting infrastructure along Latvia’s borders, according to LSM, as Russia’s hybrid campaign in Europe has included sabotage, cyberattacks, drone incidents, and pressure on critical infrastructure. UNITED24 Media documented Russian-linked operations targeting airports, defense sites, energy networks, and government systems.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Border guards will be permitted to use physical force, special combat techniques, special equipment, firearms, and service dogs to stop attacks on facilities protected by the State Border Guard or on state border infrastructure.
LSM noted that weapons may be used without warning when giving a warning is impossible in the circumstances.
Raimonds Bergmanis, chair of the Saeima Defence Commission, previously stated that protecting the state border and its infrastructure during hybrid warfare is an important part of Latvia’s territorial integrity.
The amendments also require the Border Guard to notify prosecutors immediately, and no later than 24 hours, if the use of a weapon causes injury or death.
Separate changes to Latvia’s Criminal Procedure Law provide that alleged offenses committed by border guards while performing duties under an enhanced border-security regime will be investigated by authorized State Border Guard officials.
Latvia’s enhanced border-security regime is currently in place through December 31, 2026, LSM reported.
The changes follow an incident in early October in which masked and armed escorts from Belarus attempted to push a group of migrants across the border into Latvia.
According to LSM, the armed escorts threatened Latvian military personnel while forcing the group toward Latvian territory.
Responsibility for the incident was later claimed by a little-known group calling itself “Black Rus.” Analysts cited by LSM described the group as a possible cover structure created by Belarusian and Russian security services for hybrid operations.
Latvia’s State Security Service opened a criminal investigation into the creation of a criminal organization, while the government decided on October 13 to expand the use-of-force powers available to services involved in border protection.
Latvia has faced migration pressure organized by Belarus since August 2021. Its Vilkatis operation against illegal migration, launched on August 11, was later extended through the end of 2026, according to LSM.
The changes come as Belarus continues upgrading infrastructure that could support Russian military movement toward NATO’s Baltic states. A recent report found that Belarus is modernizing railways, communications networks, and defense production along routes leading toward Latvia, Lithuania, and Poland.

articles.title: French jihadists clashes with Syrian authorities show Al-Sharaa's struggle for control - analysis
articles.body:
Clashes involving French jihadists in Syria's Idlib province highlight the continuing challenges facing Damascus as it seeks to consolidate control over the country and address the legacy of Syria's civil war. The challenge for Syria is that after the civil war ended with the fall of the Assad regime, there were still a number of extremists in Syria who did not want to lay down their arms. These are primarily foreign fighters who arrived in Syria after the civil war began in 2012. They came to fight the Assad regime, but many were also involved in global Jihadist activities and other types of extremism.
Most of these fighters refuse to go home. They are also not easily integrated into the new Syrian security forces. The camp of “French jihadists,” as it is known in media accounts, is only one example. It is in Idlib, which was the heartland of the rebel group Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS), until HTS toppled the Assad regime in 2024.
According to The New Region, a “French jihadist” was killed and a civilian injured on Wednesday when Syrian security forces confronted armed members of a group based at a camp housing French foreign fighters near Harem, close to the Turkish border.
“An internal security patrol observed an armed group leaving the French camp and heading toward the Harem area in Idlib,” the provincial internal security command told Syrian state broadcaster al-Ikhbariya, according to The New Region. Authorities said the fighters violated an agreement prohibiting them from leaving the camp while armed.
However, Kurdish media outlet Rudaw reported a slightly different account of the incident, citing Rami Abdulrahman, director of the Syrian Observatory for Human Rights (SOHR). He said masked gunmen opened fire on a vehicle carrying a French commander known as Abu Ayman al-Faransi and several other people on the road between the camp and Harem.
The identity of the attackers has not been independently established.
Syrian authorities struggle to handle foreign jihadists
Rudaw also cited testimony from a French fighter who accused Syrian security authorities of staging an ambush and confiscating surveillance equipment to conceal evidence. These allegations have not been independently verified.
The camp, according to the accounts, is associated with Firqat al-Ghuraba, also known as the Strangers Division or Muhajirun, a group led by Omar Omsen, also known as Omar Diaby, a French jihadist of Senegalese origin. The Jamestown Foundation once noted he had been called the “Spielberg of French Islamism.” It said that in France, an “unassimilated Muslim community” had Islamist “produced scores of jihadists from the Nice region.” Le Monde in France said “Syrian authorities struggle with foreign jihadists…Clashes between Syrian authorities and French jihadists entrenched in the Harem camp demonstrate the challenges the new [government].”
According to Rudaw, the fortified camp houses approximately 100 foreign fighters, as well as 25 women, 25 teenagers and 75 children. Omsen was placed on a United Nations sanctions list in 2014 over his role in facilitating the movement of foreign jihadists to Syria. He was also designated a terrorist by the United States. The group accused Syrian authorities of imposing restrictions on its movement and access to food supplies.
“For three months now, you have besieged us, imposing an embargo and stepping up surveillance. We have committed no act to justify such hostility,” the group said in a statement on Telegram quoted by Rudaw.
The group also accused Damascus of acting on instructions from France, an allegation for which no evidence was provided.
Clashes between the camp, Syrian authorities are a persistent issue
Tensions between the camp and Syrian authorities are not new. In October 2025, security forces surrounded the compound following allegations that fighters linked to Omsen had kidnapped an 11-year-old girl. The confrontation led to clashes and an agreement intended to regulate the group's activities.
The latest incident illustrates the difficulties facing President Ahmed al-Sharaa's government in dealing with foreign jihadists who established themselves in Syria during the civil war.
The foreign fighters have kept their arms and operate as their own unit and seek to run their own small area. Attempts to restrict their activities have led to clashes.
Rudaw also reported that a leader of Hurras al-Din, an al-Qaeda-linked organization, was killed in a separate airstrike earlier in the week. The group of French jihadists attributed that strike to the United States, although the account did not establish independent confirmation of responsibility.
The incidents demonstrate that the toxic legacy of foreign jihadist networks remains a significant challenge for Syria's new authorities. Damascus is attempting to rebuild international relations and demonstrate that it can control armed groups operating on its territory. However, the presence of foreign fighters, some wanted by European governments, continues to complicate those efforts.
The story is not only unfolding in Syria. In Iran the government recently sentenced a number of French ISIS members to long prison terms. This illustrates how the foreign extremist threat affected both countries.

articles.title: Russian citizen faces spying charges in Poland after photographing railways
articles.body:
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk speaks with authorities near a railway damaged overnight between Warsaw and Lublin, Poland. | Chancellery of the Prime Minister via Getty Images
A Russian citizen was charged with espionage in Poland after he was caught taking photographs of the country’s railway infrastructure, police in Lower Silesia said Friday.
Authorities said officers patrolling after a football match in Świdnica, south-western Poland, stumbled upon the 55-year-old Russian national as he was taking photographs of passing trains at an unguarded railway crossing.
“Everything indicates that the photos he took could be used against the security of the state,” the regional police authority wrote in a press release.
Advertisement
Police found a large amount of evidence suggesting that the man took pictures of strategic infrastructure systematically. “There were photographs of various places and important communication facilities, not only in Poland,” Łukasz Dutkowiak, a spokesperson for the Lower Silesian police, told Radio Wrocław.
Prosecutors are now investigating “activities for foreign intelligence against the Republic of Poland,” the regional authority added.
Poland has faced multiple sabotage attacks against its military and railway infrastructure over the past year. Prime Minister Donald Tusk accused Ukrainian nationals of “cooperating with Russian services” after a November 2025 attack damaged a rail line close to the Polish-Ukrainian border.
Fires broke out at a drone-components plant in Skarżysko-Kamienna and an aircraft-parts facility in Lublin in late August. In September, a Starlink communications station was set on fire near Warsaw.
“Russia does not even have to cross our border,” Tusk said after the September attacks. “It is already waging a hybrid war against us using drones, acts of sabotage and disinformation on the internet.”
European officials have pointed to an escalation of sabotage attacks from Russia over the past few months, as President Vladimir Putin seeks to disrupt military support for Ukraine and raise the political cost of backing Kyiv.

articles.title: Ukraine Strikes Iskander-M Launcher Inside Russia—Cutting Into Moscow’s Ballistic Missile Threat
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Strikes Iskander-M Launcher Inside Russia—Cutting Into Moscow’s Ballistic Missile Threat
Ukrainian forces struck a Russian Iskander-M ballistic missile system in the Kursk region, Ukraine’s General Staff reported on October 30. The attack directly reduces Moscow’s ability to launch ballistic strikes against Ukrainian cities.
The Iskander-M is a mobile short-range ballistic missile system designed to hit high-value targets well behind the front line.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Its transporter-launchers and support vehicles allow Russian missile units to relocate quickly, fire from dispersed positions, and move again before they can be targeted.
Ukraine’s General Staff stressed that every Iskander-M launcher destroyed reduces the Russian military’s capacity to conduct ballistic missile attacks.
The strike in Kursk was part of a broader series of Ukrainian attacks against Russian military infrastructure.
Ukrainian forces also hit ammunition depots near Maloyanisol in the temporarily occupied parts of the Donetsk, Kharkiv, and Luhansk regions.
Other strikes targeted logistics storage facilities near Bilovodsk in temporarily occupied Luhansk region, a Russian repair unit near Rubizhne, and a repair-and-recovery base near Pysarivka.
The Iskander threat has also continued to evolve. Russia used its newest 9M723-2 ballistic missile—commonly referred to as the Iskander-1000—against Kyiv for the first time during a combined strike on the Ukrainian capital this summer.
According to Ukrainian intelligence, the upgraded missile offers significantly greater range than the earlier 9M723-1 used by the standard Iskander-M system.
The most important changes include a larger rocket motor and a correspondingly enlarged launcher. Ukrainian military intelligence says those modifications increase the missile’s maximum range to roughly 550 kilometers, compared with around 390 kilometers for the earlier 9M723-1.
Previously, reports emerged that Ukraine’s intensified hunt for Russian missile systems has reportedly forced Moscow to move some launchers roughly twice as far from the Ukrainian border.
Russian forces had previously launched ballistic missiles from positions around 100 kilometers, or 62 miles, from Ukraine. That pressure has reportedly pushed some Russian systems back to positions roughly 200 kilometers, or 124 miles, from the border.
