articles.title: Ukraine to co-found defense bank aimed at financing weapons production
articles.body:
Ukraine and eight partner countries plan to sign an agreement establishing a new international defense bank on Nov. 30, potentially opening another source of long-term financing for weapons production, the governments said in a joint statement published Oct. 29.
The Canada-led Defense, Security and Resilience Bank (DSRB) aims to begin operations in 2027. It would help governments finance their defense needs, and manufacturers expand production, with benefits tied to participation in the institution.
As Russia’s war drags on, Ukraine needs sustained funding to keep its military supplied. The proposed bank could give allies another way to help finance Ukraine’s defense over the long term, supporting weapons production and military purchases.
Canadian Finance Minister Francois-Philippe Champagne said on Oct. 26 that the bank would be headquartered in Canada, with a European hub in Luxembourg. Its mandate would cover industrial expansion, critical supply chains and eligible procurement, including financing gaps affecting smaller defense companies.
read also
Reuters reported in August that the project was targeting about 100 billion euros ($111.3 billion) in capital: 20 billion euros ($22.3 billion) paid in and 80 billion euros ($89 billion) callable from members if required. The latest official statements do not specify a capital target or announce funding earmarked for Ukraine.
President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed Canada's invitation for Ukraine to become a founding member back in July in a Telegram post following talks with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney.
“It will work to attract capital and develop defense-industrial capacity and technologies tested in real combat conditions,” Zelensky said.
Alongside Ukraine and Canada, the founding group includes Albania, Belgium, Greece, Latvia, Luxembourg, Romania and Turkey.
The announcements do not specify Ukraine's contribution, borrowing terms or potential allocation. The November signing would mark another step toward establishment, rather than the start of lending.

articles.title: Shmyhal: Russia has carried out more than 350 attacks on Ukraine’s energy sector since September
articles.body:
Shmyhal: Russia has carried out more than 350 attacks on Ukraine’s energy sector since September
This was stated by First Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Energy Denys Shmyhal during Question Time with the government in the Verkhovna Rada, according to a Ukrinform correspondent.
“Since September, the enemy has carried out more than 350 strikes, damaging more than 800 units of various types at substations and power generation facilities,” Shmyhal said.
He noted that a second level of protection has now been installed for 235 transformers. At the same time, only one instance of protected equipment being hit by a ballistic missile has been recorded over the past six months.
The minister also emphasized that, without this protection, given the current intensity of Russian shelling, the restoration of energy facilities would take months.
As reported by Ukrinform, a number of Ukrainian energy companies have called on international partners to expedite the provision of assistance—particularly in the area of air defense—and to intensify sanctions pressure on Russia.
Illustrative photo: DTEK

articles.title: Germany growing weary of Zelensky’s requests for more assistance — media
articles.body:
BERLIN, October 30. /TASS/. Germany is growing more and more tired of Vladimir Zelensky’s non-stop requests for weapons and financing, Berliner Zeitung columnist Nicolas Butylin said.
"Plus a noticeable general weariness with Ukraine. We have been seeing one and the same scene for four and a half years now: Vladimir Zelensky, dressed in olive or black, either in parliament, at a conference, or via video link - and almost always asking for more weapons and money," he wrote in his column.
Since the outbreak of the Ukrainian conflict, Germany’s population has been "bearing the burden" of rising prices for electricity, gas, and food, as well as encountering its highest inflation rate in decades, while Kiev is demanding $27 billion more from the European Union," he noted, adding that whereas in 2022 such requests looked like a "cry for help," now they are perceived as an "endless cycle."
According to Butylin, the Germans have changed their opinion about sending Ukrainian citizens back to their homeland. "If, back in the spring of 2022, the Christian Social Union leader or the foreign minister had demanded that refugees from Ukraine be sent back to the frontlines, they would have been subjected to fierce political shaming," he noted, adding that now even officials often suggest this be done.
Germany is Ukraine’s largest donor, Since February 24, 2022, Berlin has provided Kiev with around 43.3-billion-euro worth of humanitarian and 57.6-billion-euro worth of military aid. In addition to official channels, various private and public German organizations regularly send humanitarian aid to Ukraine. Meanwhile, the Russian side has repeatedly stated that arms deliveries to the Kiev regime only protract the conflict.

articles.title: Italy tightens security as students, unions launch nationwide protests
articles.body:
Italy tightens security as students, unions launch nationwide protests
Rallies across the country target living costs, investment in education, and the wars in the Middle East.
Italy has tightened security as tens of thousands of students and unions took to the streets across the country.
Marches were held in dozens of cities nationwide on Friday. Rome, Milan and Naples were among those affected by the protests, which targeted soaring living costs, demanded investment in education and called for an end to the wars in the Middle East.
A large police presence was on hand, as the hard-right government tightened security measures in a bid to control potential unrest seen in Italy and other European states in recent weeks.
In Rome, security was stepped up around the Colosseum, Italy’s most visited tourist attraction, while Milan’s cathedral also received special protection.
A few skirmishes between protesters and riot police occurred at the start of a protest in Turin, with other rallies in Bologna and Genoa.
The USB trade union called for a general strike that attracted large numbers of demonstrators, including truck drivers, taxi drivers and farmers. Rallies in recent weeks have demanded an end to higher fuel prices and rising defence spending.
Unions have also issued a joint call with peers in France, Greece, Spain, Turkiye and Morocco to demand an end to the wars in the Middle East, including the war in Gaza and “an end to the militarisation of ports”.
“Ports must not be used for the transport of weapons, ammunition, military equipment and troops,” the statement said. “Dockworkers do not work for war!”
The government last week agreed on a 175 million euro ($195 million) aid package for truck drivers, farmers and fishermen hit by soaring fuel prices linked to the war in the Middle East.
The prices paid in Italy for food, energy, transport and bills have risen by 68 percent since 2000, while the average wage fell by almost 5 percent.
Measures to support young people and families – such as an annual bonus of 2,500 euros for workers under 30 – have also been inserted into the draft 2027 budget currently being discussed among the various governing parties.
“I hope this can provide answers for young people in general… who feel that the state doesn’t care about them,” Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said at a news conference on Wednesday, stressing that the measures were “not for those who smash windows”.
Following clashes over the weekend of October 17-18 between youth and police in Milan, in which groups of mainly young people looted shops and smashed windows, Meloni toughened laws on public gatherings and eased restrictions on the detention of minors.

articles.title: Houthis threaten alleged Saudi military command network in Yemen
articles.body:
SANAA, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- Yemen's Houthi group on Friday threatened to target what it described as a Saudi military command network overseeing operations across government-held areas of Yemen.
In a statement on social media platform X, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Sarea said the group had obtained information about the "operational management and field military command" of Saudi forces in Yemen.
Without providing evidence, Sarea said the network included command and support structures and operational bases in the southern port city of Aden, the oil-rich provinces of Shabwa, Marib and Hadramout, the eastern province of Al-Mahrah and the Socotra archipelago.
The claims could not be independently verified.
The spokesperson threatened that the Houthis would continue to "pursue and target" Saudi military personnel and facilities, warning civilians to stay away.
Saudi Arabia and Yemen's internationally recognized government did not respond immediately.
The statement comes as fighting has intensified between the Houthis and government forces backed by the Saudi-led coalition, alongside Saudi airstrikes in Yemen and Houthi missile and drone attacks on government-held areas and targets inside Saudi Arabia.
Yemen has been mired in conflict since late 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and much of the north, prompting the Saudi-led coalition to intervene in 2015 in support of the government. ■

articles.title: 'We don't work for war': Dockworkers strike at 113 ports across 5 continents
articles.body:
Melike Pala
30 October 2026•Update: 30 October 2026
Dockworkers in 21 countries staged strikes and demonstrations on Friday at 113 ports across five continents, protesting the use of commercial ports for military purposes.
Under the slogan "We don't work for war," more than 25 dockworkers' trade unions took part in the International Day of Action, demanding that ports serve people's needs rather than military operations, according to 902, the Communist Party of Greece's news portal.
Strikes and demonstrations were reported in countries including Greece, France, Italy, India, Türkiye, Denmark, Sweden and Germany.
In Greece, a massive strike rally took place in the port city of Piraeus, where demonstrators unfurled a large banner near the port bearing the message: "Workers do not work for war."
The mobilization also affected operations at the port of Thessaloniki, where more than 200 containers and trucks were reportedly brought to a standstill during a three-hour work stoppage.
Workers at the ports of Patras and Piraeus also staged strike actions.
In France, hundreds of workers at the port of Fos-sur-Mer, west of Marseille, joined the mobilization under banners opposing war and the militarization of ports.
In Italy, dockworkers in Reggio Calabria received support from workers and young people, who joined the mobilization with banners and pickets.
Separately, young dockworkers and apprentices in Germany staged a solidarity gathering and demonstration at the Port of Hamburg.
Sweden's Port Workers' Union voiced opposition to the militarization of European ports and warned against the use of security legislation to restrict trade union activities and put pressure on workers.
In Denmark, trade unions and federations also expressed solidarity, saying dockworkers should not be made complicit in wars or war crimes through the transport of weapons.
Dockworkers and seafarers in India joined the international action, calling for "ports of peace and jobs with dignity."
According to the No Harbour for Genocide campaign, several participating ports, including Genoa, Livorno and Gioia Tauro in Italy, Marseille in France, Piraeus in Greece and Tangier in Morocco, have been linked to weapons shipments to Israel.
The campaign said it had tracked 315 shipments of components for Israel's largest arms manufacturer, Elbit Systems, that passed through 56 commercial ports in 29 countries between August 2025 and September 2026.

articles.title: ‘A big bright lighthouse has been swept away by a murky wave’: Russian journalists, writers, and public figures react to Novaya Gazeta’s closure
articles.body:
‘A big bright lighthouse has been swept away by a murky wave’: Russian journalists, writers, and public figures react to Novaya Gazeta’s closure
For more than 30 years, Novaya Gazeta operated under constant pressure. Its journalists were threatened, attacked, and murdered; the newspaper was stripped of its media registration, and Russia’s Justice Ministry designated it a “foreign agent.” In October 2026, Novaya Gazeta was ordered to vacate its office in central Moscow and lost the ability to collect donations. Shortly afterward, its editors announced that the newspaper was shutting down.
Meduza is collecting reactions to Novaya Gazeta’s closure.
Arina Borodina
This is all unbearably painful, and there aren’t enough words for it — all we can do is sympathize and offer support however we can. Novaya Gazeta represents several epochs of our time.
Galina Yuzefovich
This morning calls for all of us to cry. I’ve spent several days writing about the markers that tell you how high the floodwaters have risen. Now another one — not just a marker, but a milestone, a big bright lighthouse — has been swept away by a murky wave. Thank you, dear colleagues. Thank you for everything. There was never anyone better than you, there’s no one better now, and there’s no guarantee there ever will be.
Katerina Gordeeva
This is a statement, not a request for help, since there’s hardly anything that can be done. The Russian authorities have killed Novaya Gazeta, a newspaper with a brilliant history, a newspaper that raised a whole generation of the country’s best journalists — and for some of them, the profession cost them their lives.
A newspaper that stood upright right to the very end — I think that’s exactly the problem.
It’s very hard to explain to anyone who never worked in the Novaya Gazeta newsroom why this place matters so much to Russian journalism, why so many journalists — even those who never worked there — considered it home. Here are three episodes where the newsroom appears. Watch them. This will never happen again.
Vera Chelishcheva
head of Novaya Gazeta’s court news desk
Now for the sad part. A symbolic coincidence of dates, for me personally: exactly 20 years ago, on November 1, 2006, I was hired onto Novaya Gazeta’s staff. And on November 9, 2026, my newspaper will no longer exist. It was stripped of its life. Stripped by a junta that treats the country as its own fiefdom.
Kirill Martynov
editor-in-chief of Novaya Gazeta Europe and former head of the politics desk at Novaya Gazeta
Today Novaya Gazeta announced its closure. A 33-year history has come to an end. For me, Novaya Gazeta was an experience of living through freedom together in an unfree country. The less freedom remained in Russia, the more we sought it out at home, at 3 Potapovsky Lane. My first piece for Novaya Gazeta was published in March 2014. It was about Ukrainian cadets in Sevastopol who sang their anthem at the entrance to the naval academy as their home was collapsing around them. My last piece ran in the paper on February 25, 2022, in both Russian and Ukrainian. I didn’t know what to call it, so I titled it “Come and See.”
Novaya Gazeta Europe issued a statement today: “We are confident that the values of the newspaper founded by Mikhail Gorbachev will still be of use to the homeland. For now, its readers remain the keepers of those values. Take care of yourselves, because one day, everything will be ‘Novaya’ all over again.”
Sergey Babinets
head of Crew Against Torture, a Russian human rights organization
They are killing Novaya Gazeta. But they will never be able to kill freedom of speech!
OVD-Info
Russian independent human rights monitor
For us, Novaya Gazeta’s journalists have been and remain examples of incredible courage and self-sacrifice in the name of democratic values. The authorities destroyed Novaya Gazeta because they could not tolerate people inside Russia who kept writing about what mattered even amid censorship and repression.
We know that Igor Domnikov, Yuri Shchekochikhin, Anna Politkovskaya, Stas Markelov, Anastasia Baburova, Natalya Estemirova, and other journalists who suffered for their work remain forever in history as examples of resilience for us and for future journalists. We know that the stories they told and the results of their investigations cannot be hidden by censorship or by beatings that leave people half-dead. We know that their unwavering commitment to their principles has inspired entire generations of Russians to remain themselves in difficult times.
Thank you, Novaya, for your work! It wasn’t in vain!
Nikolay Kavkazsky
activist, former defendant in the Bolotnaya Square case
Russian authorities have designated the paper a foreign agent and are evicting it from its premises, while banks have cut off its donations. Staff members have faced numerous instances of repression… When I was jailed in the Bolotnaya Square case, the paper wrote about me. Novaya ran a report from the press conference held after my arrest: “Beria’s Shadow in the Investigative Committee.” Novaya repeatedly gave me a platform to publish. I’m very sad that this outlet’s history is coming to an end. It’s yet another defeat for civil society and a victory for Putin’s nomenklatura.
Ksenia Sobchak
The closure of Novaya Gazeta is a gut punch. I don’t want to believe it, but I’ll have to.
Novaya is a team of brave journalists and people. For many of us, they’re a point of reference. As long as they were allowed to work in Russia, there seemed to be hope for honesty and objectivity — and hope that Muratov would come up with something, would shield them, a man who commands respect not only because he’s a Nobel laureate but because he’s done a great deal to help sick children, and that’s still something our country respects and values regardless of one’s political views. But no one is all-powerful.
The newsroom writes — and in private conversations people say the same — that they didn’t shut down, they were killed. And indeed, for the sake of journalism, free speech, and our society, people from Novaya have sacrificed their lives, more than once. As I understand it, a criminal case is now looming on the horizon, along with labels like extremism and designation as undesirable. And a Russian prison is something you wouldn’t wish on every enemy, let alone your own people — especially over politics, over words.
Someday the time will come when Novaya Gazeta returns — both to the media and to its office on Chistye Prudy.
Ilya Ber
I don’t know what to say here. Unfortunately, I don’t believe that the darkest night comes right before dawn. If anything, I know there’s no bottom.
But that a newspaper renting office space in Moscow managed to hold out — and hold out with such dignity! — through 4.5 years of Russia’s criminal full-scale war against Ukraine is a feat and a miracle. Well, that miracle has ended. But I think my colleagues’ journalistic feat will continue in one form or another.
Vitaly Mansky
Novaya Gazeta has died. Any death is a tragedy. But I think there’s an error in that formulation. It’s not Novaya Gazeta that died. What died is a country in which an independent, free media outlet opposing the war could exist. Today, such a country and such a newspaper are two mutually exclusive realities. They cannot exist in the same space, under the same jurisdiction, under the same pseudo-constitution.
So the so-called death of Novaya Gazeta — as cruel as that sounds — is merely bringing what’s happening to its logical conclusion. Strength to its contributors. Strength to Dmitry Muratov. Strength to survive and to preserve themselves individually in this nightmare.
And thank you, Novaya Gazeta, for hosting Artdocfest on its website for so many years. For the honor of being named person of the year. For putting the poster of my film Rodnye “Close Relations” on its cover just a couple of days before the full-scale war began. That will never die. And it will definitely come back someday — even if not in our lifetime…
Natalya Sindeeva
Dear Novaya newsroom, dear Dima, and every journalist, producer, engineer, archivist!! Dear readers and viewers of Novaya Gazeta!! Russian history is impossible to imagine without you — you are the most important part of these past three decades. And I’m certain you’ll find a way to keep working for all of us after a short break. We’re waiting for you!! And the darkness will lift, I believe it!
Ilya Azar
journalist, former correspondent for Novaya Gazeta
Honestly, I don’t believe Novaya Gazeta has closed for good, and I have no doubt this is temporary. There’s just one thing I want to say: I’ve worked at many newsrooms, and I’ve heard about all the rest from colleagues, and I can say with confidence that there has never been, is not, and is unlikely ever to be a newsroom better — more humane, both toward Russians in general and toward its own staff — than Novaya Gazeta, or an editor-in-chief better (more dignified and more magnificent) than Dmitry Muratov.
Dmitry Gudkov
politician, former State Duma deputy
For me, Novaya is the people I’ve spent many years alongside. Here’s one story that matters a lot to me. In 2012, we tried to stop the “Scoundrels’ Law,” which banned Americans from adopting Russian orphans. Many of the children were seriously ill, and the law was literally killing them.
Novaya Gazeta collected more than 100,000 signatures calling for the law’s repeal at the time. I invited Dmitry Muratov to a meeting of my Duma committee — the Committee on Constitutional Legislation and State-Building — to present the petition. We wanted to bring it to a plenary session, but the committee rejected the proposal. Ilya Ponomaryov, Valery Zubov, and I then used Novaya’s petition as the basis for a bill in the State Duma to repeal this barbaric law. We understood there was no chance of it passing, but we felt obligated to do everything we could to protect children whom the authorities had turned into hostages of political revenge.
Fourteen years have passed. Today, that same government is destroying Novaya Gazeta itself. I’m proud that we were together then and remain together now. Dear friends at Novaya, thank you for your work. I’m certain this isn’t the end of the story.
Alexander Arkhangelsky
The day after the birthday of Novaya Gazeta’s creator [Dmitry Muratov], it closed, stopping exactly at the line beyond which the threat of persecution becomes a guarantee.
Sergey Titov
editor-in-chief of the Russian Telegram news channel Ostorozhno Novosti
Note: this post contains profanity.
Everything that’s been happening for years now has long been a “shameful page in the history of Russian media” (and of the country, for that matter), but even by the standards of today’s dark twenties, this particular installment of the clusterfuck lands with a lot of pain. An outlet that led many good journalists to choose this profession in the first place, one that is essentially our national treasure and a source of pride, has finally been crushed.
None of this is surprising, and honestly, it’s a huge achievement that they held out for so many years — they kept going no matter what. But now they’re out of strength, and another source inside the country has been killed off, one that let people know what was really happening there, rather than relying only on the bulletins of our dear ruling party’s official bodies.
Ekaterina Fomina
journalist, former correspondent for Novaya Gazeta
The first photo shows my very first press card. I came to Novaya Gazeta at 18 and spent eight years at that newsroom on Potapovsky Lane. As of today, the paper no longer exists — Russian authorities finished it off. In truth, this had been planned for a long time. The slow killing went on for years, it’s just that in recent years, real journalism in Russia has become flatly impermissible.
Novaya and I are the same age: as I grew up, it documented what modern Russia was becoming, pointing to its ugly, terrifying flaws. Journalists who were killed, journalists who suffered attacks. All of it so that Russia’s history would be written even a little more honestly, and so the names of those responsible for evil would be named.
My eight years at Novaya were difficult — it was where I came of age as a journalist. It was real higher education, given that journalism school offered none. Watching something sacred to you be killed is hard and painful.
Boris Akunin
A few months ago, I took part in a discussion (how tiresome these have become!) about whether Russia should still be considered an authoritarian state or has already become a totalitarian one. No, it shouldn’t, my learned opponent argued. And as proof, he pointed to the existence of Novaya Gazeta: in a totalitarian state, he said, a media outlet like that couldn’t exist.
Indeed, in recent years Novaya Gazeta had looked like a strange aberration. Now everything has fallen into place. I hope we won’t have to debate this question anymore. The paper is closed, and the question is closed. And I’ll say it again. People who, while in Russia (rather than in a safe remove), behave with courage and dignity deserve enormous respect.
Thank you to them.
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.
If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at [email protected].

articles.title: ‘No food, no medicine’: Alyoshki evacuees recount Ukrainian siege (VIDEO)
articles.body:
‘No food, no medicine’: Alyoshki evacuees recount Ukrainian siege (VIDEO)
People who were evacuated from Alyoshki in Kherson Region, Russia told RT of hunger, relentless Ukrainian drone attacks, and homes being destroyed, describing how Russian soldiers brought supplies and helped them escape.
The frontline town, across the Dnieper River from Ukrainian-held Kherson, has been largely cut off from essential supplies for months. Evacuees described the targeting and destruction of vehicles carrying food and the threat of drones making even a few minutes outdoors dangerous.
“There’s nothing to eat. No medicine. Drones are constantly hovering above you,” one resident said, adding that people could barely step outside for a cigarette before another drone appeared.
He said three vehicles attempted to bring supplies in the spring. “They blew up the first one, then the second, then the third. So they wouldn’t let us get anything in.” People had to rely on vegetables from their gardens, he said, with no vehicles able to reach them.
Another evacuee, Sergey, described living without running water, electricity, and gas after flooding devastated the area. Russian soldiers and volunteers brought supplies. “That’s how we survived,” he said.
For some, escape followed the loss of family members. One woman said her husband died after encountering mines while cycling to collect potatoes. Russian troops guided her to safety using drones and a radio during a five-hour journey from her village to a hospital.
Another woman, whose husband was killed in a Ukrainian attack, described repeated bombardments that forced her to move out of her damaged home and shelter in an adjoining kitchen.
“Houses were just being blown away,” she said. Russian soldiers supplied food, drinks, and gas as residents struggled to survive.
One evacuee said Ukrainian forces were responsible for the attacks, while Russian soldiers evacuated them.
“Ukraine believes that we are traitors, that we are scum. We just want to live a normal life, a regular life,” he said, noting that soldiers shared cigarettes, canned meat, grains, and offered further help.
The humanitarian operation is underway under a temporary Russia-Ukraine ceasefire around Alyoshki. The ceasefire began on October 27 and is scheduled to continue through November 1, following mediation involving US First Lady Melania Trump.
A convoy carrying food, medicine, drinking water, hygiene supplies, and fuel for generators arrived in the town on Friday. The operation also provides the opportunity for those who wish to leave to evacuate.
Russian officials accused Ukrainian forces of obstructing deliveries and evacuations by targeting access roads and scattering mines from drones. Russian military engineers have been clearing the routes to allow the humanitarian convoy through.

articles.title: Fire Point’s FP-1 Drones Strike Russian Refinery Producing Jet Fuel for Moscow’s Military
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Fire Point’s FP-1 Drones Strike Russian Refinery Producing Jet Fuel for Moscow’s Military
Ukrainian long-range FP-1 drones struck the Novokuibyshevsk oil refinery in Russia’s Samara region, sparking a fire at the facility, Ukrainian defense manufacturer Fire Point reported on October 30.
“Ukrainian defense forces used FP-1 drones to strike the Novokuibyshevsk oil refinery in Russia’s Samara region. Multiple strikes hit the facility—which has an annual capacity of ~8.8 million tons—including its diesel hydrotreating unit,” Fire Point wrote.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Residents of Novokuibyshevsk reported explosions and Russian air-defense activity during the attack. Significant flight delays were also reported at Samara airport as the drone strike unfolded.
The Novokuibyshevsk refinery has been part of Russian state oil giant Rosneft since 2007 and can process approximately 8.8 million metric tons of crude oil annually.
The facility produces gasoline, diesel, and jet fuel, including fuel used by the Russian Aerospace Forces, as well as bitumen and petroleum coke.
The refinery has repeatedly come under Ukrainian drone attack during the war.
On April 18, 2026, another drone strike sparked a fire at the facility. The refinery later shut down its AVT-11 and AVT-9 primary crude-processing units following the attack.
Previously, Alexander Shokhin, head of the Russian Union of Industrialists and Entrepreneurs (RSPP), acknowledged that Russia cannot provide comprehensive air defense coverage for its vast industrial infrastructure, with many of the country’s largest factories and production complexes too extensive to be fully protected against Ukrainian drone strikes.

articles.title: Ukraine resumes attacks on oil refineries after pause — Russian deputy PM
articles.body:
MOSCOW, October 30. /TASS/. Ukraine has resumed drone attacks on Russian oil refineries following a pause, with three refineries and a gas chemical complex targeted on Friday, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak told reporters.
"Yes, another attack on Russian oil refineries took place today. Four processing facilities were targeted - three oil refineries and a gas chemical complex. One of the facilities sustained minor damage but overall, our air defenses and protection systems worked," he said.
"There was a pause but attacks resumed today, and our facilities are working to ensure protection," the deputy prime minister added.
US President Donald Trump said earlier that Vladimir Zelensky was not seeking a peaceful solution to the conflict, adding that Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries were negatively affecting the entire world. The US leader also described Zelensky as the wrong person for the US to deal with.
Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump held a phone call on October 9, during which they discussed, among other things, supplies of petroleum products. The Russian leader said that Moscow had reiterated its readiness to supply oil and petroleum products to the United States and global markets. Trump, in turn, commended the diesel deal with Russia.

articles.title: Dockworkers in 22 countries strike over arms shipments, Gaza war
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Dockworkers launch 'largest coordinated mobilisation' against arms shipments, Gaza war
A global dockworkers’ strike involving 113 ports began on Friday in protest against military supply chains supporting Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza- as Palestinians in the besieged territory have also rallied in support of the movement.
Organised by the dockworkers’ union coalition Dockworkers Don’t Work for War, the action has been described by activists as the largest coordinated port mobilisation of its kind.
Organisers said more than 25 unions across five continents would refuse to handle weapons shipments to Israel, staging 24-hour strikes and other actions, including work stoppages and demonstrations of varying durations.
Their demands include an end to the transportation of weapons and military equipment through civilian ports to conflict zones.
Local unions in France, Italy, Greece, Spain, Turkey and Morocco issued a joint call for an end to wars in the Middle East, including the war on Gaza, and “an end to the militarization of ports”.
No Harbour for Genocide (NHG), a pro-Palestine organisation campaigning to halt maritime transfers supporting Israel’s war, told The New Arab that its research had identified 315 consignments of components for Israel’s Elbit Systems passing through 56 commercial ports in 29 countries between August 2025 and September 2026.
NHG said many of the ports detected in its research were among those whose workers were taking part in Friday’s strike.
"The same military, shipping and oil interests driving war and genocide in Palestine, Lebanon, Yemen, Sudan, Congo, and beyond are driving fuel poverty, cost-of-living crises and unsafe conditions in our own ports and communities," a spokesperson for NHG told The New Arab.
"It helped provide examples materially backing the workers who were already moving toward action and found the information useful. The credit for today belongs to the workers themselves."
Organisers said that participation would range from full-day strikes to shorter walkouts and demonstrations, however the extent of the disruption remained unclear as industrial action and protests having been taking place across several countries.
In Greece, the ENEDEP dockworkers’ union called a strike at Piraeus, the country’s largest port, as part of the international day of action.
Additionally, protesters in Turkey's Istanbul gathered outside Haydarpaşa port beneath a banner reading: “No to war, no to armament!”
Italy’s Unione Sindacale di Base (USB) said demonstrations were planned at major ports, including Genoa, Trieste and Gioia Tauro.
In France, the CGT ports and docks federation called a one-day strike at major ports, including Le Havre, Marseille, Dunkirk and Rouen, in opposition to “the militarization of port facilities” under European policies.
"International coordination is the only way forward, and the evidence is in what workers have 
already won," the NHG spokesperson told The New Arab.
"We've seen arms vessels call at different ports once workers turn against the ship, and we've seen Maersk quietly cut ports like Fos from their weapons supply routes when the opposition there stood alone."
They continued: "Earlier this year, 26 containers of military steel were seized, and that 
would not have happened without coordinated action to reject three different MSC vessels from 
ports in Greece, Spain, Türkiye and Italy."
"The supply chain of imperialism is global, and workers have learned the lesson it teaches: it can only be materially disrupted if action is taken globally too."
The pro-Palestine maritime campaign Global Sumud Flotilla (GSF) also announced its participation, saying it would join land-based mobilisations across four continents as part of the global shutdown for Palestine.
The group said a flotilla of five vessels would operate in international waters between Sicily and Malta.
GSF added that around 20 of its activists had launched a 24-hour campaign of non-violent direct action to obstruct and challenge three major commercial vessels bound for, or servicing, Israeli infrastructure.
Prominent Spanish-Palestinian flotilla activist Saif Abukeshek told The New Arab that, as strikes take place around the world, GSF is communicating with local unions, including Italy’s USB, to offer support and amplify voices of solidarity with Palestine.
He said the group hopes to expand the movement to countries such as South Africa, India and Australia.
"I believe the message is that we are tired of continually waiting for governments to take the dignified action of ending their complicity and preventing our ports and seas from being used for war purposes and for transporting materials used in the genocide against the Palestinian people," Abukeshek said.
"People, civil society, unions, organisations and students are taking a step forward to prevent this situation from continuing."
He continued: "The message is clear. We are taking a step forward in our mobilisation and we will be adding this as part of our strategy, in addition to the sea missions and flotillas that try to break the Gaza siege."
"We will also continue mobilising through our flotillas to block ships carrying such materials and complicit in the war, as well as organising actions at sea that expose the roots of the genocide and the companies that continue to benefit from and invest in the genocide and the war."
Palestinians in Gaza back global strike
The international mobilisation has drawn support from Palestinians, particularly in Gaza, where residents and the Palestinian General Federation of Trade Unions have voiced solidarity with the movement.
On Thursday, Palestinians gathered at the fishermen’s port near Gaza City ahead of Friday’s strike, hoping to draw attention to the plight of fishermen who have faced killings, injuries and arrests during Israel’s assault on the territory.
Shaher Saad, secretary-general of the Palestinian General Federation of Trade Unions, told The New Arab that Friday’s international action reflected growing opposition to Israel’s brutal war on Gaza, which has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and injured over 175,000 since 2023, most of them women and children.
Saad also highlighted the situation facing Palestinian fishermen, who have endured destruction and been prevented from accessing the sea since Israel launched its assault.
He said his organisation firmly supported the international mobilisation, describing it as "one form of solidarity with the Palestinian people".
"We knew that many unions affiliated with the Palestinian General Federation of Trade Unions wanted to express solidarity with the Palestinian people and oppose the transfer of lethal weapons to the Israeli government, which is killing Palestinians in Gaza, the West Bank and Jerusalem."
Saad said the federation had formally backed the initiative after learning of plans for workplace strikes and protests.
"When we learned about this trade union initiative, which involved calling for strikes and protests at workplaces, we formally supported it."
The union leader stressed the importance of the action in calling for governments to intervene and impose a full arms embargo on Israel.
"This is an important form of solidarity because these weapons are being used to kill Palestinian children, women, elderly people, medical staff and journalists," Saad told The New Arab.
"All of this is happening while weapons are being transported through ports around the world to Israel, where they are used to kill the Palestinian people."
Saad confirmed that the federation was coordinating with Palestinian workers and fishermen in Gaza, while expressing hope that Friday’s mobilisation would lead to sustained international cooperation rather than remain a one-day show of solidarity.
"The workers who took part in today's strike have performed a heroic act of solidarity. They have raised their voices in support of the Palestinian people and stood alongside them," he told The New Arab.
"The Palestinian people have been deprived of their freedom. They seek to establish an independent and democratic Palestinian state, with East Jerusalem as its capital."
He added: "The Palestinian people want peace, but peace must be based on their rights and dignity, and above all on the establishment of an independent Palestinian state. It cannot simply mean concessions granted by the Israeli occupation to those it chooses."
"We do not want this occupation on our land, and there can be no lasting solution while it continues to remain on our homeland."

articles.title: Entrepreneur Māris Martinsons: we know how to spend money, but do we know how to earn it?
articles.body:
Latvia has no shortage of political promises, but it lacks a long-term strategy, the courage to make unpopular decisions, and the ability to create a business-friendly environment. This is how entrepreneur Māris Martinsons assesses the situation in Latvia in a conversation with former Foreign Minister Jānis Jurkāns and the news portal mmnews.eu. Jurkāns, meanwhile, draws attention to the constant calls for austerity: “The Russians are coming, the Russians will attack, so we must tighten our belts,” while enormous sums are allocated to security. Whether that money is being wasted or spent effectively is another question. The discussion covers government formation, the electoral success of the United List, the risks of a minority government, national debt, public passivity, bureaucracy, challenges facing the construction industry, the future of airBaltic, partnerships in big business, investment attraction, and Latvia’s economic development prospects.
The Country Waits While Politicians Celebrate
Jānis Jurkāns: The country is not exactly in danger, but it is waiting. Elections have taken place, a new government needs to be formed, yet political uncertainty continues. Surely politicians should be thinking about the country.
Māris Martinsons: I get the impression that the winners are so euphoric about the election results that the country has become a secondary concern. It’s quite simple: they announce that government formation talks are being postponed for a week. That means forming a government is not a priority. They feel so good about themselves that it is no longer their main concern.
Jānis Jurkāns: I watched how Kulbergs behaved in Brussels. He was extremely self-confident. Today, all that success has probably gone to his head, because the number is enormous: 41 seats. Latvia has never seen a result like that before. The question is how they feel internally.
Māris Martinsons: In my opinion, they feel far too comfortable. My impression is that wherever there are two Latvians, there are two political parties. The United List consists of four different groups, and that will become one of the main issues. Disagreements will begin, followed by disputes over positions.
Some MPs have never even met one another. Perhaps their first joint meeting will be the first time they all see each other.
My prediction is that ambitions will grow over time. The Prime Minister will most likely establish a new party. And that, so to speak, will be the beginning of the end.
Jānis Jurkāns: And who forms the core of the party?
Māris Martinsons: The core is already clear. But internally, people are manoeuvring against one another. Initially, they tried to attract people from other parties who might be willing to become independents. Now the reshuffling is happening within their own ranks, with people deciding who belongs to which faction.
“That alone suggests there is unlikely to be much unity within the party.”
A Minority Government: A Solution or a Dead End?
Jānis Jurkāns: What do you think about Kulbergs potentially forming a minority government and relying on Šlesers’ goodwill?
Māris Martinsons: Šlesers has indicated that he would be prepared to support a government on the condition that Unity is not part of it. Perhaps a minority government would not be the worst option in this situation. But I cannot see how they would manage to work together and deliver results with a minority government.
Jānis Jurkāns: I have never seen a minority government function successfully in Latvia.
“A minority government in Latvia is essentially a dead end, because there is always the possibility of political blackmail.”
We will see how the situation develops. But I assume that, at this point, he cannot afford to join forces with Unity.
Māris Martinsons: If they join forces with Unity, they will have betrayed their own principles. They have always declared that their partner is the National Alliance. Most likely, that is how it will turn out. And 51 votes still constitute a majority.
Jānis Jurkāns: The demands have already begun. People are openly discussing how positions will be divided, including who wants the Foreign Minister’s seat. They will start fighting among themselves, and then we will see what happens.
Māris Martinsons: I think there will be a great deal of internal disagreement. They are already acting independently of one another: each has their own political base, interests, and priorities. For now, this is not yet so apparent. But as soon as they start working on the budget and distributing ministerial portfolios, everyone will pull in their own direction.
I have never seen a government or political party from which nobody eventually broke away.
Jānis Jurkāns: That depends on whether the party is in power. In the past, nobody left Latvia’s Way because it was in power, distributing positions, and people stayed together. Even today, it is difficult for an independent MP to act against the mandate given to them by voters. So, in my opinion, the United List could function quite well for a while. What do you think?
Māris Martinsons: Everyone looks after their own interests first. That is how it has always been, and how it will remain. Kulbergs was Prime Minister for a few months, but that was merely a warm-up.
“The real test will come when they have to prepare a budget, make promises to everyone, and then actually deliver on them.”
And that is far from simple, because the country is facing a more serious crisis than many people realise. Latvia’s external debt continues to grow, and we are planning to borrow even more.
Debt Keeps Growing, While We Strive to Be Model Europeans
Jānis Jurkāns: Why have neither finance ministers nor prime ministers so far attempted to discuss postponing debt repayments or restructuring the debt?
Māris Martinsons: We are too rigid in our decision-making. We are among the most exemplary countries when it comes to complying with European Union requirements.
“We want to meet every criterion, and sometimes it seems that this matters more to us than the well-being of our own people and the interests of our country.”
Latvia can, in a sense, be compared to one large company. If we cannot manage it properly, even in terms of ensuring people’s well-being, that is a major problem.
Jānis Jurkāns: Let’s assume the money is available and the government borrows it. Where should it be invested? Which sectors should be developed?
Māris Martinsons: That is precisely the biggest problem: we have no strategy. First and foremost, we need to improve people’s standard of living. Secondly, healthcare and education reforms. So far, these have largely been empty words.
Unpopular decisions must be made, for example, regarding health insurance. A system had been developed, but because people did not like it and elections were approaching, nothing was done.
It will be interesting to see how the Prime Minister reacts when he comes under pressure from his own party and ministries demanding more budget funding, and he has to say no.
“Right now, we are spending more than we earn. And we are covering the difference through borrowing.”
Why Latvians Do Not Take to the Streets
Jānis Jurkāns: How much patience do people have? There are problems in healthcare, education, and elsewhere, yet nobody takes to the streets in sufficient numbers to force the government to listen. Look at what happens in France. How long will Latvians simply keep tightening their belts and accepting everything?
Māris Martinsons: Historically, Latvians have been an extremely resilient people. They wait and keep hoping that something will change.
In Italy or France, people express their dissatisfaction much more actively. In France, there is a strike almost every week. Society actively voices its dissatisfaction and demands change.
Jānis Jurkāns: France has a different political culture. They have trade unions. Do we have trade unions?
Māris Martinsons: In theory, yes. But you hardly ever hear anything about them. And that is a problem.
In Construction, Everyone Fights for Themselves
Jānis Jurkāns: Construction is one of your businesses. Do construction workers have a trade union?
Māris Martinsons: Historically, the largest construction companies came together and reached a sector-wide collective agreement on wages. That was a significant achievement.
But today, businesses are largely fighting for themselves. Industry organisations are gradually losing influence. That is one of our biggest problems. And that is also why we do not really have functioning trade unions.
Jānis Jurkāns: Every industry should also play a role in improving legislation. Who are the construction industry lobbyists who go to Parliament and say: this law doesn’t work, this one needs to be changed?
Māris Martinsons: Historically, the largest construction companies were members of the Latvian Construction Contractors’ Partnership (renamed the Latvian Construction Contractors’ Association in 2022 — Ed.). Over time, however, the major construction companies have withdrawn from the organisation.
Communication with government institutions continues, but in my opinion, the industry’s representation of its interests is very weak.
“In Latvia, lobbying is often perceived as corruption or a violation of competition rules.”
I get the impression that Latvia’s large construction companies have lost the role they once played. Today, medium-sized companies dominate, and sometimes it seems as though the country no longer needs large businesses at all.
Jānis Jurkāns: What about skilled workers in the industry? Is there a shortage of welders?
Māris Martinsons: That is a very serious problem. If we look at the volume of construction activity in Latvia, we can no longer meet demand using only the domestic workforce.
We have to accept that recruiting foreign workers is necessary if we want projects to be completed to a high standard and on schedule. That is a reality we cannot ignore.
The Kulbergs Phenomenon
Jānis Jurkāns: What do you think explains the success of Andris Kulbergs and the United List?
Māris Martinsons: A new face emerged: someone who made people believe that change was possible in this country. Many factors and coincidences contributed to that.
Even today, a large proportion of voters cannot distinguish between the Union of Greens and Farmers (ZZS) and the United List. When they go to the polls, they see the name Kulbergs and tick the box.
Secondly, voter turnout was very low. People do not believe that anything will change, and they do not want to waste their time.
It is difficult to assess Kulbergs after just a few months as Prime Minister. Compared with his predecessors, he stood out, and people liked that. Looking at the people involved, some new faces have emerged, and perhaps that is a good thing.
“But fundamentally, nothing has changed. Essentially, they are the same people, just in different roles.”
Security: A Slogan Used to Justify Everything?
mmnews.eu: In your opinion, what should be the main priorities in the new government’s policy declaration, apart from national security?
Jānis Jurkāns: Security is the moment when people are told to tighten their belts. The Russians are coming, the Russians will attack, so we must tighten our belts, and enormous amounts of money are allocated to security. Whether that money is being wasted or spent effectively is another question.
“Security is a very convenient slogan for any government to justify financial problems.”
Māris Martinsons: I agree with Jānis. Who is going to vote against the defence budget? Security is a priority today, and that is why many people exploit the issue. But we sometimes include expenditure under the security budget that has no direct connection to security. Meanwhile, there is not enough money for healthcare and education.
We are exemplary in our commitments to NATO and the European Union, yet education reforms are lacking and healthcare is struggling. It cannot be right that we find money for one area while others remain underfunded.
I believe everything needs to be balanced. And most importantly, it is not enough for the state simply to spend money. The state must also think about how to generate revenue.
We Could Cut the Number of Civil Servants by Half
Jānis Jurkāns: This is something I keep coming back to: how are we going to make money in Latvia?
Māris Martinsons: First, we need to put our own public administration in order. Ministries and various government agencies have overlapping functions. We have an enormous administrative apparatus. Has anyone genuinely assessed how much of it is actually necessary?
“I believe we could cut the number of civil servants by as much as half, and nothing significant would change in how the state operates.”
We live in an age when technology and artificial intelligence make it possible to automate a great many processes. For example, if someone submits all the required documents and they comply with the regulations, why should the decision depend on the subjective judgement of an individual civil servant?
The more such subjective decisions there are, the greater the risk of bureaucracy and potential corruption.
Jānis Jurkāns: But civil servants need jobs too.
Māris Martinsons: That raises an interesting question about artificial intelligence and its impact on employment.
There is even a philosophical theory that, in the future, artificial intelligence could generate such enormous economic value that it might be more beneficial for society to provide benefits to some people rather than employ them.
I am not saying that is what we should do. It is simply one possible scenario worth discussing.
Jānis Jurkāns: Nevertheless, every normal person wants to be employed. Whether they work from home or in an office, people want to have a job.
Corruption: Years Without Progress
Jānis Jurkāns: Kulbergs has spoken about fighting corruption. Latvia’s position in international rankings has been disappointing for years, and everyone knows it. So I would like to understand what he has actually done about it.
Māris Martinsons: That really is an interesting question. Year after year, those rankings show us standing still. We appear to be fighting everything at once, yet at the same time, achieving nothing.
airBaltic: It Must Be Saved, but First We Need to Define the Goal
mmnews.eu: Turning to airBaltic, how do you assess the government’s handling of the company?
Māris Martinsons: First, we need to clearly define the objective. What do we, as a country, want from this airline? What role do we expect it to play in the economy, tourism, and international connectivity? Has anyone actually assessed tourist flows?
We keep talking about losses, but nobody has clearly explained why airBaltic continues to lose money.
Jānis Jurkāns: There is another aspect: the political one. I know two Latvian brands that are recognised internationally: airBaltic and Latvijas balzams. I’m not joking. That is why airBaltic should be saved, if only as a national brand. I don’t know exactly what should be done, but we must not let it go under.
Māris Martinsons: I completely agree. It is one of the things Latvia can be proud of. Neither Estonia nor Lithuania has anything quite like it.
I believe we should keep airBaltic alive for as long as possible. A former business partner of mine once said: don’t just think about spending money; think about how to earn more. In my opinion, that applies perfectly to airBaltic as well.
Perhaps it would be worth considering turning it into a kind of people’s airline.
“I think many people would be willing to get involved, offer support, and even donate money to keep airBaltic alive.”
But first, we need to understand why the company is making losses and how to eliminate them. If we can afford to pay the head of an organisation a substantial salary, we can just as easily bring in world-class experts to identify the causes and recommend solutions.
And one more thing: no politician wants to deliver bad news before an election. That is why I believe airBaltic will soon become one of the main issues on the political agenda.
The situation with Latvijas balzams is very similar. But that is another story.
Šķēle, Shefler, and Partnerships in Big Business
Jānis Jurkāns: Have you been following the relationship between Shefler and Šķēle? They used to be close friends, but now there is a conflict between them. I haven’t looked closely into what caused it. But I’ve noticed that in big business partnerships, one partner often eventually tries to get rid of the other. It’s better to be on your own than to have someone constantly breathing down your neck. Is that how it works?
Māris Martinsons: I actually think the opposite. A partnership is about sharing risks while also bringing additional value. The question is whether responsibilities are properly divided. That is a matter of corporate governance.
When it comes to Shefler, he essentially wants to do everything himself. He owns one of the world’s largest vodka brands and runs it himself, without bringing in world-class specialists.
“If someone wants to manage everything personally, they cannot be an expert in every field.”
Jānis Jurkāns: He is impulsive. He likes to show off.
Māris Martinsons: He is capable of organising any event on a grand scale. But at the same time, he can make one decision today, change his mind tomorrow, and come up with a third decision the day after. That is his biggest mistake. There was no shortage of potential buyers, but in my opinion, it was precisely this inconsistency in decision-making that made reaching an agreement difficult.
Why Should Investors Choose Latvia?
mmnews.eu: Judging by the headlines, a great deal seems to be happening in investment attraction: business missions to Germany and the United States involving dozens of Latvian companies. But compared with neighbouring countries, the question arises whether Latvia is competing successfully enough for major investors. What should the government do differently?
Māris Martinsons: First and foremost, we need to create an environment where investors actually want to come and do business.
We must not forget that there is a war taking place close to our borders. Many investors from Europe and Scandinavia are cautious about this region. They have adopted a wait-and-see approach and do not believe they should take unnecessary risks.
That is why Latvia must be able to offer something that outweighs those risks: faster decision-making and less bureaucracy. There are countries where governments can respond to a crisis within a few months, whereas our bureaucratic system is so cumbersome that even a simple decision takes an extremely long time.
We need to ask ourselves a simple question: why should an investor choose Latvia over another European country?
Can we name even one reason why we are better than other countries in Europe?
“The only thing we have going for us is that we are members of the European Union and NATO. Beyond that, there is nothing.”
Jānis Jurkāns: We also pride ourselves on having an educated workforce.
Prohibit or Regulate?
mmnews.eu: You have also criticised Latvia’s approach to business regulation. What do you think should change?
“We have a tendency to prohibit things rather than create opportunities.”
Māris Martinsons: For example, we talk about banning casinos or introducing various restrictions on electronic cigarettes. But a ban does not necessarily mean that people stop using a particular product or service.
They simply find other ways to obtain it. As a result, we may end up encouraging the illegal market and losing tax revenue.
I believe that in many cases, we should focus on sensible regulation and tax policy rather than automatic bans.
For example, if someone wants to buy cigarettes, the government can impose a high tax and use the revenue for public needs. But bans alone will not solve the problem.
Why do we keep making the same mistakes over and over again?

articles.title: How the record-breaking $6.3 billion heist in crypto history unfolded
articles.body:
How the record-breaking $6.3 billion heist in crypto history unfolded
Hackers stole $6.3 billion in cryptocurrency from Binance in a record-breaking heist, prompting issuers to freeze roughly half of the stolen assets. The breach, which US analysts suspect was done by North Korean hackers, has shaken confidence in the crypto market.
Hackers stole $6.3 billion from Binance, the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange, in a record digital asset theft.
Here's what we know so far:
What happened ?
About $6.3 billion of cryptocurrencies were drained from wallets that Binance uses to process transactions, according to the exchange and expert analysis of blockchain records.
Read moreBinance hit by $6.3 billion security breach in potential record crypto heist
Binance said in a statement on X that it initially thought the attack involved a compromised laptop. "However, our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach," it added, without elaborating.
The exchange operates a secure asset fund for users, a $1 billion bitcoin reserve designed to protect customers in the event of a security breach, according to its website.
Co-CEO Richard Teng said losses would be covered by the fund and company resources.
According to US blockchain analytics firm TRM Labs, the attackers compromised Binance's "signing infrastructure", which authorizes transactions, allowing them to issue instructions that emptied the affected wallets.
The bulk of the heist unfolded in about 20 minutes, blockchain records show, beginning shortly after 2000 GMT on Thursday.
Once the funds were moved, the attackers raced to shift them beyond the reach of Binance counterparties and stablecoin issuers, which have frozen roughly half of the stolen assets.
An unusual feature of some cryptocurrencies, including major stablecoins such as Tether's USDT and Circle's USDC, is that their issuers can freeze them remotely.
"In layman's terms, the attacker may not have stolen the vault key, they may have hijacked the system that tells the vault to release money," said Joshua Chu, a Hong Kong lawyer who works on crypto cases.
Who's behind it?
Several US blockchain analysis firms said the attack bears similarities to previous operations attributed to North Korean hackers.
Teng said Binance's investigation had not yet identified the attackers, while North Korea routinely denies involvement in cyberattacks and cryptocurrency thefts. North Korea's mission in Geneva and embassy in China did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
TRM said the breach shared characteristics with last year's attack on crypto exchange Bybit, which the FBI attributed to North Korean hackers. The firm said it was highly confident the same group was behind the Binance theft.
Chainalysis said funds stolen in an attack last month on Bitget were being mixed with proceeds from the Binance breach.
Where's the money?
About half the stolen assets were stablecoins that have since been frozen by issuers including Tether, Circle, Ripple and World Liberty Financial, the Trump family's crypto venture.

One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
That doesn't mean the coins will be returned to Binance, but it significantly limits the attackers' ability to convert them into cash.
TRM said some of the funds had already been posted as collateral to borrow ether and estimated that about $2.4 billion worth of bitcoin and ether is beyond reach.
"No company issues bitcoin or ether and no company can freeze either one," said Patrick Tan, general counsel of ChainArgos, a blockchain intelligence firm in Singapore.
"The bitcoin and ether can be stopped only if the attacker sends them to a crypto-asset exchange or broker that is able and willing to freeze them, or if law enforcement obtains the private keys."
Market participants said the attackers would likely mix the stolen coins with other assets or use lesser known coins and exchanges to try to move the proceeds.
"The more time passes, the less likely they will be able to fold those funds into other exchanges or payment providers – they essentially get blacklisted," said Bernardo Brites, CEO of Trace Finance, a stablecoin infrastructure company.
"In reality a lot of the proceeds of hacks ... (can only be laundered) in the first few hours, but after that happens, you have a lot of different players who know those are marked funds ... and they usually sit there for years."
What next?
The theft is the latest in a series of major digital asset breaches. Attackers stole $2.9 billion of cryptocurrency across nearly 150 incidents last year, according to TRM Labs.
The attack has also rattled confidence in the sector. Cryptocurrencies fell on Friday and the total market value of stablecoins declined, suggesting investors were pulling money from digital assets.
(FRANCE 24 with Reuters)
