articles.title: UN finds Israel persecuted Palestinian children based on age. Can justice follow?
articles.body:
The deliberate killing and injuring of Palestinian children in Gaza and the occupied West Bank by Israeli forces amounts to age-based persecution, a United Nations commission of inquiry has found.
In a report presented on Monday to the UN General Assembly, the Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including East Jerusalem, and Israel concluded that Israeli forces had persecuted Palestinian children on the basis of age in the occupied West Bank, extending its earlier finding on Gaza.
The commission said the repeated attacks and severe physical and psychological harm inflicted on children were part of a broader pattern of intentional violence.
Persecution as a crime against humanity entails a severe deprivation of fundamental rights on discriminatory grounds, according to Nasir Qadri, an international law practitioner and critical legal scholar at Koc University.
“Age-based persecution applies that discriminatory ground specifically to children as a group. In this context, their age was the basis for the use of lethal and injurious force against them, rather than children simply being part of the population caught up in a military campaign,” Qadri tells TRT World.
“War crimes require proof of specific prohibited acts, while genocide requires proof of the intent to destroy a group as such,” he adds.
“Persecution falls into a different legal category. It requires a widespread or systematic attack, a severe deprivation of rights, and discriminatory intent directed at the group being targeted.”
“The Commission found all three, with age as the discriminatory ground, across the occupied Palestinian territory as a whole. The West Bank finding extends a conclusion previously confined to Gaza. Age-based persecution is now the Commission’s determination for both,” he says.
The commission investigated seven cases involving killings and serious harm to Palestinians in the occupied West Bank between November 2023 and June 2026, and documented six.
In most cases, the victims were children, including an infant. The commission found that they were unarmed, posed no imminent threat, and were targeted without warning, often in the head or upper body.
It concluded that Israeli soldiers intentionally killed the victims, despite being in a position to recognise that they posed no immediate danger.
In one case, an Israeli soldier fired on a car carrying a Palestinian family in Hebron on June 5, 2026, killing a seven-month-old baby with a shot to the head and injuring both parents.
Video footage showed the father slowing down, stopping the car and raising his hands as he approached the soldiers.
The Israeli army said the soldier had fired because the vehicle was accelerating towards them, but the commission found that the soldier had a clear, unobstructed view of the occupants from a distance of about 10 metres. The family received no medical assistance.
In another incident, a 14-year-old Palestinian boy was shot in the chest and killed near the entrance to Jenin refugee camp on September 8, 2025.
Israeli forces had closed the camp in January, displacing its residents.
When rumours spread that troops might be withdrawing, around 50 to 60 residents went back to check on their homes. Israeli forces arrived by vehicle and opened fire without warning, killing the boy.
What is age-based persecution?
Persecution is a crime against humanity under international criminal law. It involves the intentional, severe deprivation of fundamental rights because of a person’s identity or membership in a particular group, with discriminatory intent.
Age-based persecution applies this legal framework to harm inflicted on people because of their age.
Not every killing or injury of a child automatically amounts to persecution. The legal determination depends on the severity of the harm, evidence of discriminatory intent, and the broader context in which the acts took place.
In the case of Palestinian children, the commission concluded that the attacks’ recurrence and widespread nature revealed a pattern of intentional violence, rather than children merely being caught up in military operations.
The legal finding depends on the nature and severity of the harm, evidence of discriminatory intent and the wider context in which the acts took place.
The report also found that Palestinians in the occupied West Bank were being targeted on the basis of their nationality, race, ethnicity, gender and age.
Qadri points to the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia's (ICTY) Kupreskic case, which examined the persecution and killing of Bosnian Muslim civilians during the 1993 attack on Ahmici, Bosnia and Herzegovina.
“In the Kupreskic case, the ICTY established that discriminatory intent can be demonstrated through the cumulative effect of acts that may appear ambiguous when viewed individually, but which reveal a pattern when considered alongside an established policy,” Qadri says.
In other words, discriminatory intent need not be established by any single incident if the evidence as a whole demonstrates a pattern.
“The Commission found that Israeli forces applied permissive rules of engagement exclusively against Palestinians, concentrating lethal force on children approaching designated lines, as part of a coordinated attack across the occupied Palestinian territory,” Qadri adds.
A wider pattern of violence
The report describes a sharp deterioration in the human rights situation in the occupied West Bank since October 7, 2023, as Israeli forces' attacks and sustained settler violence have increasingly endangered Palestinian civilians.
The scale of lethal force has changed dramatically. According to the commission, six Palestinians were killed by air strikes in the occupied West Bank between 2008 and October 6, 2023.
Between October 7, 2023, and September 30, 2026, air strikes killed 254 Palestinians.
The commission concluded that Israeli military operations and settler violence were part of a widespread, systematic attack on Palestinian civilians in the occupied West Bank.
It also linked the violence to territorial expansion and displacement.
Israeli military operations since January 2025 have led to the largest displacement of Palestinians in the occupied West Bank since 1967, with 34,176 people still displaced as of August 2026, according to the report.
The findings add to a growing body of evidence concerning alleged and established violations of international law against Palestinians. But documenting crimes and securing accountability remain separate challenges.
“The ICC Pre-Trial Chamber’s arrest warrants for Netanyahu and Gallant mean that the situation in Gaza is already part of active proceedings. The Commission’s finding of age-based persecution could also provide evidentiary material for the Office of the Prosecutor as it builds its case,” Qadri says.
“The ICJ is continuing to hear South Africa’s case under the Genocide Convention, and the Commission’s findings on the West Bank add to the factual record the Court can consider when assessing Israel’s compliance with its January 2024 provisional measures order.”
“So the legal avenues are already open and active. The main obstacle is not jurisdiction, but enforcement,” Qadri adds.
Accountability efforts
The commission's conclusions go beyond documenting individual abuses.
By classifying the deliberate killing of Palestinian children and the serious physical and psychological harm inflicted on them as age-based persecution, the commission has identified this conduct in both Gaza and the occupied West Bank as a crime against humanity.
The report also found that Israeli authorities and forces continued to commit genocidal acts in Gaza after the October 2025 ceasefire, with the intent to destroy Palestinians, in whole or in part.
In the occupied West Bank, it documented other crimes against humanity, including extermination, torture, rape, and other forms of sexual violence.
The commission called on Israel to end its unlawful occupation of Palestinian territory, remove settlements and settlers, reverse the confiscation of Palestinian land, and return seized property to its owners.
“Under Article 41 of the Articles on State Responsibility, all states must refrain from recognising as lawful situations resulting from serious breaches of peremptory norms of international law, and must cooperate to bring those breaches to an end,” Qadri says.
“States that continue to provide military, financial or political support to Israel in the face of this evidence may also face legal consequences. The Commission made clear that states must use all means available to prevent and punish genocide and cooperate with the ICC.”
“When states choose not to act despite the evidence available, that is a political choice. The Commission has already set out its legal assessment,” he adds.
As of September 30, 2026, the commission was unaware of any effective investigations, disciplinary proceedings, or judicial measures in the cases it had examined.
Even in four cases where Israeli authorities acknowledged mistakes, the victims' families had received no remedy.
The commission warned that this lack of accountability had helped entrench a discriminatory system in which violations against Palestinian children were repeatedly committed with impunity.

articles.title: Economic Watch: AI takes on bigger role in China's express delivery during Singles' Day peak
articles.body:
BEIJING, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- A drone hovers overhead, calibrating its position as a smart locker below opens its double doors. A package is lowered precisely into the compartment before the doors close. Later, a customer collects it with a code, with no courier on site.
Scenes like this are becoming common during this year's Singles' Day shopping rush, as China's express delivery industry pushes artificial intelligence (AI) deeper into frontline operations. From sorting centers to last-mile delivery, delivery companies are deploying intelligent agents, robots and predictive models to streamline the entire delivery chain.
The Singles' Day shopping festival, also known as Double 11 because it falls on Nov. 11, is China's annual online shopping carnival and one of the world's biggest retail events.
The most visible change this year is that AI is no longer confined to back-office analytics. STO Express, one of China's major couriers, has deployed AI "digital employees" through its SClaw intelligent-agent platform. The system can assist with customer inquiries, intercept abnormal shipments, plan trunk-line routes and help couriers make outbound calls and optimize delivery sequences. A digital quality-control system is also flagging risks for fresh produce and other sensitive parcels.
"The core change at STO Express this year is using AI computing power to take on part of the frontline physical workload, while proactive services help absorb peak pressure. We are raising efficiency without compromising safety, ensuring the entire network can steadily handle this prolonged peak season," said Luo Jian, who oversees Double 11 operations at STO Express.
Beyond frontline support, delivery companies are using intelligent decision systems to improve resource allocation. JD Logistics, the logistics arm of Chinese e-commerce giant JD.com, has rolled out its upgraded Super Brain 3.0 large model as a decision-making hub, forecasting order volumes by region and adjusting nationwide logistics capacity in real time. The company said AI-recommended delivery routes have an adoption rate of more than 90.2 percent.
In specific operational scenarios, logistics robots are expanding their reach. JD Logistics is deploying embodied intelligent robotic arms at scale in sorting centers, and the arms have achieved a parcel tracking accuracy rate of 99.9 percent. Drones are also delivering to remote villages in southwest China, where mountainous terrain and river crossings have long made last-mile delivery difficult.
AI applications are also extending into broader supply-chain management. SF Express is using sales forecasts and digital supply-chain tools to move inventory closer to consumers in advance, shortening the last-mile delivery distance. YTO Express has embedded more than 100 intelligent agents into route optimization, dispatch analysis and customer-service workflows, and put 28 digital employees to work in operations and customer service. Digital-twin systems now cover its entire network of consolidation hubs.
The changes are not limited to the logistics chain itself. Zhang Yi, vice-president of the Guangdong Internet Society, said AI applications are now used across the entire e-commerce operation cycle, from product selection and content creation to traffic acquisition, customer service and competitor analysis.
This shift is reflected in the latest data. A recent report by the China Federation of Logistics and Purchasing showed that AI adoption in China's logistics and supply chains had exceeded 37 percent, with transport at 78 percent, safety and compliance at 52.73 percent, and smart warehousing at 47.27 percent.
China's express delivery sector handled 151.3 billion parcels in the first nine months of 2026, up 4.3 percent from a year earlier, according to the State Post Bureau. The scale of the market continues to provide diverse real-world scenarios for AI deployment across the logistics chain.
Hu Dajian, vice-president of the China Federation of Logistics and Purchasing, said AI is shifting from isolated applications to whole-chain coordination, extending from single enterprises to broader industrial-chain collaboration.
This whole-chain push is backed by national policy. The deployment comes as China promotes deeper integration of AI into the real economy. In 2025, China released a policy document to advance the "AI Plus" initiative, setting out goals and priorities for integrating AI across the economy and society.
As these efforts take hold, industry observers said the broad commercial rollout of AI, from drones and unmanned vehicles to robotics and digital employees, has become a major highlight of this year's Singles' Day shopping peak, signaling that the next competitive edge will come less from scale than from AI embedded across the entire operational chain. ■

articles.title: Strike on Donetsk on August 26: Chief of Engineering Troops of Russia’s Central Military District Was Killed
articles.body:
In Donetsk, Colonel Andrey Romanchuk, chief of the engineering troops of the Russian Federation’s Central Military District, was killed in a strike on a command post.
This was reported by researchers from the KIU project, who track casualties among Russian Army officers, and the publication Vesti Nizhny Novgorod.
According to available data, the high-ranking Russian officer was killed during shelling of the headquarters in occupied Donetsk on August 26.
Romanchuk had previously participated in the Russian Federation’s military operation in Syria, for which he received state awards.
The Central Military District is an operational-strategic territorial unit of the Armed Forces of the Russian Federation, covering the territories of the Volga, Ural, and Siberian federal districts, with its headquarters in Yekaterinburg.
It is the Russian Federation’s largest military district by area, covering about 40% of the country’s territory and responsible for ensuring security in central Russia and in Central Asia.
As a reminder, journalists identified the names of at least 20 Russian Federation Army officers who were killed in a missile strike on Donetsk.

articles.title: US oil giants report profit surge again on Iran war
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
US oil giants report profit surge again on Iran war
US oil giants reported Friday another quarter of soaring profits reflecting higher oil prices and refining margins due to the US-Israeli war on Iran.
ExxonMobil's profits in the period came in at $15.4 billion, slightly more than double the $7.5 billion in the year-ago period, while Chevron's profits were $9.9 billion, compared with $3.5 billion in the year-ago quarter.
The surge in US petroleum earnings comes on the heels of similar increases at European companies as the US-Israeli war on Iran drags on. The impacts have been most dramatic in refining, where the profit margins for processing crude oil into gasoline, diesel and other petroleum products have exploded in recent months.
Steep price increases and supply shortfalls in some cases have sparked protests in parts of Asia, Latin America and Europe. In the United States, President Donald Trump's Republican party faces a stern test in next week's midterm elections, with high gasoline and diesel prices souring the mood of consumers.
At ExxonMobil, oil prices averaged around $85 per barrel during the period, about a third more than in the 2025 quarter.
Refining margins were $50.3 per barrel, almost three times the level in the year-ago period as the company cited efforts to boost output of diesel and other key products that have seen supplies tighten.
"Refining capacity in Russia and the Middle East remained curtailed, with roughly 10 percent of global capacity offline," the company said in prepared remarks ahead of a conference call.
"North American refineries sustained high operating rates during the quarter but were unable to fully offset reduced global refining capacity availability," according to the remarks.
The efforts to boost output translated into 100 percent crude unit utilization at US Gulf Coast refineries, ExxonMobil said in its press release.
Chevron scored higher profits in its upstream business, but also won its greatest increases in the downstream area, where profits of $4.9 billion were more than four times the level in the year-ago period.
The NGO 350.org, which advocates for clean energy and other measures to address climate change, called for "permanent levies" on "exceptional" oil industry profits, with the funds going to consumers and to finance the energy transition.
"As we head into the midterms, energy affordability is on everyone's minds," said Candice Forten, US campaigns manager for 350.0rg.
"Families and small businesses want reliable electricity they can afford, and communities want a say in how their land, water and energy resources are used," Forten said. "Yet as people struggle with energy bills and the impacts of extreme weather, the biggest oil companies are forecast to make billions."
Forten called for policies to ensure that data centers for artificial intelligence do not drive up electricity bills and that oil companies "pay their fair share towards the costs of the crisis, rather than leaving the public to pick up the bill."
Shares of ExxonMobil rose 2.0 percent in pre-market trading, while Chevron climbed 1.7 percent.

articles.title: Former Palestinian prisoners are being abused, taken by Israel
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
One year on since freedom, former Palestinian prisoners in the West Bank are being re-arrested and abused by Israel
Israa Nasrallah never imagined that the release of her husband, 35-year-old Bakr Khreiwesh, in the most recent prisoner exchange deal last October 2025 would be followed by continued harassment and his re-arrest.
21 August brought an unpleasant surprise to Isra and her husband; their home in the city of Tulkarm in the occupied West Bank was raided by the Israeli army. Once again, her husband was taken under "administrative detention", a practice that allows for indefinite imprisonment without charge or trial, repeatedly renewed.
The Palestinian Prisoners' Club has warned that Israel has been re-arresting, harassing, and interrogating at least 80 former Palestinian prisoners who have been released as part of previous exchange deals between Hamas and Israel.
In a statement, the organisation noted that these security and judicial measures prevent former detainees from resuming their normal lives and exacerbate the suffering of the families of those who were deported or exiled, leaving them unable to see their loved ones.
Bakr was one of 1,968 Palestinian prisoners released in the latest deal. He was among the small number of individuals whom Israel permitted to return to their homes in the occupied West Bank, rather than being deported elsewhere.
He had been serving a nine-year prison sentence, of which he had completed six years. During his time in prison, he and his wife had twins, conceived through sperm smuggled out of the Israeli prison.
Isra described to The New Arab how her husband’s release as part of the prisoner exchange deal was the end to the family's nightmare. Throughout the seven months since being free, Bakr spent with his family, Israeli intelligence repeatedly summoned him for questioning and interrogation.
"Israeli officers would constantly call to threaten him or summon him for interrogation, during Ramadan, during the Eid holidays, and at other times. They made sure he felt he was always being watched, signaling that his release under the deal didn’t guarantee he wouldn't be arrested again," she said.
At one point, Israeli intelligence threatened the landlord of the apartment the family was renting, warning that if he didn’t evict them, the Israeli army would take the landlord instead. Consequently, the family was forced to leave and move in temporarily with a relative.
"The pressure extended even to our housing; Israeli intelligence kept a close watch on our situation and threatened anyone who might rent a home to us. We felt as though we were constantly under their gaze," Isra explained.
Bakr is currently being held in the Naqab prison. His lawyer has been able to visit him only once since his arrest; afterward, Bakr asked his family not to send the lawyer again. When Isra inquired why, she learned that any prisoner is subjected to severe beatings immediately following such visits.
She is also deeply concerned about his health. He has begun to suffer from scabies due to a lack of hygiene. Furthermore, at the time of his release under the prisoner exchange deal, he had already lost a significant amount of weight and was suffering from chronic pain in his back and knees to the point where he could barely walk, as a result of the brutal beatings he endured prior to his initial release.
The New Arab contacted several former Palestinian prisoners; none were willing to comment, citing Israeli threats that they could be re-arrested.
Violation of international law
The Palestinian Prisoners' Club has linked these pursuits to an escalation in abuses including mistreatment, starvation, denial of medical care, and solitary confinement within Israeli prisons since the onset of the aggression on Gaza.
The organisation pointed to the severe physical and psychological toll observed among those released, particularly those from the Gaza Strip.
Approximately 3,985 Palestinian prisoners, men, women, and children, have been released through three separate exchange deals. These include a November 2023 agreement (240 prisoners), a deal spanning January and February 2025 (1,777 prisoners), and an October 2025 agreement (1,968 prisoners and detainees).
Helmi Al-Araj, director of the Hurriyat Center for Civil Rights, told TNA that Israel has never adhered to the terms of these agreements even those with clear and specific provisions.
He cited the "Shalit deal" as an example; in 2014, Israel re-arrested more than 50 prisoners who had been released under that agreement. Many remained in prison for long periods, and some were only released again during the more recent exchange deals.
Al-Araj explained that Israel is employing the same tactic regarding the latest agreement, re-arresting released prisoners, both men and women, in an apparent attempt to signal that it won’t bide by any conditions, and that anyone can be taken back into custody at any time.
He added that this serves as a message to the released prisoners; they remain under surveillance, subject to pursuit and arrest and even killing or assassination, as is currently the case in the Gaza Strip.
"The Israeli occupation’s underlying message is an attempt to terrorize the released prisoners, their families, and the Palestinian people at large, by asserting that everyone is being pursued and remains subject to arrest regardless of whether or not they are currently engaged in any activity," he added.
According to Al-Araj, Israel was compelled to release these prisoners but refuses to fully accept this reality; consequently, it pursues them more aggressively than others, under the pretext that they pose a threat to its security.
"As far as is known, none of these released prisoners are engaged in any activities in the West Bank. Yet, Israel is violating the terms of the prisoner exchange deal, as well as international law and international humanitarian law. It arrests these individuals without charge, subjects many of them to administrative detention, and fails to uphold the standards required for fair trials," he concluded.
As of 5 October 2026, the number of prisoners held in Israeli jails reached approximately 9,300, according to the Addameer Prisoner Support and Human Rights Association.
This figure includes 3,101 individuals held under administrative detention, as well as approximately 350 children and 91 women. The organisation also documented 1,419 detainees from the Gaza Strip whom Israel classifies as "unlawful combatants", though these figures don’t necessarily account for everyone held within Israeli military camps.

articles.title: Russians teach children to operate drones and fire assault rifles in occupied Crimea – Ukrainian intelligence
articles.body:
Russians teach children to operate drones and fire assault rifles in occupied Crimea – Ukrainian intelligence
The Russians in occupied Crimea are training children and young people to fly drones, fire assault rifles and take them apart. Ukrainian intelligence says the training uses drones and other equipment belonging to the Russian military.
Source: Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU) on Telegram
Details: In late October, around 50 schoolchildren aged between seven and 18 in Sevastopol qualified for the regional stage of competitions organised by the Russian Movement of the First and the so-called Drone Racing Federation.
The Russians are also teaching university students in the city to operate drones. They use simulators, actual drones and equipment used by Russian forces in the war.
Quote: "The aggressor state of Russia is creating an environment in Ukraine's temporarily occupied territories where military technology and participation in war are becoming a normal part of childhood."
Details: In schools across occupied Crimea, the Russians hold classes where children learn to shoot, strip down Kalashnikov assault rifles and march in formation on command. They also organise "military and patriotic" games and challenges involving participants in Russia's war against Ukraine and force students to learn songs by Russian pro-war propagandist singers.
The occupation authorities are also recruiting people into Russian security agencies and encouraging them to sign contracts to serve in the Unmanned Systems Forces. Those who have fought against Ukraine are being appointed to senior positions in the occupation administrations, and schools are putting up memorial plaques commemorating Russian soldiers killed in Ukraine.
DIU says the Russians are using these measures to justify their aggression and teach children to accept war as a normal part of life.
Quote: "Its goal is not only to maintain control over Crimea, but also to raise a generation for whom Russia's war, military training from the school desk and hatred of Ukraine will become the norm."
Background:
- In March, Ukrainska Pravda.Zhyttia (Life) reported on Russian efforts to teach schoolchildren to operate combat drones. According to Ukraine's Foreign Intelligence Service, the classes are conducted by Russian military personnel who have fought against Ukraine, and training drone operators is part of a federal course called Fundamentals of Security and Defence of the Motherland.
- The classes have been introduced in Kursk, Nizhny Novgorod and Vologda oblasts, among others. In Vladivostok, there were plans to include the subject of drones in school mathematics and physics courses.
- Ukrainska Pravda.Zhyttia previously also reported on the militarisation of education in Ukraine's occupied territories, where the Russians are introducing school subjects that focus on "patriotic" education and loyalty to Russia.

articles.title: A Xi-Trump-Putin summit in Shenzhen could kick-start peace in Ukraine
articles.body:
A Xi-Trump-Putin summit in Shenzhen could kick-start peace in Ukraine
There will be no diplomatic masterstroke in Ukraine’s absence but serious consideration of a ceasefire can lay the groundwork for peace
At the recent Valdai Discussion Club, I asked Russian President Vladimir Putin if he would be open to meeting Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) forum in Shenzhen. I also asked, more broadly, what role China could play in promoting peace in Ukraine, mediating and contributing to peacekeeping.
Some in the United States and Europe question the value of such a summit. They may fear restoring Putin’s standing or normalising the conflict without yielding any real progress towards an end to the war. That risk is still real but these largely Western fears must be tempered by the very real, very human cost of letting the war continue unabated.

articles.title: My Word: Negative political thinking - opinion
articles.body:
Talk about a split vote. Ask the average Israeli how they voted this week, and the answer is likely to be 50:50 – half in favor of a particular politician, and half against someone else. And the negativity continues long after the ballots are counted and a coalition somehow formed.
The question became less a matter of “Whom am I voting for?” and more “Whom am I voting against?” Above it hovered the political joker: “Whom am I likely to end up with?”
Voter turnout at 77.7% was high, particularly in the Arab sector. In my Jerusalem neighborhood, Election Day had a buzz to it. The streets felt festive, and a local “social cafe” held election-themed activities for families with young kids.
There were fewer political banners hanging from windows and balconies. Some (mis)interpreted it as a sign of apathy; others saw it as a reflection of the way the battle for voters had moved from the streets to social media. Perhaps it’s also because so many parties kept merging and changing their names.
It is not yet clear who will ultimately lead the next government; it ain’t over until it’s over. The Israeli system is built on blocs. The prime minister is not automatically the leader of the party that gains the largest number of votes, but the person who can present to the president the likelihood of the most stable coalition – usually a collection of parties amounting to at least 61 seats out of the 120-member Knesset.
Hence, the myriad small parties are a sign of a vigorous democracy but also detract from it, placing an inordinate amount of power in their hands. Remember how Naftali Bennett became prime minister in 2021 for a short-lived term with just seven mandates? Here is where the Arab parties’ gains can have an impact.
Netanyahu’s outgoing government lasted its full four-year term is why he’s earned the title “The Magician.” To have survived the chaos of the backlash to the proposed judicial reform and then the horrors of the October 7, 2023 Hamas invasion and mega-atrocity and resulting war on seven fronts is remarkable.
Ultimately, however, this election also came down to the same question that has shadowed Israeli politics for three decades: To vote “Only Bibi” or “Anyone but Bibi.”
While both Left and Right agree on the need to topple the Iranian regime, too many politicians are more concerned with bringing down a perceived enemy closer to home – a rival party leader.
There will always be political wheeling and dealing in coalition bargaining – either before or after the elections, or both. The question is whether politicians are held accountable for promises made, paid for, and broken.
Expect “a fighting opposition”: infighting among the various parties that compose it. Even worse, there could be paralysis in a coalition because of the disparate nature of its numerous components.
Among the challenges are the splits within different parties and the so-called “change bloc” itself. Tellingly, ahead of the election this week, the parties led by Bennett (B’Yachad), Gadi Eisenkot (Yashar), and Avigdor Liberman (Yisrael Beytenu), among others, could not even agree on who would head the bloc – who potentially would be prime minister or official leader of the opposition.
Road map to forming a government
Election campaigns included promises about which lists each party would not sit with, but it is hard to see how a government can be formed without either the ultra-Orthodox (haredi) or the Arab parties.
The coalition will be its own opposition. Neither the haredim nor the Arab parties are likely to support a law on mass conscription, despite this being a hot topic in the wake of the massive burden on reservists (and their families) during the three years of war.
The public needs to consider the price of these constant changes. When ministers believe they might not have long in office, they do not plan ahead. They want to cut as many red ribbons as possible even if it means cutting corners.
The judicial reform launched by the outgoing government as soon as members had sat in the leather seats around the Cabinet table is a product of this phenomenon: the ministers and MKs involved had not hidden their desire for a judicial overhaul – the need for a reform was acknowledged across the political spectrum – but the speed and intensity took some by surprise. But following five elections in four years, the new government did not want to risk losing time.
The protests against the judicial reform were accompanied by calls to stop serving in the military, to emigrate and create a brain drain, and to transfer businesses and finances abroad. In effect, to boycott Israel under the Netanyahu government.
Even some of those demanding a commission of inquiry into the events of October 7 acknowledge that the rifts – verging at some points on a call for a military coup by veterans – weakened the country and contributed to the timing and scope of the Hamas-led attack.
Headlines social media posts warned of post-election clashes that would mimic the storming of the Capitol in January 2021 after Donald Trump’s loss to Joe Biden. The warnings could be considered part of some campaigns.
Israel’s ballot system makes mass voter fraud difficult (but not impossible), but the greater threat lies in delegitimization – that one side won’t accept the other’s victory. This can happen from either side, Left or Right.
News stories leading up to the election noted the Shin Bet security given to Yashar’s Eisenkot, Democrats leader Yair Golan, and Amcha Yisrael head Ofer Winter (who didn’t pass the threshold) – who were all assumed to be under threat from the Right.
There is a missing story: what happened to anti-government activist Tamar Gershuni who was arrested in July 2025 for plotting to assassinate Netanyahu and released to house arrest? The assassination threat seems to have fallen off the mainstream media’s radar. Or, more likely, it was deliberately dropped.
The left and center-left parties boycotted Netanyahu’s government after the November 2022 elections, citing his criminal trials. Four years later, the trials are ongoing, although the central case involving bribery charges appears to have collapsed, with even the judges twice telling the prosecution they should be dropped. Former attorney-general Avichai Mandelblit on the witness stand admitted serious irregularities concerning the investigation and prosecution.
Among the scenarios that cannot be discounted is that the new Knesset, which is sworn in before the government is formed, could appoint a Speaker from the current opposition, who could then help promote legislation regardless of whomever ultimately is appointed prime minister.
Liberman last week began promoting the “Defendant Law,” under which an indicted politician would be prevented from forming a government. The theory sounds noble. The intent, less so.
It is obviously an attempt at blocking Netanyahu from becoming prime minister. If passed, it is likely to lead to a flurry of charges against politicians of different political persuasions – and to hell with the right to be presumed innocent.
Ultimately, it will place even more power in the hands of the judiciary – to decide whom to prosecute and when – at the expense of the democratic voice of voters and parliament’s right to rule.
No matter who wins, the world will be watching. If Netanyahu forms a government, Israel can expect more of the same or even a worsening of sanctions; but don’t expect a lovefest if someone else takes the reins.
The global wave of antisemitic sentiment and actions are about the existence of the State of Israel itself, not who its citizens have elected, or ended up with, as their leader. On Election Day itself, the Netherlands, for example, announced it would boycott the Eurovision Song Contest again this year over Israel’s participation.
Few imagined that Israel’s first peace treaty would have been signed by Menachem Begin’s Likud government with Egypt. And the Abraham Accords, drawn up under US President Donald Trump and Netanyahu, have proven their worth during the years of war, particularly due to the shared threats from Iran.
Not only will the results of the Israeli elections have an impact, but also next week’s US midterms.
Meanwhile, I’ll let Winston Churchill have the last word. As he said in November 1947, “No one pretends that democracy is perfect or all-wise. Indeed, it has been said that democracy is the worst form of government, except for all those other forms that have been tried from time to time…”

articles.title: 'No' to peace bond, 'yes' to INDIA bloc: Has Neha Bora outsmarted CJP leaders?
articles.body:
AISA president Neha Bora and CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke
NEW DELHI: When Neha Bora recently said “AISA will not be a part of normalising the signing of peace bonds”, she inadvertently highlighted a contrast that the Jantar Mantar 2.0 protests against SIR and "vote chori" had brought to the fore. Neha’s refusal to sign the peace bond before a special executive magistrate and her subsequent challenge to the police move drew an obvious parallel. Did the CJP leaders - Abhijeet Dipke, Ashutosh Ranka and Sourav Das - give in to peace bond pressure easily?“Peace bonds are being weaponised to curb democratic protests. Signing such peace bonds is no less than signing away our democratic right to dissent,” the AISA national president said and claimed that she was detained within 10 minutes of protesting at Mandi House on October 16 and was told that she and other protesters were in breach of peace.“On one side, the Constitution gives us the right to dissent. On the other hand, such peace bonds are invoked only to detain people in the name of breach of peace. Therefore, signing such peace bonds is a principally wrong decision for us. It is no less than signing away our democratic right to dissent,” Bora said defending her decision.
Neha Bora on why she would not sign peace bond
Bora has still not signed the bond and is awaiting copies of 6 FIRs cited as her criminal antecedents in peace-bond proceedings.
This, after she insisted for all documents relied upon in the show-cause notice seeking execution of her peace bond.Now, let’s rewind to October 10.The CJP’s call for Jantar Mantar 2.0 on October 10 had, as expected, evoked great national interest and anticipation. All eyes were on Abhijeet Dipke and his associates Sourav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, who had in June-July this year led a successful youth mobilisation against NEET paper leak. The CJP-led protests had ensured that Dharmendra Pradhan was forced to resign as Union education minister. After all, they were the new heroes of GenZ, who had left the politicians far behind.But ahead of October 10, the national capital saw an unprecedented clampdown. The Delhi Police closed down anything and everything that could facilitate the movement of protesters to Jantar Mantar. For the CJP leadership, the message was loud and clear - they will not get a free passage, unlike in June when they were allowed to gather and mobilise youth at Jantar Mantar for their protests against NEET paper leak.But October 10 morning started with an anticlimax. The top 3 CJP leaders Abhijeet Dipke, Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das travelled together from Mumbai to Delhi and were detained from aircraft as soon as they landed in the national capital. Thousands of protesters who had responded to their calls, braved the police clampdown. They were all detained.The CJP leaders were released a day later after giving an undertaking to maintain public order. Delhi Police said a surety bond of Rs 50,000 was furnished for CJP activists Abhijeet Dipke, Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das for maintaining peace and good behaviour for one year, following their preventive arrest on October 10.The CJP leaders made two more attempts to reclaim the streets - when Sourav Das and Ashutosh Ranka tried to reach Jantar Mantar and again when Dipke urged people to join the "Lehra Do Tiranga" march with the national flag at Central Park in Connaught Place.However, they were detained again and made to sign peace bonds to come out of detention. And while the CJP leaders failed to recreate the magic of Jantar Mantar 1.0, AISA leader Neha Bora took the centrestage. The AISA national president was detained 5 times between October 2 and October 11. However, every time she was released, she would come back to the streets and continue with her protests.During the peak of the protests, Neha Bora hogged the headlines for foxing the police. On October 11, Neha Bora announced a gathering at RK Ashram Marg Metro Station around 2:30pm as part of demonstrations heading toward central Delhi and Jantar Mantar.Heavy police deployment and barricades were set up around RK Ashram Marg to prevent demonstrators from moving toward Jantar Mantar. During the confrontation, police mistakenly chased and detained another protester whose face was partially covered, believing her to be Neha Bora.While police attention was focused at RK Ashram Marg, Neha Bora surfaced near Connaught Place (CP), breaching barricades and running alongside fellow demonstrators in a dash that went viral on social media.Little wonder then, when a user on X called Neha Bora "more talented" than CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke and described her as a "complete GenZ icon", Dipke responded simply: "I agree." The X user had posted: "Maturity is realizing Neha Bora is more talented than Abhijeet Dipke. A complete GenZ icon with an absolutely ridiculous aura.” It was a comparison that manifested all along the “vote chori” protests.
Neha Bora was on the streets every time she was released from detention by the police. She was everywhere - with the CJP leadership, the social activists and also the politicians. When Rahul Gandhi chose to walk behind her during one of the protest marches of INDIA bloc, it spoke volumes about the impact she had made with her street politics. Clearly, the campaign against “vote chori” had put the spotlight on Neha Bora, even as the CJP struggled to find their way to the centre stage of the protests.
Neha Bora, along with Lok Sabha leader of the opposition Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi, during the opposition's protest.
For the CJP, it was a harsh realisation that a lot had changed between July and October. Unlike the anti-NEET paper leak protests in June-July, the Congress-led INDIA bloc this time around were already on the streets demanding resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. Interestingly, while the INDIA bloc’s original protest schedule had only one announced street protest on October 6, the group returned back to the streets four days in a row till October 9, which was a day before the announced CJP protest.The CJP and the Congress had stayed away from each other during the anti-NEET protests. After Jantar Mantar 1.0 was over, the 'cockroaches' carried out their own campaigns in different states, while the Congress shifted focus to protests against SIR and CEC Gyanesh Kumar.
Abhijeet Dipke has announced that he has no political plans and would prefer to keep CJP as a pressure group. So when CJP announced support for INDIA bloc’s November 1 rally, it set tongues wagging about their political ambitions.
With CJP’s Jantar Mantar 2.0 not shaping out as they would have hoped, perhaps its leadership should take a leaf out of Saurav Das’s advice on X to a Congress “soldier” who had questioned why youth Congress and NSUI activists were being detained as soon as they hit the streets and cockroaches were allowed to roam free. Responding to him, CJP co-founder Saurav Das had then said: “if u guys r detained immediately, then u must rethink ur strategy. don’t blame others for ur failures.”The context of that remark was different and CJP’s Jantar Mantar 2.0 campaign was in no way a failure, but Sourav's take on “rethinking strategy” perhaps holds true for the cockroaches at present.

articles.title: Islamic states prosecutors call for global enforcement coalition
articles.body:
Law enforcement heads from 46 Islamic states gather in Baku to tackle cross-border financial crime, artificial intelligence and international asset recovery.
As transnational criminal networks deploy increasingly sophisticated technology to conceal illicit wealth, authorities across the globe are accelerating efforts to dismantle international financial crime.
These priorities framed the agenda in Azerbaijan as delegates convened for the Third High-Level Meeting of the Heads of Anti-Corruption Law Enforcement Agencies of Member States of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC).
At the core of the summit was the implementation of the Makkah al-Mukarramah Convention.
According to the OIC, the landmark treaty represents the first multilateral anti-corruption law enforcement agreement tailored specifically for Islamic Cooperation member states, establishing a unified legal foundation to track illicit financial flows across borders.
Overcoming bureaucratic borders
Cross-border financial investigations often face significant legal barriers, a challenge highlighted alongside Malaysia’s recent asset recovery experience.
Abd Halim Bin Aman, Chief Commissioner of the Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission, detailed his agency’s multi-year effort to trace and repatriate stolen funds following the 1Malaysia Development Berhad (1MDB) case.
"We managed to achieve our goal of tackling the 1MDB matter and as of today we managed to bring back home about 75% to 80% to outside countries, and we managed to bring back about 33 billion Malaysian ringgit worth of loss," he revealed.
Originally established in 2009 as a state-owned strategic development fund, 1MDB became well-known for being embroiled in one of the world's largest financial kleptocracy scandals, after billions of dollars were systematically siphoned off through offshore shell companies and international bank accounts.
According to the US Justice Department’s website, between 2009 and 2015, money was "laundered through major financial institutions worldwide, including in the United States, Switzerland, Singapore, and Luxembourg" and "misappropriated more than $4.5 billion (approximately €4 billion) in funds belonging to 1MDB through a criminal scheme."
The Justice Department stated it "repatriated an additional $156 million (approximately €139 million) in misappropriated 1MDB funds" to people from Malaysia and brought the total of returned funds to approximately $1.4 billion (approximately €1.2 billion).
Bin Aman also shared his views on what typically slows down such international matters.
"Bureaucracy is always being an obstacle to any investigation," he said.
He said that the summit provides a necessary platform to share legislation and best practices to speed up investigations irrespective of legal backgrounds.
Ivica Bošnjak, Deputy Minister of Security for Bosnia and Herzegovina, outlined the unique structural and geographical pressures facing his country.
"Bosnia and Herzegovina is complicated and complex in the political part, and therefore the organization of the entire security system is complex," Bošnjak stated.
He noted that national authorities must coordinate "16 police agencies and a whole series of other law enforcement agencies" operating across the security sector.
While the state has adopted extensive legal regulations and action plans, Bošnjak told Euronews that "much still needs to be done to refine a couple of more crucial laws" and operational strategies to tackle cross-border financial crime effectively.
Building a global enforcement coalition
Tugay Rahimli, Special Assistant to the Prosecutor General of Azerbaijan, outlined the scale and primary objective of the summit.
"Today's event brings together more than 250 participants from 46 member and service states as well as eight international organisations," Rahimli said.
"The main objective of today's event is to facilitate and foster international cooperation among member states, facilitate exchange of information and best practices, as well as to enhance the joint efforts to recover the assets obtained through crime," he added.
Rahimli also pointed to a key leadership development for the host nation.
"Particularly important outcomes of today's event that I would like to highlight is the election of Azerbaijan to chair the bureau for the next two years," he told Euronews.
A unified legal framework
Kamran Aliyev, Prosecutor General of the Republic of Azerbaijan, confirmed the host nation's immediate legislative steps regarding the agreement, the Makkah al-Mukarramah Convention, which is an agreement designed to facilitate mutual legal assistance, the exchange of information, and the recovery of assets derived through corruption.
"This convention first was adopted in 2022 in the city of Makkah, of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, and this is a new platform in fighting corruption at a regional level," Aliyev said.
The agreement operates under a framework, which incorporates 57 nations, with the intention to bypass lengthy diplomatic channels and to allow law enforcement agencies to share intelligence quickly, conduct joint investigations, and trace, freeze, and return stolen state funds to their countries of origin.
Aliyev said that Azerbaijan has joined international initiatives and international and regional conventions against corruption and has also "implemented all provisions of the conventions into our legislation."
Fighting tech with tech
Imed Hazgui, President of the High Authority for Administrative and Financial Control in Tunisia, talked about the global nature of the conference and how the meeting "brings together about fifty Islamic states who are interested in the development of cooperation between them in the fight against corruption."
He warned about the methods modern criminals may use to evade international sanctions.
"Today we all know that terrorist groups and organised crime groups are increasingly using developed technologies to commit their crimes, to hide the necessary means of having them, and also to escape all sanctions," he said.
He is urging member states to integrate advanced digital tools into their law enforcement strategies to keep pace with these threats, which he says "requires a great cooperation at the level of the exchange of developed technologies, of the exchanges of the good practices in this sense, through also the increasingly use of artificial intelligence today in the fight against corruption, in the prediction of dangers and in the treatment of dangers."

articles.title: Russia’s Murena-300S Sea Drone Suspected in Black Sea Container Ship Sinking, Analysts Say
articles.body:
- Category
- World
Russia’s Murena-300S Sea Drone Suspected in Black Sea Container Ship Sinking, Analysts Say
A container ship identified as CONTSHIP JET sank off the coast of Bulgaria in the Black Sea following an apparent attack by an unmanned surface vessel believed to be of Russian origin, according to Reuters on October 29.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Footage verified by Reuters showed a maritime drone moving alongside the ship before changing course toward its hull. Another video captured an explosion, after which the vessel gradually began to list.
According to analysts at Ambrey Analytics, the drone measured approximately five to six meters in length and featured a matte-black hull.
The analysts also noted that the vessel’s maneuvering patterns suggested it may have been remotely controlled.
Based on its appearance and operational characteristics, specialists believe the unmanned vessel could be a modified version of Russia’s Murena-300S maritime drone or a system developed from the same design, Reuters reported.
On October 28, Bulgarian Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov reported that three maritime drones targeted a Liberian-flagged container vessel approximately 21 miles from Bulgaria’s Black Sea coastline.
The container ship CONTSHIP JET was en route from Haifa, Israel, to Constanța, Romania, when the attack occurred near Cape Kaliakra, within Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone.
The vessel suffered severe damage along its starboard side, with local fishermen reporting a fire aboard the ship. The crew abandoned the vessel using life rafts, while a tanker operating nearby was dispatched to assist with the emergency.
The attack on CONTSHIP JET comes amid a series of drone strikes targeting commercial vessels near Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast earlier in October. On October 13, three aerial drones struck Chelsea 3, a Maltese-flagged vessel owned by a Ukrainian company, approximately 18 nautical miles east of Byala, prompting all 15 crew members to abandon the ship.

articles.title: Five Questions About Trump’s ‘America First’ Approach to Fighting Corruption
articles.body:
Shortly after taking office in early 2025, the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump paused the enforcement of the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (FCPA), the nearly 50-year-old law that prohibits American citizens or companies from bribing foreign officials for business.
When the FCPA was resumed six months later, the U.S. Department of Justice was ordered to narrow its focus to limit “undue burdens” on American companies operating outside the country. That action was in line with the Trump administration’s “America First” unilateral approach to foreign policy, which has seen the U.S. withdraw from dozens of international organizations on the grounds that they are inefficient and not in line with the country’s priorities.
Lorenzo Crippa, a lecturer at the University of Strathclyde who quantitatively studies how recorded instances of corruption affect financial flows, discusses the repercussions of these changes and worrying trends that have emerged under the new U.S. approach to global anti-corruption enforcement.
The U.S. has changed the way it applies the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act, and last month it was announced it will officially withdraw from GRECO, the Council of Europe’s anti-corruption body. U.S. officials reportedly said the government would instead use unilateral tools like sanctions and visa restrictions to fight corruption, which they described as more effective. Based on your research, do you think the rejection of collaborative global standards in favor of mechanisms a country controls itself can be more effective?
I would say hardly so. In the anti-corruption space, likely the opposite is true. It's just enough to look at history: the U.S. adopted the FCPA (Foreign Corrupt Practices Act) in 1977, and for 20 years, the law was basically silent until a global regime on anti-corruption was passed at the OECD (Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development) with the OECD Anti-Bribery Convention.
The law was on the books, but it was effectively not enforced, because the fear was that enforcing the law would disadvantage American companies at a time when German competitors and French competitors could even deduct bribes from tax statements.
That all changed with the OECD Anti-Bribery Convention. At the end of the ‘90s, that's the moment we see enforcement of the FCPA, effectively for the first time.
The same could be said when we think of other areas of governance, more generally. There's research in political science and international relations that clearly shows that coordination among countries is the most effective way to address global issues, rather than unilateral actions. So, I'm at the very least skeptical that that could be the case.
In unrelated research of mine with some co-authors, we looked at the effect of American sanctions on financial markets, and we find that they can actually backfire for American firms that are connected to the sanctioned entities. So there's even evidence that a multilateral solution could probably be more desirable.
You co-authored an article in Foreign Affairs this year on how Washington may now be weaponizing anti-corruption law. Many critics of the U.S. say that its laws were hardly neutral before, and often applied for geopolitical or economic leverage, or even amounted to a form of imperialism. How would you respond to that line of argument?
Certainly it's true that the FCPA had been enforced in the past also for geopolitical reasons. I'm sympathetic to these claims. What has changed is that the approach of the Trump administration seems to be one where American firms get a free pass, and non-American firms would be subject to harsher enforcement. Or at least the expectation seems to be this one. And if that's the case, this is a significant change from the past.
If we compare it from the past situation, [despite] the fact that non-U.S. firms might have been significantly charged under the FCPA, American firms were still subject to this policy to a full extent. Whereas here, what we're observing is the possibility of a double standard. That could genuinely be concerning, because that would be outright weaponization.
Like I said, I'm sympathetic with these critics of the FCPA but it did manage to get some massive cases of corruption brought to justice — even of American firms. I think the largest fine in FCPA history is Goldman Sachs. It was certainly far from ideal, but probably closest to the best that was realistically adoptable as an anti-corruption policy. So its reshaping under the Trump administration is, to me, concerning.
What are your specific concerns? What could be the broader effects on corruption around the globe if they don't target U.S. firms and selectively target non-U.S. firms?
When Trump initially halted enforcement of the FCPA in 2025, I was initially puzzled. The FCPA has been used as a tool of foreign policy as well, so getting rid of this or pausing it altogether, was puzzling to me.
But when the period of pause was over and enforcement resumed, under new revised guidelines, what seems to be the case is that it's going to be enforced primarily with the purpose of defending American foreign interests. At the moment we just have a handful of new cases after this change in enforcement, which makes it a little bit difficult as of now to understand if that's really the direction that this is going.
What my co-authors and I found was that at the very least markets seem to have priced in that expectation. We found that the moment the FCPA was suspended, firms that had been targets of FCPA actions in the past significantly experienced a boost in their stock price, which reflects the idea that probably investors expected a lax enforcement environment coming, for the rest of the Trump administration at least. That essentially means putting a bonus on the possibility of corrupt activity. It's a very robust change that we observe from the moment enforcement was made laxer.
In the past decades, we got used to the idea that corruption was bad for business, that investors would prefer a cleaner firm. These results, at least in this historical moment, seem to indicate the opposite: That these market actors would be willing to bet on more corruption. This is somewhat of a step change when it comes to corporate governance and good governance of business. Then again, this gain in stock price was concentrated on American firms. Non-American firms saw no improvement to their valuation, which seems to reflect this idea that there's going to be weaponization going forward.
With those same co-authors, you published another paper this year studying the effects of the OECD Anti-Bribery Convention, finding that the drop in bribery by companies who comply with the convention was basically offset by an increase in bribery from non-signatory competitors. What can we conclude from this? Is it casting doubt on whether the OECD convention or any “supply side” treaty targeting bribers can work?
That's a tricky question, because that paper clearly shows two faces of the same coin. On the one hand, it shows that these treaties are working because they generate strong incentives for those outside the treaty to make the most out of the advantage that they can get. That shows firms covered by the treaty that cannot bribe with impunity. The other face of the coin, that this is offset by corruption from firms outside the treaty, is really concerning. It means that something should be done.
We had a meeting with the OECD working group on bribery about this when we were disseminating the results of our findings. I think they're very aware of this problem. My main takeaway from this is that the solution is [an] expansion of these treaties. As long as there are double standards, as long as there are firms outside of the treaty who can bribe with impunity, the risk of this leakage (that’s what we call it where corruption sort of leaks to the group of firms outside of the treaty) becomes larger.
Historically, the way this has been solved was by trying to expand participation to the treaty. In the ‘90s, that meant having France, Germany, and Japan in the treaty. Right now, probably that means trying to expand to China, Singapore, Taiwan — jurisdictions with firms that are very heavily involved in business, but who can bribe with impunity. I understand that calling for more multilateralism these days seems idealistic, but really that's the only way that we can ensure that these supply side treaties can work in a sense.
My research doesn't do much on this, but existing research of others does show that in the past a strategy has been to use domestic anti-corruption needs of countries. When the OECD Anti-Bribery Convention was signed, the U.S., who was heavily pushing for this treaty, managed to sort of exploit the fact that European countries were facing their own domestic corruption scandals. In Italy, for example, the Mani pulite [“clean hands”] scandal was a big thing in the ‘90s, and that was a significant reason why the U.S. managed to put pressure on this treaty to exist. So if treaty members were able to exploit the fact that, domestically in other parts of the world, there might be a need for more anti-corruption reforms, this could be one lever to try and extend participation.
I wouldn't be certain that these [multilateral treaties] are the ideal solutions, but of the ones that have been tried, they seem to have been quite effective. At least in the shape that they used to have, with a multilateral agreement, and within that agreement, the United States playing a significant role in enforcement, for the good and bad that that was. This role as a global sheriff, in a sense, has managed to reduce corruption and bring large cases of bribery to justice. Now, whether that is the ideal solution, I'm not sure. There certainly is evidence that this was working, and jeopardizing that with the recent moves of the Trump administration makes me somewhat worried.
Could the U.S. look to resume its role as “global sheriff” if U.S. President Donald Trump’s Republican Party suffers the kind of losses currently being predicted in polling for next week’s U.S. midterm elections?
There's a group of senators led by Elizabeth Warren who are trying to propose a bill called the FCPA Reinforcement Act. The idea is to extend the statute of limitations of the FCPA so that it could effectively be protected by future political decisions to halt enforcement again. This specific bill is very unlikely to pass — it’s mostly like a signalling device.
But under a flip [of congressional power in next week’s elections] … that’s a hypothetical. [but] Mmy expectation would be that it would counteract the negative effect that we saw on stock market movements at least. By protecting the FCPA from political swings it should reinforce the idea that enforcement is going to happen, and that good anti-corruption governance is the expectation, and that companies and investors shouldn't deviate from that. So at the very least, I would expect it should reassure markets of that and prevent investors from betting on corruption. I'm not sure this would do much to change this idea of enforcing the FCPA more strongly on non-American companies. I'm not sure that would be something that the bill itself could address. But at the very least, it should remove part of the problem.

articles.title: Russian man arrested in Poland on espionage charges after photographing trains
articles.body:
Russian man arrested in Poland on espionage charges after photographing trains
Police detained a 55-year-old Russian man in the city of Świdnica, in Poland’s Lower Silesian Voivodeship, after he photographed trains and railway infrastructure, the newspaper Rzeczpospolita reported.
The detention came during a police operation to secure a soccer match. After the game ended, officers patrolling the city noticed a parked car near a railroad crossing. The man inside tried to flee when he spotted the police.
After stopping him, police found professional photography equipment and files showing he had photographed trains and critical railway and transportation infrastructure, not only in Poland.
He has been charged with espionage, and a court ordered him held in custody for three months. Under Polish law, the offense carries a minimum sentence of five years in prison. His name has not been released.
Poland’s special services coordinator Tomasz Siemoniak called the detention of the Russian man an “exceptional case.” He explained that Russia is conducting subversive activity in Europe, which requires preliminary reconnaissance and documentation. However, he said, Russian intelligence services have so far avoided sending Russian citizens “to the front lines,” preferring to use local agents who are paid for their work.
