articles.title: Repeaters for Russian drones continue to operate in Belarus — Demchenko
articles.body:
Repeaters for Russian drones continue to operate in Belarus - Demchenko
Kyiv • UNN
Repeaters periodically transmit signals from Belarus for Russian drones. During massive attacks, the UAVs move along the border.
In Belarus, repeaters for Russian drones continue to operate. This was stated by State Border Guard Service spokesperson Andrii Demchenko during a national telethon on October 30, UNN reports.
Unfortunately, they are operating. Signals originating from the territory of Belarus are periodically detected, which allow Russian drones to move more freely toward our western regions. And it cannot be said that the repeaters operate 24 hours a day, but those components of the Defense Forces that have the technical capabilities continue to note that, in various locations, the repeaters resume operation for a certain period of time—especially when a more massive attack is underway as Russia launches drones toward Ukraine. The routes are specifically plotted so that these drones follow the border line with Belarus

articles.title: Bollywood and the underworld — together in the spotlight?
articles.body:
Bollywood and the underworld — together in the spotlight?
October 30, 2026
"In the entire film industry, whoever works without aligning with us, or works with Salman Khan, will be killed."
This warning was delivered in an audio message by presumed attackers on Indian actor Tiger Shroff in Mumbai earlier this month, as they claimed responsibility for the shooting.
The apparent perpetrators said they were connected to Lawrence Bishnoi, a student-politician-turned-gangster who has been in prison since 2014. Notably, police have not confirmed the gang's involvement.
The shots fired at Shroff, which injured his driver, were only the latest in a string of attacks targeting prominent figures from the Mumbai-based film industry, popularly known as "Bollywood".
Since 2022, gunmen fired shots at actor Salman Khan's apartment and at the home of filmmaker Rohit Shetty in Mumbai, as well as actor Disha Patani's family home in northern India. Actor Ranveer Singh also reportedly received an extortion demand of nearly $1.1 million (around €980,000).
The attacks have spread to the other side of the globe, with a cafe owned by comedian Kapil Sharma in Surrey, Canada, also hit three times.
For an industry that once lived in the shadow of organized crime, the attacks have revived old fears, harking back to the crime bosses of the 1990s. But experts say the threat facing Bollywood today looks very different from the one it faced three decades ago.
When the underworld ruled Bollywood
In the 1990s, Mumbai's underworld was deeply entangled with the Hindi film industry.
"The mafia was always fascinated with the movie industry," said S. Hussain Zaidi, crime journalist and author of "Dongri to Dubai: Six Decades of the Mumbai Mafia," who has covered organized crime in the city for over three decades.
Gangsters like Dawood Ibrahim, Abu Salem and Chhota Shakeel "were totally obsessed" with Bollywood, he told DW, much like mafiosi who sought a foothold in Hollywood.
To the gangsters, films offered glitz and glamor, but also a way to launder their profits. They invested in films "so that they could control the industry and have a legitimate way of making money," Zaidi added.
When producers didn't cooperate, the consequences could be fatal. In 1997, music mogul Gulshan Kumar, founder of the label T-Series, was shot dead. In 2000, filmmaker Rakesh Roshan, father of Bollywood star Hrithik Roshan, was shot and wounded.
Mumbai's streets were "made red with blood" in 1998, Zaidi said, describing the year as the pinnacle of gang killings.
D. Sivanandhan, the former Police Commissioner of Mumbai, who led the crackdown, says 101 businessmen were shot dead in 1998 alone, or one "every third day," mostly over unpaid extortion demands.
Police efforts were reinforced by a tough new organized crime law passed in 1999, which Sivanandhan calls the "ultimate weapon." Security forces used electronic surveillance and preventive detention, and seized some 2,500 illegal weapons.
"A few encounters also happened, but that is not a policy nor a strategy,” he told DW, referring to police shootouts.
By the early 2000s, the gangs' hold had been broken, and a new Mumbai seemed to be emerging.
A gang run from a prison cell
The man believed to be behind the latest wave of attacks is not from Mumbai.
Bishnoi, 33, comes from a landowning family in the northern state of Punjab and was studying in Chandigarh when he was drawn into violent student politics. Then, he was arrested, incarcerated and eventually turned to crime, says journalist Jupinderjit Singh, author of "Gangs of Punjab."
"He was introduced to the University of Crime through the jail," Singh told DW.
Bishnoi went on to build what Singh describes as one of the first criminal syndicates spanning several northern Indian states. Investigators say he still directs operations from prison using concealed phones and messaging apps.
Currently, Bishnoi is held in a jail in Prime Minister Narendra Modi's home state of Gujarat.
His network stretches beyond India's borders. In September 2025, Canada designated the Bishnoi gang a terrorist entity. Last month, the FBI added Satinderjeet Singh, popularly known as Goldy Brar, to its Ten Most Wanted list, offering up to $1 million for information leading to his arrest. US prosecutors described him as the alleged leader of Bishnoi's group in North America.
While Bishnoi comes from an affluent landowning family, his shooters are mostly poor. The gang usually recruits them online.
"There are so many youngsters who want to do something… they are just pulled by the lore attached to Lawrence Bishnoi," Singh explained. "Recruiting is no big issue… They offer money, protection, weapons."
Why target film stars?
For Bishnoi, it seems personal.
In 1998, Salman Khan was accused of killing a blackbuck, an antelope revered by Bishnoi's community. Bishnoi vowed revenge, and many of the attacks targeted people close to the actor, including the 2024 killing of politician Baba Siddique, which police have linked to the gang.
Singh sees the feud as a bid for respectability. Criminals "always try to find something that makes them a moral guardian," he says, and this case was Bishnoi's "chance to redeem himself."
But money and intimidation matter too.
"Bollywood has a lot of money," Singh added, pointing that the previous generation of gangsters was no longer in position to take advantage.
"With Dawood Ibrahim and his counterparts away, there was a vacuum, and Lawrence Bishnoi is trying to exploit that."
Sivanandhan explained the old Mumbai gangs ran a whole "basket" of illegal businesses, from smuggling to protection rackets and cricket match-fixing. Their members were "local boys," while the Bishnoi gang has “nothing to do with Mumbai,” he added. It targets Bollywood because the industry is "loaded with money" and a "soft underbelly."
"They are using Bollywood as an ATM," he told DW. "Insert a card and collect your money."
Meanwhile, Zaidi sees the attacks mainly as publicity. "It's a way to grab headlines," he told DW. Within hours of the recent attack on Shroff, someone claimed on social media that he was targeted for being close to Khan, a logic Zaidi called "absolutely illogical and absurd."
But publicity is useful to gangs that live off extortion. "The base material of extortion is: create fear," a security professional responsible for the protection of several Bollywood stars, who asked not to be named because of the sensitivity of the issue, told DW.
Is Bollywood under siege?
Still, experts say its hard to argue that the ongoing violence is comparable to the 1990s crime wave.
"I won't say resurgence, because that would be a bit of an exaggeration," Zaidi said. In the 1990s, several rival gangs fought for control of Mumbai. Today, other than Bishnoi's faction, other gangs are not considered active in Mumbai.
The film industry is also not paying up the way it once did, because the shift to digital payments has made large cash transactions hard to hide, he added.
Sivanandhan disagrees. The shootings at walls and gates, followed by quick claims on social media, are "all aimed at collecting… extortion money," he said. In his view, "cash-rich Bollywood would be coughing up so much, which is enough to run an army of people."
At any case, the fear remains real.
And even if violence is not as prevalent, hundreds of thousands of people rely on the Mumbai film industry for their livelihoods.
"If the fear of the underworld continues, leading names may be forced to leave Mumbai," the All Indian Cine Workers Association (AICWA) President Suresh Shyamlal Gupta wrote to Home Minister Amit Shah.
"Mumbai will not be allowed to go back to the underworld days of the 1990s, and Bollywood will not be allowed to work in the shadow of fear," Gupta wrote.
With security forces seemingly on the back foot, gangsters are likely to continue their campaign.
Several Bollywood stars have already stepped up their security.
Edited by: Darko Janjevic

articles.title: Strikes on camp in Ethiopia kill at least 15, sources say
articles.body:
Strikes on camp in Ethiopia kill at least 15, sources say
NAIROBI, Oct 30 - At least 15 people, many of them children, died in a series of drone strikes that hit a camp for displaced civilians in Ethiopia's Amhara region, two sources involved in a rescue operation said on Friday.
It was not clear why the camp was targeted or who was behind the attack, but the strikes highlight continuing clashes in the area despite a lull in the heavy fighting that erupted last month between an alliance of rebels from northern Tigray region and the government in Addis Ababa.
"There were around five explosions. Then ... we started collecting bodies," a community representative involved in the burials told Reuters, asking not to be named due to the sensitivity of the issue.
The representative said they helped bury 13 people at the camp, which is known as Jari 2 and is home to more than 1,700 people who fled previous violence.
Two of the injured later died at a hospital in Hayk, a town 17 km away.
A spokesperson for Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed did not immediately respond to requests for comment but a local official said they were aware of the incident and were helping get medical treatment to 36 people who had been injured.
A resident of Hayk who was helping provide shelter to survivors also said 15 people had been killed. "Those from the camp are now sheltering in a school," they said.
The dead included five children, the two sources said.
Both sources said there had been no fighting in the area when the strike took place, but members of the Amhara Fano National Movement, which is part of the rebel alliance spearheaded by fighters from Tigray, had been nearby.
Government troops have driven back the rebel alliance since their offensive was launched on September 23.
They retook the capital of Tigray region earlier this month and advanced towards the border with Eritrea, which Ethiopia accuses of supporting the rebellion by sending troops over the border.
Asmara denies the accusation and says Addis Ababa's allegations of an invasion by Eritrean forces amounted to a "declaration of war".
Given the web of interconnected conflicts in the Horn of Africa, with neighbouring countries and powers further afield backing their respective proxies, experts have warned that war in Ethiopia could trigger a broader conflict in the region. REUTERS

articles.title: US economy, soaring living costs dominate voter concerns ahead of November midterms
articles.body:
Economic pressures from high inflation, rising energy prices, cooling job growth and affordability issues take center stage for voters ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections in the US, which will determine the balance of power in Congress.
Soaring living costs dominate voter preferences, public opinion polls ahead of the elections show.
Some 84% of registered voters consider the state of the economy very important to their vote, including 82% of Republicans and 88% of Democrats, a survey by the Pew Research Center on Oct. 8 found.
Accelerating inflation, weakening consumer confidence and persistently high borrowing costs just days before the elections underscore these concerns.
Energy costs continue to strain households amid tensions in the Middle East that began with the joint US and Israeli strikes on Iran at the end of February.
The American Automobile Association (AAA) reported that the average price of gasoline stood at $4.23 a gallon as of Oct. 29, marking a surge of more than 39% from the $3.04 average recorded during the same period last year.
Diesel prices remain at record highs of around $6.33 per gallon, up 72%. Since diesel is used in the transportation and agriculture sectors, soaring prices drive up costs throughout the supply chain.
The US is paying the heaviest toll of the Middle East conflict and the oil shock in the Strait of Hormuz, shouldering around $160 billion of the $468 billion in additional costs added to the global fuel bill, according to the nonprofit Center for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA).
Inflation remains well above the US Federal Reserve’s 2% target as the country’s consumer price index (CPI) rose 0.6% month-on-month and 3.7% year-on-year in September, pushing monthly and annual inflation to five-month and four-month highs, respectively.
The core CPI, excluding food and energy, rose 0.3% month-on-month and 2.6% year-on-year in September.
The producer price index (PPI) surged 1.3% month-on-month and 6.3% year-on-year in the same month, marking multiyear highs.
Fed Chair Kevin Warsh recently said Americans have been facing inflation that has remained above the bank’s target for nearly six years.
The Fed raised rates in September for the first time since 2023, hiking them by 25 basis points before maintaining rates at a range of 3.75%-4% this month. The bank had cut rates by a total of 75 basis points last year and maintained them at its first five meetings of this year.
The labor market also started to cool, with nonfarm payrolls rising by only 29,000 in September, well below estimates, while the figures for July and August were revised downward by a combined 60,000 jobs.
The number of initial jobless claims fell to 194,000 in the week ending Oct. 24, the lowest level since mid-July.
While the unemployment rate rose slightly by 0.1 percentage points to 4.2%, representing 7.1 million people, the US economy showed resilience in the third quarter, growing at an annual rate of 3.4%, driven by private consumption and massive tech investments.
This performance failed to positively influence consumer sentiment, as the University of Michigan’s consumer sentiment index dropped to a five-month low of 48 in October amid a rise in short-term inflation expectations to 4.7%.
Consumer confidence declined by 10% year-on-year and 15% compared with February, before tensions with Iran escalated.
Meanwhile, inflationary pressures and expectations of tighter monetary policy kept bond markets under selling pressure, with the US 10-year and 30-year Treasury yields hitting 24-year highs earlier in October before retreating somewhat, although they remained elevated.
At the same time, the housing market came under pressure from high financing costs as 30-year fixed mortgage rates hovered around 7.37%, according to the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA).
Pending home sales dropped 11.3% year-on-year and 7.3% month-on-month in September, data from the National Association of Realtors (NAR) showed.
The US federal budget ran a deficit of $1.99 trillion in fiscal year 2026, marking the highest level since the COVID-19 pandemic, while total public debt hit $40.4 trillion.
Net interest payments on the massive debt exceeded $1 trillion as debt servicing became the federal government’s third-largest spending item, surpassing defense and overall health care, while ranking behind Social Security and Medicare.
Trade protectionism also drove up domestic cost pressures. Although the Supreme Court struck down initial tariffs under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), Washington imposed new tariffs of 10%-12.5% on the EU and other countries under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974.
Some 69% of registered voters disapproved of US President Donald Trump’s tariff policies, according to a poll by Fox News in mid-October.
Some 81% of participants in an Ipsos poll conducted in September think tariffs directly drove up prices.
A recent poll by The New York Times/Siena College showed that 64% of registered voters disapprove of the current administration’s handling of the US economy.
Some 69% of voters disapproved of Trump’s stance on the cost of living, while 65% disapproved of his approach to the war in Iran.
Some 73% expressed dissatisfaction with the policy Trump has pursued regarding gasoline prices, the survey showed.
Economic pressures will decide the outcome of the elections, given that key races for seats in the House of Representatives and the Senate are neck and neck.

articles.title: A statement from from Meduza’s editorial team and fellow journalists in support of Novaya Gazeta
articles.body:
A statement from from Meduza’s editorial team and fellow journalists in support of Novaya Gazeta
Novaya Gazeta has announced it is shutting down. We never thought we would have to write these words — and yet that’s the reality. The story of the most important independent news outlet in modern Russia has come to an end.
Novaya was a unique newspaper from its founding to its final day. No other newsroom has a record like this: an extraordinary body of investigative reporting and exceptional journalism, an impressive array of awards — including Dmitry Muratov’s Nobel Peace Prize — and a list of journalists who were murdered.
By every measure, it was the best media outlet in Russian history. In a testament to that distinction, Novaya Gazeta was the only major independent outlet that kept operating inside the country after 2022, in defiance of wartime censorship, dictatorship, and even the instinct for self-preservation.
We admire your loyalty to the profession. We thank you for everything. And we promise to continue your work for as long as we can. We also know that you are unbreakable and never give up. You’ll find a way, as you have so many times before.
That is why we refuse to say goodbye to you. Novaya Gazeta will not disappear.
Thank you.

articles.title: Nvidia CEO sees Kazakhstan as potential AI hub for Europe
articles.body:
During his first visit to Kazakhstan, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said the country's growing computing capacity could make it a major AI hub for Europe, as Kazakhstan expands its energy and digital infrastructure.
Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang has visited Kazakhstan for the first time, saying the Central Asian country could emerge as a major AI computing hub for Europe.
Huang made the remarks during a fireside chat with Zhaslan Madiyev, Kazakhstan's Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development, at the Alem.ai International Artificial Intelligence Centre in Astana.
During the discussion, Madiyev said Kazakhstan plans to nearly double its installed power capacity to more than 40 gigawatts by 2035 as the country expands the infrastructure needed to support its growing AI sector.
One of its flagship projects is the Data Center Valley, a large-scale AI computing campus under development in Ekibastuz, one of Kazakhstan's main power-generating centres. Its first 50-megawatt phase is expected to begin operations in 2027, while the project's energy infrastructure could eventually scale up to one gigawatt.
Huang said Kazakhstan's energy resources and growing computing capacity could give the country a significant role in Europe's AI ecosystem.
“Kazakhstan has a lot of real estate. It also has a lot of energy,” Huang said. “You're going to have a lot of compute right here in Kazakhstan. It's going to be a hub, a computing hub, an AI factory hub for all of Europe.”
Huang described the country's abundant energy resources as a potential competitive advantage in the AI economy, arguing that electricity could increasingly be used to generate computing power and AI rather than simply being exported as energy.
“Kazakhstan has a fundamental advantage because you have so much natural resource already. You have so much energy, and instead of just exporting energy in the future, you could transform the energy into intelligence and export intelligence,” Huang said.
Sovereign AI
But energy alone, Huang argued, will not be enough. Kazakhstan will also need to retain control over another resource — its data.
Madiyev said the country is already developing Kazakh-language large language models based on open-source foundation models and asked whether Kazakhstan should eventually build its own foundation model from scratch.
Huang said building a domestic foundation model “makes complete sense”, describing it as a national security concern.
He argued that countries should retain control over both their data and the AI infrastructure used to serve their citizens, comparing it to other essential national infrastructure.
“In the future, you will have your own electric grid, your own internet, your own telecommunications and your own intelligence grid,” Huang said.
The potential of Physical AI
Beyond computing infrastructure and sovereign AI, Kazakhstan is also looking to position itself in the emerging field of Physical AI — systems that can interact with and operate in the physical world.
Pointing to Kazakhstan's industrial base in mining, agriculture, transport and logistics, Madiyev asked whether the country could become a hub for developing and training Physical AI models and robots. Huang called the idea “fantastic”, saying these industries could be among the first to benefit.
“Physical AI is not just robotics,” Huang said. “It includes everything from seismic understanding to mapping mines and wells, to understanding geography and geology — where to mine, how best to mine — understanding material science, the processing of chemicals.”
With the technology still at an early stage, Huang said Kazakhstan has an opportunity to help shape the emerging industry.
Investing in AI startups
The discussion also turned to Higgsfield AI, a Kazakh-founded generative video startup in which Nvidia has invested.
Asked what attracted Nvidia to the company, Huang said the decision ultimately came down to its founders.
“The first thing and the last thing is you invest in people, not companies,” Huang said, describing Higgsfield's founders as “visionary” and capable of competing with leading AI companies globally.
Huang also pointed to the company's presence in both Kazakhstan and the United States, saying it could help bridge the two ecosystems.
Later that day, Huang met President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, who described the development of artificial intelligence and digitalisation as a national priority.
“This visit is very important for us in terms of giving a serious boost to cooperation with Nvidia,” Tokayev said.
Huang welcomed Kazakhstan's ambition to become an “AI nation” and said the country had the potential to become a global hub for Physical AI.
Huang's first visit to Kazakhstan came at the close of AI Month, a nationwide initiative launched in September as part of the country's Year of Digitalisation and Artificial Intelligence.

articles.title: Finland to establish military space operations center at Tikkakoski
articles.body:
Finland to establish military space operations center at Tikkakoski
Finland will establish a military space operations center at Tikkakoski, according to Defense Minister Antti Hakkanen, Qazinform News Agency reports.
In a post on X, the Finnish minister said that the Defence Forces' Space Operations Centre will be located at the Air Force Headquarters in Tikkakoski. It will start operating on January 1, 2027.
“It will serve as the command and control of defence space activities and the space operations of the Finnish Defence Forces, while also developing the Defence Forces’ space capabilities,” an official statement reads.
The center will initially employ 20 personnel, and the number will increase in the coming years.
“The founding of a space operations centre is part of a broader process to improve Finland’s defence by reinforcing the Finnish Defence Forces’ space capabilities. It is also our response to the growing importance of space as an operational domain for defence,” Minister Häkkänen said.
The Ministry of Defence is also preparing a space strategy for defence to create a long-term vision for developing space defence in the defence administration. The strategy is nearly complete, and the establishment of the space operations centre is one of the first tangible steps towards reaching the objectives set out in the strategy.
The priorities and objectives for space defence are outlined in the Government Defence Report. As part of its Programme, the Government has also adopted a Space Strategy, which sets out Finland’s vision and objectives for space activities through 2030, highlighting the importance of the space economy, security and defence policy, and security of supply.
Earlier, it was reported that Finland's Licensing and Supervision Agency had ordered Google's subsidiary, Tuike Finland Oy, to suspend environment-altering preparatory work at two planned data center sites in Muhos and Kajaani until environmental impact assessments are completed.

articles.title: Andreas Malm condemns UK travel ban as ‘drift into authoritarianism’
articles.body:
The Swedish climate academic Andreas Malm has condemned a travel ban imposed on him by the UK government as a “drift into authoritarianism” amid criticism of the move.
Malm, the author of How to Blow Up a Pipeline, said he had been “kept in the dark” by the UK’s immigration authorities over the reasons for his electronic travel authorisation (ETA) being revoked.
He said he had only been told that his presence in the UK was “not considered to be conducive to the public good”, as the Guardian revealed.
Speaking to Radio 4’s Today programme on Friday, he speculated that the only plausible rationale for the ban was his advertised appearance at a conference next Wednesday alongside Huda Ammori, a co-founder of the proscribed group Palestine Action.
He said: “I cannot see any other explanation than the scheduled appearance of me on stage for a panel on Wednesday evening in London, together with Huda Ammori. That … makes me somehow a terrorist or associated with terrorism, and therefore barred from travelling to the UK. That’s pretty scandalous.”
He added: “What I am going through here is just a very small part of a major trend: this drift into authoritarianism that is targeting the Palestine movement, the climate movement, and others who oppose the destructive forces that are in control of this world. And that’s a very sad thing.”
Malm confirmed to the Guardian that he would speak via video link at the event organised by Tribune magazine.
In his BBC interview, he denied supporting or helping to finance Palestine Action. But Malm, who has long campaigned for Palestinian rights, added: “You might be able to guess my opinions and sympathies.”
The Home Office said it could not discuss individual cases. However, a source said: “Decisions to refuse or cancel an ETA on the grounds that presence in the UK may not be conducive to public good are based solely on an assessment of the potential risk an individual may pose to UK society.”
Malm said: “I don’t have any concrete evidence for what this is all about. I’m left in the dark. I have asked for clarification, explanation. I haven’t received any.”
Malm was challenged on Today over whether his description of the Hamas attacks on 7 October 2023 as an “act of liberation” could be the reason for the ban.
He replied: “It could be. But my views about what happened on 7 October and in Palestine have been in the public realm for a long time. I was most recently in the UK in May.”
Malm added: “I’ve done nothing in public that is associated with Palestine Action. I have not publicly supported them or promoted them in any way.”
Malm said he was invited to speak alongside Ammori to discuss the war in Iran.
“So, what they’re preventing here is for us to have a discussion about the drivers of the imperial aggression in the Middle East,” he said.
“The only link to Palestine Action is her [Ammori] as a person. If you continue with these guilt-by-association links, then presumably if I am a threat to the public good in the UK by dint of talking to her, then someone who talks to me presumably is also a threat to the public good. Where does that end?”
The travel ban has been widely criticised. The author Sally Rooney said it was a “sad and frightening act of cultural self-harm”.
In a post on X, the Green party leader, Zack Polanski, said: “This all feels very much Starmer’s Labour government 2.0. An extraordinary attack on free speech from Andy Burnham.”
The Labour MP Clive Lewis, who last year offered to stand down from his Norwich South seat to allow Andy Burnham the chance to return to parliament, said: “When any government starts barring academics for their political views, alarm bells should be ringing.
“If ministers have evidence Andreas Malm is dangerous, produce it. Otherwise, this looks like political censorship dressed up as public safety. That’s a dangerous road for any democracy.”
How to Blow Up a Pipeline, which inspired a film of the same name, argues that sabotage and destroying property are morally and strategically justified forms of activism.

articles.title: Lavrov flew to the G20 summit in the United States for 20 hours, bypassing “unfriendly” countries
articles.body:
Lavrov flew to the G20 summit in the United States for 20 hours, bypassing “unfriendly” countries
Kyiv • UNN
The Russian delegation, headed by Lavrov, flew to Atlanta for 20 hours and 10 minutes, avoiding the airspace of “unfriendly” countries. A meeting of the G20 foreign ministers will take place in the United States.
The Russian delegation headed by Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov had to fly to the G20 summit in the United States for almost a day. Due to the need to avoid the airspace of "unfriendly" countries, the flight lasted 20 hours and 10 minutes, Russian "media" report, according to UNN.
Details
On the night of October 30, Lavrov arrived in Atlanta, where a meeting of the foreign ministers of the G20 countries will take place. The event will be key ahead of the G20 leaders’ summit, scheduled for December 14–15 in Miami. U.S. President Donald Trump said he wanted to see Vladimir Putin at the meeting, but the Kremlin noted that no decision had yet been made on the matter.
Additionally
After the start of the full-scale war in Ukraine, Lavrov has already flown to the United States, bypassing "unfriendly" countries. In July 2024, for example, the Russian minister took part in meetings of the UN Security Council. At the time, Russian "media" reported that the flight from Moscow to New York lasted more than 12 hours.
It is also reported that Lavrov is the last Kremlin representative to have visited the United States amid growing ties between Washington and Moscow.
Meanwhile, Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov, who was also sanctioned, took part in the G20 meeting in North Carolina in September. There, he met with his American counterpart, Scott Bessent.
Recall
The Kremlin stated that the next round of peace talks on ending Russia’s war against Ukraine could take place after November 4. At the same time, the Russian side has not yet named a specific date for the meeting.

articles.title: BAE Systems wins modernization deal for littoral combat ship St. Louis
articles.body:
- The U.S. Navy awarded BAE Systems a $66.5 million contract on Oct. 28 for a dry-dock availability on USS St. Louis (LCS 19).
- Work in Mayport, Florida, is due to finish by December 2027, and options could raise the contract value to $80.7 million.
The U.S. Navy has awarded BAE Systems’ Jacksonville ship repair business a $66.5 million contract to dry-dock and overhaul the littoral combat ship USS St. Louis (LCS 19) in Mayport, Florida, with work due to finish by December 2027. Naval Sea Systems Command awarded the firm-fixed-price contract on Oct. 28, and options could raise its value to $80.7 million.
Of the $66.5 million obligated at award, $58.8 million comes from fiscal 2027 U.S. Navy other procurement funds, $7.5 million from fiscal 2026 funds and $234,355 from fiscal 2025 money. The Navy ran the competition as full and open and received two offers. The announcement does not list the systems to be repaired or modernized, and it does not say when the ship will enter dry dock.
A docking selected restricted availability is depot-level maintenance, alteration and modification work done while the ship sits in dry dock, scheduled by the Chief of Naval Operations. Under the contract, BAE Systems Maritime Solutions Jacksonville supplies the labor, supervision, equipment, facilities, production, testing and quality assurance for the job.
The ship left Naval Station Mayport on Sept. 13 to take over U.S. Northern Command’s maritime mission along the southern border, relieving USS Cooperstown (LCS 23), and stopped in Nassau, Bahamas, on Sept. 21. It flew the same mission in a surge deployment that ended on Nov. 10, 2025. The U.S. Navy has not said how long the current deployment will last.
St. Louis is the 22nd littoral combat ship delivered to the U.S. Navy and the 10th of the Freedom variant, the steel monohull design built at Marinette, Wisconsin. The ship was christened and launched there on Dec. 15, 2018, commissioned at Mayport in 2020 and assigned to Littoral Combat Ship Squadron 2. On its first deployment, eight months with U.S. 4th Fleet in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific, the U.S. Navy said the crew disrupted and seized more than $100 million in illicit cargo in five operations.
In late 2020, the U.S. Navy declared a class-wide flaw in the Freedom variant’s combining gear, the gearbox that links the ship’s diesel engines and gas turbines, after a failure on USS Little Rock (LCS 9) in March of that year. German manufacturer RENK developed a fix that replaced the gear’s ball bearings with journal bearings, and the U.S. Navy stopped accepting new Freedom-variant ships until it was proven. St. Louis was the last ship delivered before that pause and, in 2022, became the first already-delivered ship to receive the correction.
The U.S. Navy’s fiscal 2023 budget sought to decommission nine Freedom-variant ships, St. Louis among them; Congress allowed four. In 2023, the U.S. Navy still planned to retire St. Louis, Wichita, Billings and Indianapolis in 2025 and make them available for foreign military sales, even though St. Louis had just been repaired. That retirement did not happen, and in January 2026, U.S. Navy officials said the service had shelved plans to decommission five Freedom-variant and two Independence-variant ships.
The class has been shrinking at the old end and growing at the new one. USS Fort Worth (LCS 3), one of four early hulls designated as test ships in 2016, was decommissioned in July 2026, the sixth Freedom-variant ship to leave service. USS Cleveland (LCS 31), the 16th and last of the variant, was commissioned on May 16, 2026, in Cleveland, Ohio, and joined the Freedom-variant fleet at Mayport.
BAE Systems’ Jacksonville yard handles much of the surface-ship docking work at Mayport. In 2023, it won a $83 million docking selected restricted availability for the destroyer USS Ramage (DDG 61), with options worth up to $93 million, after a competition that drew three offers. In 2021, Naval Sea Systems Command set up two multiple-award contracts worth up to $2.27 billion combined to sustain Mayport-based littoral combat ships, including docking availabilities. BAE Systems Jacksonville Ship Repair and Fincantieri Marine Systems North America held the larger of the two, with an ordering period expected to end in August 2026. The St. Louis work was awarded as a separate contract, N00024-27-C-4405.

articles.title: Russia’s last major independent newspaper Novaya Gazeta shuts down after 33 years amid Kremlin pressure
articles.body:
On Oct. 30, the independent Russian media outlet Novaya Gazeta has announced its plan to close, publishing a statement titled “They Killed Us.” The newspaper’s staff, who occupied a building in Potapovsky Lane in central Moscow, received a notice of eviction the day before.
“They killed us. On November 9, we will turn off the lights in our home where we have lived for 30 years, shut down the servers, and leave. There is no more newspaper. The Russian authorities and Russian security services forced the editorial team to stop working,” the statement read.
The journalists expressly blame Russia’s security services, the Ministry of Justice, and the prosecutor’s office, those who “privatized the state and usurped power”:
“Stop saying that Stalin’s Great Terror is not happening as we speak, and that the repressions have some kind of ‘digital nature.’ These are state repressions. And it is people, not numbers, who die in cells. Period. A human life has lost its meaning and been devalued.”
The editorial team also thanked its readers. The newspaper’s last issue, which was being prepared for publication, will still be released.
The editorial team also said that it continues to face financial restrictions, with private companies and banks refusing to provide services allowing for the receipt of donations, citing “internal corporate rules.” These refusals are linked to pressure from Russian security services.
The Anna Politkovskaya Museum, located in her former office, will close along with the newspaper.
Novaya Gazeta was founded in 1993 by a group of journalists including Dmitry Muratov, who would hold the post of the newspaper’s editor-in-chief throughout most of its history, sharing the Nobel Peace Prize in 2021. In March 2022, shortly after the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the newspaper suspended its print edition because of warnings from the consumer rights watchdog Roskomnadzor. In September 2022, a court revoked its registration as a media outlet, but it had continued to publish up until now.

articles.title: The Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine called on UNESCO to respond to Russian propaganda events at the Khan's Palace in Crimea
articles.body:
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine called on UNESCO to respond to Russian propaganda events at the Khan's Palace in Crimea
Kyiv • UNN
Ukraine is protesting against Russian events at the Khan's Palace on October 31–November 1. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs is asking UNESCO to strengthen the protection of the heritage site.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine has expressed its protest over propaganda events planned by Russia on the grounds of the Khan's Palace in occupied Bakhchysarai, scheduled to take place from October 31 to November 1. The MFA called on UNESCO to respond to the actions of the Russian Federation and strengthen the protection of Crimean Tatar cultural heritage. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine reports this, writes UNN.
The Khan's Palace is a historical and cultural landmark of global significance, included by Ukraine on the Tentative List of UNESCO World Heritage Sites. The Russian Federation continues to systematically wage war against the Crimean Tatar people, their culture, historical memory, and the world's cultural heritage. The occupiers' criminal actions are documented during monitoring conducted by UNESCO in temporarily occupied Crimea since 2014
The ministry noted that Ukraine had already officially informed UNESCO's leadership and the organization's member states of the Russians' intention to hold the event in temporarily occupied Bakhchysarai.
We call on the Director-General of UNESCO, its relevant bodies, and the Organization's member states to immediately employ all available international instruments aimed at ending Russia's practice, as the power temporarily occupying Crimea, of turning the cultural monuments of the indigenous Crimean Tatar people into an instrument of imperial propaganda and the justification and glorification of the occupation
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine calls on UNESCO to take the following measures:
-  Provide a principled assessment of Russia's propaganda activities in the temporarily occupied Crimea. 
-  Strengthen international mechanisms for protecting Ukraine's and the Crimean Tatars' cultural heritage. 
-  Consider strengthening the Russian Federation's accountability for the systematic destruction of Ukraine's cultural heritage, which bears signs of war crimes.

articles.title: Russia set to return to international hockey tournaments after top sports court's ruling
articles.body:
Controversial court ruling paves way for Russia's return to world ice hockey. European nations push back
Editor's note: The story has been updated with the latest details.
The Court of Arbitration for Sport ruled the International Ice Hockey Federation's exclusion of Russian athletes from its tournaments unlawful, in a ruling announced on Oct. 30.
Russia is increasingly returning to international sporting and cultural events, using them to whitewash its reputation on the world stage and distract from its war against Ukraine.
"The International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) expresses its disappointment with the decision of the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) to allow the Russian Ice Hockey Federation to enter a Russian Team in all IIHF Championships with immediate effect," reads a press statement from the IIHF.
"While the IIHF respects the authority of CAS and will act in accordance with its ruling, the outcome does not remove the concerns that informed its assessments," reads the statement.
In a press release, the CAS says that the IIHF cited safety and security concerns for barring Russian participation, but that for them "the evidence was insufficient."
"The Panel unanimously concluded that... only substantiated security concerns could outweigh athletes of a particular nationality to participate in competitions," reads the CAS statement.
The CAS ruling means that Russia will be able to participate in a sweep of forthcoming ice hockey tournaments in Canada, Czechia, the U.S., and Germany.
The Czech, German, and Austrian hockey associations criticized the court's decision, saying their position on Russia's participation remains unchanged and that they would evaluate their next steps.
The Finnish association called the CAS's ruling "incomprehensible" and said that no player or team official is under obligation to take part in competitions in which Russia or Belarus is involved.
The EU is mulling ideas on how to restrict Russia's access to sporting events, and even a Russian visa ban to the bloc for anything other than necessary travel.
However, Lithuania's recent refusal to issue visas to Russian and Belarusian athletes led to it being stripped of the right to host a world pentathlon tournament.
The European Commission has expressed "regret" over decisions to allow Russia to return to world sports events, but has said it would respect the "autonomy" of sporting organizations.
With CAS serving as the supreme decision-maker in disputes between sports organizations, the Oct. 30 ruling raises the question of whether it sets a broader precedent that Europe will be unable to stop.
But CAS's own press release also mentions an Oct. 13 decision to maintain a ban on Russian participation in World Curling events, and it reads that all cases are assessed "on their individual merits."

articles.title: China Focus: Shenzhen's electronics hub finds new global audience ahead of APEC
articles.body:
SHENZHEN, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- Andrea Triboldi stepped into Shenzhen's Huaqiangbei, the well-known electronics hub, with a handwritten shopping list of more than 20 products, noting model numbers, prices and stall locations. At the top was a DJI drone for the Italian tourist's 11-year-old son.
Next month, leaders of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) economies are expected to gather in Shenzhen for an annual summit. The theme of this year's summit is "Building an Asia-Pacific Community to Prosper Together," while China has identified openness, innovation and cooperation as the three priority areas for this year's APEC cooperation.
The city's Huaqiangbei, one of the world's largest wholesale markets for electronic products, offered a tangible window to see how these priorities translate into commercial reality.
Long known for bulk electronic components and low-cost gadgets, the bustling market's merchandise mix has shifted toward a growing range of smart consumer goods, a reflection of the city's push for digital innovation. This ability to roll out new items quickly grows out of its tightly integrated industrial cluster.
Spanning just 1.45 square kilometers, Huaqiangbei hosts 35 specialized markets and over 115,000 registered businesses, stocking more than a million kinds of parts and finished goods. Designers, suppliers, prototyping workshops and exporters operate in close proximity, creating an environment where new product ideas can move swiftly from concept to market.
"Foreign buyers used to come mainly for electronic accessories," said Meng Hangfang, co-founder of local supply-chain platform Zhipinku. "Now smart robots, wearable AI devices and small home appliances are popular. Many visitors come as soon as new items launch."
On the market floors, travelers from across the region test these new offerings. A Vietnamese visitor tried a sensor-controlled aircraft model, drawing onlookers to film. Nearby, a group of Vietnamese tourists picked up portable neck massagers. Nguyen Thi Hong Ngoc said the 150-yuan (about 22 U.S. dollars) massager outperformed pricier alternatives back home, and nearly everyone in her group bought one.
Figures from Huaqiangbei subdistrict authorities show that AI-related products accounted for 61 percent of electronic products in the area as of July, up from 41 percent in 2025.
Sales of AI products rose more than 55 percent year on year in the first seven months of 2026. Sales of AI glasses doubled, while those of drones and robots increased by 60 to 70 percent.
Choi Minjee, a journalist with the Republic of Korea (ROK)'s Kyunghyang Shinmun newspaper who previously covered the technology industry, said she was surprised by the low prices of AI-enabled accessories in Huaqiangbei.
"Such accessories are not yet widely available in the ROK, but they are ubiquitous in Shenzhen," she said. "You can directly feel the advantages brought by the city's complete and mature electronic information industrial chain."
Overseas customers favor smartwatches, headphones, game consoles, affordable phones and hair dryers, as well as foldable electric bikes and smart suitcases, said trader Xiao Wenlong. Some 70 percent to 80 percent of his orders are from abroad, mainly Europe, the United States, the Middle East and Southeast Asia.
"There used to be more large bulk buyers," Xiao said. "Now foreign visitors often combine family travel with shopping." He added that China's visa waiver and tax refund policies have made it easier for individual shoppers to cross borders, supporting broader open trade exchanges.
In the first half of 2026, Shenzhen's trade with other APEC members rose 33 percent year-on-year to 1.98 trillion yuan, nearly 70 percent of the city's total foreign trade.
Huaqiangbei sees roughly 750,000 visits daily, including more than 8,000 overseas business visitors, said local official Chen Jiongwen.
Janwick Hattingh, a Hong Kong-based South African, squeezed in a day trip. He bought a power bank, got his MacBook and daughter's watch repaired, and headed home by late afternoon.
"You can find everything," he said. "If you can't find it here, it doesn't exist." ■

articles.title: The Rutte way or the Carney method? Scaramucci says Europe’s Trump strategy is off the Mark
articles.body:
European leaders are using the wrong strategy to deal with U.S. President Donald Trump, according to Anthony Scaramucci, who briefly served as the White House’s communications director during Trump’s first term.
“You have to be firm with him. He doesn’t respect people that aren’t. I think you have got to wait him out,” Scaramucci told WELT AM SONNTAG, which, like POLITICO, is part of the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network.
Scaramucci described two ways of handling Trump: the Carney approach and the Rutte approach.
Advertisement
“There’s two models of behavior: one is [NATO Secretary-General] Mark Rutte and one is [Canadian Prime Minister] Mark Carney. I think Mark Carney is handling him better. The Canadian people are with him, even if it causes some level of economic hardship,” Scaramucci said.
“Rutte, on the other hand, is making a big mistake. Because when you equivocate or flatter him, when you act in the manner that Mark Rutte has acted, all you’re doing is losing his respect. You’re not gaining anything,” he added.
Rutte has often lauded the U.S. president: “I just like the man. I think what he is doing for NATO is great news,” the military alliance chief said in an interview with POLITICO this summer.
Europe has seemingly yielded to Trump’s wishes on numerous occasions. The EU-U.S. trade deal was criticized as playing in Washington’s favor, while European allies agreed to a 5% of GDP spending target by 2035 at last year’s NATO summit in The Hague, matching Trump’s headline demand.
Carney, by contrast, has been more unwilling to bow to Trump’s pressure. He walked away from U.S. trade talks, saying Ottawa could not accept the offer or the demands — and promised to match Washington’s new tariffs dollar for dollar.
In the interview, Scaramucci also lambasted members of Trump’s own Republican Party. “That is the other side of this story: the cowardice of the political servants that are supposed to check Donald Trump, the members of the Republican Senate caucus and the House caucus,” he said.
Advertisement
He added that lawmakers had failed to speak out against Trump’s decision to waive key provisions of the Russian sanctions law championed by the late South Carolina senator, Lindsey Graham.
“They’ve done nothing to speak out against that or to rebuke Trump, even though they could override him,” he said. “This is a case study in what you would call the strong arm tactics. People that believe in authoritarianism operate with levels of intimidation. That’s what Trump has done.”
The Axel Springer Global Reporters Network harnesses the resources of the company’s newsrooms to publish ambitious scoops, investigations, interviews, opinion pieces and analysis. It allows journalists — including those from POLITICO, The Telegraph, Business Insider, WELT, BILD, Onet and Fakt — to collaborate on major stories for an international audience of hundreds of millions across platforms: online, print, TV and audio.

articles.title: Cybersecurity Is Economic Security
articles.body:
Today, a locally owned coffee roaster in Colombia can reach customers in Germany and Japan, accepting payments in euros, yen, and pesos. Meanwhile, a daughter in Connecticut sends money to her parents in Morocco, and it arrives in their account in a matter of seconds. It’s easy to forget that these everyday moments, so central to our lives, were not possible until relatively recently.
Moments like these remind me of how our connected digital economy—and the technology that powers it—has opened more opportunity for more people in more places than ever before. It’s nothing short of revolutionary.
At the same time, this revolution created new risks. Connections that unlock growth can also create shared vulnerabilities that hackers, fraudsters, and scammers are quick to exploit. In 2024, cybercrime losses were equivalent to the third-largest economy in the world measured in GDP, behind only the U.S. and China. By 2029, its value is projected to reach $15.6 trillion.
Add to that the rapid evolution of AI models, and the stakes are rapidly being raised on both sides of the cybersecurity equation. While bad actors use AI to commit more convincing scams and scale attacks, defenders are putting AI to work to detect unusual activity faster, identify vulnerabilities, and prevent fraud before it happens.
Now, agentic commerce is beginning to drive a growing share of business transactions. That means cybersecurity requires further levels of verification to ensure agents are only acting as they are permissioned and empowered to do.
Our economy has long depended on cybersecurity. As technology evolves, protecting it requires a broader, shared commitment. Cybersecurity can no longer be treated as an issue only for the IT department. It is an economic priority for all of us, from government leaders to CEOs to individual citizens. We all have a role to play.
It starts by strengthening the systems that power the secure exchange of value, so they are resilient, intelligent, and inclusive for all. The need is especially acute for small businesses like the coffee roaster in Colombia.
Small businesses are the building blocks of economies worldwide, driving 70% of employment and accounting for half of global GDP. Yet, they are also often the least equipped and resourced to withstand a cyberattack. The damage from a cyberattack is rarely limited to just the targeted small business. The broader economy feels the impact too, including the employees, suppliers, customers, and communities that depend on them.
Recent Mastercard research found that only 37% of small business owners currently use cybersecurity tools, but 89% say they want to adopt more digital tools. The only question is whether our ability to protect small businesses and the broader online environment will stay ahead of evolving cyber threats. It’s our collective job to make sure it does.
No business or single organization can secure the digital economy alone. Banks, technology companies, platforms, governments, and industry groups each bring different strengths—from sharing intelligence and setting standards to building more secure products and helping businesses act early. Groups like the Alliance for Critical Infrastructure and the Cyber Readiness Institute maximize that cooperation and close gaps. Only by working together can we help protect the connections that small businesses run on.
Investing in cybersecurity for businesses and communities of all sizes isn’t altruism; it’s a potent business opportunity to drive economic growth. When strong protections are easier to access, more entrepreneurs can participate in the digital economy, sell across borders, and adopt new technologies with confidence. Strong cybersecurity becomes an economic advantage, attracting investment, supporting growth, and kicking off a virtuous cycle that further strengthens defenses. Everyone benefits.
We have to get this right. Underinvesting in cybersecurity, or restricting who benefits from those investments, is a recipe for stunting future economic growth and innovation. But when we lead with cybersecurity, we protect the trust that keeps the digital economy running. When we make it harder for bad actors to exploit vulnerabilities, we create the confidence people and businesses everywhere need to keep creating, connecting, and growing. That is a powerful return we all share.
Success on this issue should not be measured by how well the best-resourced institutions protect themselves, but by how effectively the ecosystem protects every participant. When strong protections reach businesses of every size, we strengthen trust, resilience, and growth for all.
The digital economy may have started as a revolution, but today it is the keystone of economies everywhere. It depends on technology being safe, reliable, easy to use, and above all, trusted. Cybersecurity is the key to unlocking our collective next chapter of digital growth.

articles.title: Qalamkari: The centuries-old art of printing stories on fabric in Isfahan
articles.body:
Qalamkari: The centuries-old art of printing stories on fabric in Isfahan
TEHRAN - In the historic Iranian city of Isfahan, where centuries of artistic ingenuity have shaped one of the country's richest cultural landscapes, an age-old craft continues to bring colour, patterns and stories to life on fabric. Known as Qalamkari, this traditional textile art combines hand-carved wooden stamps, carefully prepared dyes and intricate Persian designs to produce decorative fabrics that are both functional and artistic.
Rooted in Iran's long tradition of craftsmanship, Qalamkari became particularly prominent in Isfahan, especially during the Qajar era, when its printed textiles developed into some of the city's best-known artistic products. Beyond their decorative appeal, some of these fabrics served as visual narratives, portraying episodes from Persian epics, historical events and religious traditions.
Isfahan, nicknamed Nesf-e Jahan, meaning "Half the World", was the capital of Persia during the Safavid era and a major crossroads of international trade, diplomacy and artistic exchange. Under the Safavid monarch Shah Abbas I, the city experienced a remarkable cultural and architectural flourishing, helping establish its reputation as one of the most important centers of Persian art and craftsmanship. Today, it remains one of Iran's leading tourist destinations and a prominent hub of traditional handicrafts.
An art shaped by wood, color and fabric
Qalamkari, also known as Kalamkari in some transliterations, is a traditional method of decorating textiles through printing with hand-carved wooden blocks. Artisans use these stamps to transfer elaborate patterns onto fabric, often combining several colors and motifs to create richly detailed compositions.
The designs draw inspiration from a broad range of Iranian artistic traditions, including Persian carpets, architectural ornamentation and the elaborate tilework of historic mosques. Floral and botanical patterns, animals, arabesques, geometric arrangements, hunting scenes and Persian calligraphy are among the recurring motifs.
Flowers, cypress trees and other elements of nature feature prominently, often evoking the visual richness of traditional Persian gardens. The resulting compositions reflect a distinctive aesthetic in which symmetry, repetition and a harmonious combination of colors play central roles.
Cotton is among the most widely used materials for Qalamkari because of its ability to absorb dyes. Silk, canvas and fustian have also been used, depending on the intended purpose and desired finish.
The traditional production process requires considerable precision. First, an artisan prepares the design and selects the appropriate wooden stamps, each carved with a particular section of the intended pattern. The raised surfaces of the blocks are coated with dye and pressed onto the fabric to transfer the design.
Producing multicolored patterns requires several stamps, each corresponding to a different color or part of the composition. Their placement must be carefully coordinated so that the separate elements align correctly. Even a slight misalignment can disrupt the overall design.
The craft therefore involves much more than simply pressing a wooden block onto cloth. Knowledge of dyes, fabric preparation, pressure, spacing and the precise registration of patterns is essential. In some examples, hand painting is also combined with block printing to achieve more elaborate effects.
A craft with a long history
The precise origins of Qalamkari in Iran remain uncertain, and no definitive historical reference establishes when the craft first emerged. However, according to the renowned art historian Arthur Upham Pope, the art was already practiced in Iran during the Ghaznavid period.
It subsequently developed through different historical periods, reaching particular prominence under the Safavids. The reign of Shah Abbas I was especially significant for Isfahan's artistic and commercial development, as the city became an important center for the production and exchange of Persian handicrafts.
Although Qalamkari flourished under the Safavids, it was during the Qajar period that Isfahan's printed textiles became especially well known. Their popularity extended beyond decorative applications, with different fabrics serving as garments, tablecloths, curtains and large wall hangings.
Some pieces featured repeating floral and geometric patterns, while others incorporated elaborate figurative compositions. In the latter, the fabric became a surface for storytelling, bringing together characters, landscapes and historical or religious episodes.
When fabric became a storytelling medium
One particularly interesting aspect of Iranian Qalamkari is its ability to communicate narratives through images.
A number of historical examples preserved in international museum collections demonstrate that these textiles were not always intended merely as household decorations. Some depicted scenes from Persian heroic literature, while others illustrated religious beliefs and historical events.
The Weltmuseum Wien (Vienna's World Museum), for instance, houses several examples of Iranian printed and painted textiles attributed to Isfahan and dating from the 19th century.
One of them is a cotton wall hanging from the mid-19th century, during the Qajar period, measuring 176 centimeters in height and 116 centimeters in width. Originally part of the collection of Austria's Museum of Trade, the piece features a variety of traditional Iranian motifs, including scenes inspired by Persian epic stories, floral compositions, cypress trees emerging from vases and animal figures.
Another notable example, titled The Day of Judgment, is a late-19th-century cotton wall hanging attributed to Isfahan. Combining printing and hand painting, it depicts scenes associated with the Day of Resurrection from a Shiite religious perspective, including references to the Battle of Karbala and the fate of its martyrs and opponents.
The museum also preserves another late-Qajar textile, catalogued as a pictorial Qalamkari, which incorporates verses attributed to the Persian poet Omar Khayyam. Its message reflects on the passage of time and the importance of appreciating life's fleeting moments.
Together, these works illustrate the remarkable range of subjects that Iranian textile artisans could accommodate within a single piece of fabric. They also demonstrate how Qalamkari could preserve aspects of Persian literary, historical and religious culture through visual storytelling.
Challenges, decline and revival
Like many traditional Iranian crafts, Qalamkari experienced significant challenges as economic conditions and international markets changed.
During the 19th century, the arrival of cheaper and, in some cases, higher-quality textiles from Britain and Russia made competition increasingly difficult for Isfahan's producers. According to Encyclopaedia Iranica, the quality and price of locally produced Qalamkari fabrics were not always competitive with imported alternatives.
To maintain production, some manufacturers began importing unfinished white textiles and printing their designs in Iran before selling the finished products. Although this helped sustain the industry for a time, it could not fully address its underlying difficulties.
Keeping a living heritage alive
Today, Qalamkari continues to be produced in Isfahan, where generations of artisans have worked to preserve the techniques and knowledge associated with the craft.
Its products include tablecloths, curtains, decorative wall hangings and other household textiles. While traditional floral, geometric and figurative designs remain popular, contemporary producers have also adapted their products to changing tastes and practical uses.
In 2023, Isfahan's Qalamkari received international recognition from the World Crafts Council, reflecting the craft's cultural significance and the city's continuing contribution to traditional textile production.
Isfahan is widely regarded as one of the crown jewels of Iran's handicraft industry, with artisans working to safeguard skills passed down from one generation to the next. Qalamkari represents an important part of this heritage, bringing together textile production, wood carving, color-making and visual design in a single artistic tradition.
For visitors to Isfahan, discovering Qalamkari offers an opportunity to look beyond the city's celebrated mosques, palaces, bridges and historic squares and explore another dimension of its cultural identity.
AM

articles.title: Ukrainian experts launch security index to help Europe tackle rising drone threat
articles.body:
Ukrainian experts launch security index to help Europe tackle rising drone threat
Two expert organizations teamed up on Oct. 30 to unveil a new Drone Security Index (DSI), which will assess European countries' preparedness for drone attacks and inform them about measures they can take to improve their readiness.
The DSI, unveiled by New Age Defense, a European-Ukrainian defense tech alliance, and the Ukrainian think tank BRDO, "assesses national preparedness across four key areas: prevention, detection, response, and recovery," with each area given equal weighting.
Europe has been subjected to an increasing number of drone attacks, as Russia continues to probe for weaknesses in the continent's defense everywhere from Lithuania to Romania and Germany.
"From the beginning of 2022 to October 2026, 129 drone incidents have been recorded across 18 EU countries," says New Age Defense in a press release announcing the DSI.
Countries are then given a score out of 100, with scores above 87.5 considered high preparedness and scores below 50 considered totally unprepared.
"The index is not a rating or a competition between countries. It is a planning tool," said Taras Yemchura, the head of the Defense Policy Sector at BRDO.
Yemchura said that the index takes into account Ukraine's experience in repelling attacks, analyzing their consequences, and adapting countermeasures. It also incorporates NATO and EU frameworks on infrastructure resilience.
The two organizations will conduct pilot assessments in Germany and Poland in November. Germany was second only to Romania in the number of drone attacks experienced, says New Age Defense, with 23 confirmed attacks having taken place since 2022.
After this, the organizations hope to cover 16 other countries in 2027, including NATO Eastern Flank countries, Canada, and the U.K.
For Kateryna Mykhalko, head of New Age Defense, the index could also help bolster cooperation between Europe and Ukraine on drone warfare.
"The sooner Europe starts thinking in terms of modern warfare, the more productive our defense cooperation, the creation of joint ventures and arms exports will be," Mykhalko said.
"It is Ukraine, with its unique experience in the mass use of drones of various types in war, that can strengthen partners' readiness for new threats," she added.
The launch of the DSI comes the same day that European Commissioner Valdis Dombrovskis announced the opening of two drone technology hubs in Latvia and the Netherlands, and one day after the EU opened calls for funding for defense projects to support Ukraine.

articles.title: NATO top commander sees no delays in delivery of Patriot missiles to Ukraine
articles.body:
NATO top commander sees no delays in delivery of Patriot missiles to Ukraine
He made the statement to journalists while in the Latvian capital Riga on Friday, October 30, Ukrinform reports, citing Bloomberg.
“Everything has been delivered, in fact, we just had the delivery within the last week. I won’t go into the numbers or types of missiles, but deliveries have been ongoing,” Grynkewich said.
He added that “nothing that’s been put in the PURL package, that has been paid for by European allies, has been delayed.”
“Every single third-party transfer that has been requested of the U.S. government has been approved. We continue to work on the content for future PURL packages. We’re working this hard,” the NATO top commander said.
As reported by Ukrinform, President Volodymyr Zelensky recently said that Ukraine had been waiting for almost a month for U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth to sign off on the delivery of Patriot and NASAMS missiles.
